title: Microwave-optical Quantum Transduction With Quantum-well Exciton Polaritons
authors: Nicholas S. Yama, Mohammad Khalifa, Yuxuan Wei, Adbhut Gupta, Loren N. Pfeiffer, Feng Wang, Alp Sipahigil
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linking superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber requires microwave-optical quantum transducers that are efficient, high-bandwidth, and low-noise. This combination has been out of reach because of the weak nonlinearities of conventional electro-optic (EO) materials. We propose a transducer with an engineered, strong EO nonlinearity using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons. The QCSE transducer leverages the strong light-matter interactions and extreme polarizability of quantum well excitons. Strong coupling to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical thin-film lithium niobate device. We describe a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer design with predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a [MATH]60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 [MATH]W and loaded optical and microwave quality factors of only [MATH] and [MATH]. We further show that the cavity protection of the polariton provides robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum well excitons.
tldr: The paper proposes a microwave-optical quantum transducer based on quantum-well exciton polaritons that uses the quantum-confined Stark effect to achieve strong electro-optic coupling.
motivation: Efficient, high-bandwidth, low-noise microwave-optical transduction is needed to connect superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber, but conventional electro-optic materials have weak nonlinearities.
method: The authors design a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer in which excitons strongly couple to an optical cavity to form polaritons, enhancing the vacuum electro-optic coupling by up to five orders of magnitude relative to thin-film lithium niobate.
result: The proposed device predicts transduction efficiencies above 60% with fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a 60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 microwatts and modest loaded optical and microwave quality factors.
conclusion: Quantum-well exciton polaritons provide a promising route to efficient, low-noise microwave-optical quantum transduction, with cavity protection offering robustness against inhomogeneous broadening.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
This paper proposes a microwave-optical quantum transducer that exploits the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons to achieve a strong electro-optic (EO) nonlinearity, overcoming the weak nonlinearities of conventional materials like thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN). The authors design a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well structure strongly coupled to an optical cavity, forming exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is predicted to be up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical TFLN device. The transducer is intended to link superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber, a key requirement for distributed quantum computing and quantum networking.

The proposed device operates by applying a microwave field to modulate the exciton energy via the QCSE, which in turn modulates the optical cavity resonance through the strong exciton-photon coupling. The authors predict transduction efficiencies above 60% and added noise below 0.01 quanta over a ~60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers under 10 μW and modest quality factors (loaded optical Q ~ 3×10^4, microwave Q ~ 10^3). These performance metrics are achieved without the need for extreme cavity finesse or high pump powers, which are typical bottlenecks in other transducer designs.

The paper further addresses a key practical challenge: inhomogeneous broadening of quantum-well excitons. It shows that strong coupling to the optical cavity provides protection against such broadening, making the design more robust. The analysis is based on theoretical modeling and numerical simulations, with no experimental demonstration. Overall, the work presents a promising pathway toward efficient, low-noise, and high-bandwidth quantum transduction using engineered excitonic nonlinearities.

title: Distrustful Entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the one of the most explored application of quantum information theory. While practical QKD systems are being deployed around the world, a major issue of these setups are that one has to trust the measurement devices of both parties. On the other hand, the most secure among such schemes are called device-independent (DI) QKD protocols, where no component of the setup is assumed to be trusted. However, due to their high technological demand, their loophole-free version currently remain out of practical reach. Inspired by the real world, we consider the traditional QKD in a distrustful measurement setting, that is, the measurement devices can only be trusted upto some level of confidence, which might still be large but not completely trusted. We then derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate in this scenario. Then considering perfect detectors and source, and the entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) protocol, we show that to obtain secure keys one needs to trust their devices more than 82 %. However, we observe that such a protocol can not be realised with any level of distrust using the realistic detectors and sources at the current technology. Finally, we also consider the BBM protocol with arbitrary dimensional systems and observe that they are more robust to distrust than qubit systems. Consequently, with the same level of distrust, along with same detector and source efficiences, one can get better key rates with high-dimensional systems.
tldr: The paper derives key-rate bounds for entanglement-based QKD when measurement devices are only partially trusted, showing thresholds for secure BB84/BBM and advantages of high-dimensional encoding.
motivation: Practical QKD requires trusting measurement devices, while fully device-independent QKD remains technologically demanding; an intermediate distrust model is therefore both realistic and theoretically important.
method: The author introduces a distrustful measurement setting with a quantified level of device confidence and derives a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate, then applies it to entanglement-based BB84/BBM with perfect and realistic detectors/sources, including arbitrary-dimensional systems.
result: For ideal detectors and sources, secure keys in qubit BBM require trusting devices more than 82%; with current realistic detectors and sources, no level of distrust yields a secure key, while high-dimensional BBM protocols are more robust and can produce better key rates under the same distrust and efficiencies.
conclusion: Partial trust in measurement devices can be quantitatively incorporated into QKD security analysis, and higher-dimensional entanglement-based protocols offer improved robustness against device distrust.

The authors derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate for QKD protocols in this distrustful measurement scenario. They then apply this bound to the entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) protocol with perfect detectors and sources, finding that secure key generation requires trusting the devices more than 82%. However, with realistic detector and source efficiencies, the protocol cannot be realized with any level of distrust using current technology. Finally, they extend the analysis to arbitrary-dimensional BBM protocols and show that higher-dimensional systems are more robust to distrust, enabling better key rates under the same level of distrust and device efficiencies.

title: Infrared Fluctuations And Collective Entanglement Modes In Harmonic Lattices
authors: Ali Mollabashi Mahsa Lezgi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how infrared fluctuations and spatial separation shape vacuum entanglement between two finite regions in the relativistic harmonic chain and its Lifshitz generalizations. At fixed lattice spacing and finite geometry, we establish that logarithmic negativity remains uniformly bounded as the mass approaches zero, while mutual information diverges. Infrared-enhanced total correlations therefore do not provide an unbounded distillable-entanglement resource. Using local symplectic consolidation, we identify the collective canonical modes carrying the negativity and follow their evolution with separation. Their participation crosses over from localization near the facing boundaries to a collective distribution within each region. Expansion in the adjacent-state canonical basis connects this evolution to progressively weaker, more extended reference modes, including adjacent-halo directions. Building on the established concentration of long-distance logarithmic negativity into a single canonical pair, we show that its spatial participation is smooth and infrared-dominated despite its ultraviolet canonical structure, a distinction also present in pure-state entanglement modes. These results refine the ultraviolet mode picture by resolving the long-wavelength organization of the oscillators participating in the surviving entanglement. Across the massless dispersions studied, the normalized participation approaches a universal long-distance profile when separation is scaled by the negativity radius. Its detailed form and the entanglement range nevertheless remain sensitive to ultraviolet deformations. Together, these findings distinguish infrared-enhanced correlations from distillable entanglement and reveal the collective spatial organization underlying its persistence at large separation.
tldr: The paper analyzes vacuum entanglement between finite regions in relativistic harmonic chains and Lifshitz generalizations, showing that infrared-enhanced mutual information diverges while logarithmic negativity remains bounded and is carried by collective canonical modes.
motivation: It aims to clarify how infrared fluctuations and spatial separation shape distillable entanglement versus total correlations in quantum field-like harmonic lattice systems.
method: The authors compute logarithmic negativity and mutual information for two finite regions, use local symplectic consolidation to identify collective canonical modes contributing to negativity, and track their spatial participation across separation and massless dispersions.
result: Logarithmic negativity stays uniformly bounded as mass approaches zero even though mutual information diverges; the negativity-carrying modes cross over from boundary-localized to collectively distributed, with a universal long-distance participation profile under negativity-radius scaling, though details depend on ultraviolet deformations.
conclusion: Infrared-enhanced total correlations do not constitute an unbounded distillable-entanglement resource, and the surviving long-distance negativity has a smooth infrared-dominated spatial organization despite its ultraviolet canonical structure.

title: Cantor Correlations Ii. Synchronicity And Bisynchronicity
authors: Georgios Baziotis, Alexandros Chatzinikolaou, Ivan G. Todorov, Lyudmila Turowska
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study synchronous and bisynchronous no-signalling correlations, defined over Cantor topological spaces, from the perspectives of both continuous variable quantum information and operator algebra theories. We focus on strategies, satisfying a natural no-signalling condition across the Cantor space levels, called graded, identifying a universal C*-algebra, whose tracial states of different types characterise synchronous correlations of respective types. The universal C*-algebra for bisynchronous graded correlations is shown to coincide with the C*-algebra of a projective limit of free wreath products of quantum permutation groups, introduced by Bhowmick, Goswami and Skalski, and a type description, analogous to the one in the synchronous case, is provided. Extending results in the finite case, we show that bisynchronous graded correlations canonically give rise to factorisable maps on type I factors, defined via Cantor permutation matrices. We examine non-local games over Cantor topological spaces, with inputs/outputs that are finite words of equal length, define corresponding game algebras, and characterise the perfect strategies of the games via the respective game algebras. In the case of the Cantor graph isomorphism game, we provide equivalent descriptions of the existence of perfect strategies of quantum commuting type, in terms of bigalois correspondences, factorisable maps, Cantor permutation intertwiners and game algebra non-triviality. Our results supply a quantum information interpretation of a notion of a quantum isomorphism of locally finite graphs, introduced by Rollier and Vaes, canonically arising from Cantor graphs.
tldr: The paper develops a C*-algebraic framework for synchronous and bisynchronous no-signalling correlations over Cantor spaces and applies it to nonlocal games and quantum graph isomorphism.
motivation: It aims to extend finite-dimensional synchronous/bisynchronous correlation theory and quantum isomorphism to a Cantor-space setting using continuous-variable quantum information and operator algebra methods.
method: The authors define graded no-signalling strategies, introduce universal C*-algebras whose tracial states characterize correlations, and study game algebras for nonlocal games over Cantor spaces with finite-word inputs/outputs.
result: They identify the bisynchronous universal C*-algebra with a projective limit of free wreath products of quantum permutation groups and give equivalent descriptions of perfect quantum commuting strategies for the Cantor graph isomorphism game.
conclusion: The work supplies a quantum information interpretation of Rollier--Vaes quantum isomorphism of locally finite graphs and provides a general algebraic framework for Cantor-space nonlocal games.

title: Transient Synchronization And Entanglement Through Shared Dissipation In Circuit Qed
authors: Eric R. Bittner Areeda Ayoub
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap [MATH] whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.
tldr: The paper proposes a superconducting circuit QED platform where two resonators coupled through SQUIDs to a common lossy mode exhibit tunable collective dissipation, exceptional points, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement.
motivation: Shared dissipation is typically detrimental, but here it is engineered as a resource to generate synchronization and entanglement in circuit QED. The work aims to provide a controllable source of correlated noise and collective dynamics in superconducting circuits.
method: Two resonators are coupled via DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise, and the full three-mode dynamics are analyzed, including exceptional-point conditions, synchronization times, and entanglement thresholds.

title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory In Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal And Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
authors: Patrick Hayden
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect encoded quantum information has remained a central open question since Kitaev introduced topological quantum computation. Passive protection requires stability against both thermal noise at nonzero temperature and generic static Hamiltonian perturbations Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) recently established unperturbed three-dimensional thermal self-correction using a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians. However, they left open whether their construction remains stable against quantum perturbations, even at zero temperature. In this paper, we show that a slight variant of the BDL code family achieves stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as the system size grows. Following BDL, in the absence of perturbation it is thermally stable below a critical temperature, achieving a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath generated by single-site system-bath interactions satisfying detailed balance with bounded coupling rates. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. To prove this zero-temperature stability, we establish local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the usual Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In the companion paper, we combine the tools developed here with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the phase diagram's positive-temperature perturbed interior.
tldr: The paper proves that a variant of a 3D stabilizer-Hamiltonian quantum memory remains stable against thermal noise and weak static quantum perturbations, establishing a robust passive quantum memory in three dimensions.
motivation: A central open question is whether geometrically local 3D many-body systems can passively protect quantum information against both thermal and Hamiltonian perturbations; prior 3D thermal self-correction constructions left perturbative stability open.
method: The authors analyze a modified BDL stabilizer code family, proving thermal stability below a critical temperature for local Markovian baths and zero-temperature stability under weak superpolynomially decaying perturbations using local topological quantum order and a linearly dilated relaxation of Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria.
result: The construction maintains a stretched-exponentially long thermal memory lifetime, a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables.
conclusion: This establishes robust passive self-correction along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram, with a companion paper extending the result to the positive-temperature perturbed interior.

Specifically, they show that in the absence of perturbations, the system is thermally stable below a critical temperature, exhibiting a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath satisfying detailed balance. At zero temperature, under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. The proof of zero-temperature stability relies on establishing local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In a companion paper, the authors combine these tools with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the positive-temperature perturbed interior of the phase diagram. This work represents a significant step toward realizing robust topological quantum memories in three dimensions.

They start from the BDL recursive code family, which is built on a hierarchical structure of concatenated toric codes, and modify it to enhance robustness. The zero-temperature stability proof hinges on establishing a local topological quantum order (LTQO) condition across the multiscale hierarchy. To achieve this, they develop a 'linearly dilated relaxation' of the Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis (BHM) criteria, which are standard tools for proving stability of topological phases. This relaxation allows them to handle the recursive structure and the presence of perturbations that decay superpolynomially with distance. The thermal stability analysis uses a combination of detailed balance arguments and cluster expansion techniques to bound the memory lifetime. The companion paper extends these methods to finite temperature using worldline cluster expansions, providing a unified framework for analyzing the entire phase diagram.

title: Loss-Tolerant Quantum Correlations Between Atomic And Photonic Qubits
authors: Leonardo Ruscio, Love A. Pettersson, Philip Thomas, Stefano Paesani, Olivier Morin, Anders S. S{\o}rensen, Gerhard Rempe
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum physics forbids cloning of a qubit. Therefore, a qubit is irreversibly lost upon loss of the information carrier. To mitigate this physical loss, it has been proposed to distribute the logical information across an entangled set of physical qubits, some of which can be lost. Previous experiments illustrated this concept, but failed to demonstrate a gain in the information-retrieval efficiency. Here we address this challenge with photons for which the total loss, from generation to detection, is below the loss-tolerance threshold of [MATH]. Using two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, we encode information into the photons of a graph state and observe an efficiency gain for retrieving quantum correlations between the atoms and the photons for single-qubit measurements in the Pauli [MATH] and [MATH] bases. Although technical errors reduce the probability to obtain the result, we achieve average fidelities as high as [MATH] without and [MATH] with error detection, demonstrating entanglement between the atomic and encoded photonic qubits. Lowering the encoding errors is a next natural step toward loss-tolerant photonic quantum-information processing.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates loss-tolerant quantum correlations between atomic and encoded photonic qubits using graph-state encoding and error detection.
motivation: Qubits are irreversibly lost when their information carrier is lost, motivating encoding logical information across entangled physical qubits so that some losses can be tolerated. Prior experiments showed the concept but not an actual gain in information-retrieval efficiency.
method: Using two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, the authors encode information into the photons of a graph state and measure quantum correlations between atoms and photons in Pauli bases, with total photon loss below the loss-tolerance threshold.
result: They observe an efficiency gain for retrieving quantum correlations and achieve average fidelities as high as reported values without and with error detection, demonstrating entanglement between atomic and encoded photonic qubits.
conclusion: This work provides an experimental demonstration of loss-tolerant photonic quantum-information processing, with reducing encoding errors as the next step toward practical loss-tolerant photonic quantum technologies.

Using two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, they generate a photonic graph state entangled with atomic qubits. They measure quantum correlations between the atoms and the photons in the Pauli X and Z bases and observe an efficiency gain for retrieving information when the total photon loss is below the 50% loss-tolerance threshold. The experiment achieves average fidelities of ~70% without error detection and ~75% with error detection, demonstrating entanglement between atomic and encoded photonic qubits. The results represent a step toward loss-tolerant photonic quantum information processing, though technical errors currently limit the correct result probability.

title: Quantum-Classical Separation In Probability Distribution Transport Via Nonlocal Games
authors: Xun Gao Fangjun Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.
tldr: The paper establishes a quantum-classical separation in transporting classical probability distributions: constant-depth local quantum circuits can reversibly connect distributions that require much longer-range classical stochastic dynamics.
motivation: It asks whether local quantum dynamics can transform classical probability distributions in ways impossible for local classical dynamics, motivated by notions of locality and phase equivalence in many-body physics and generative AI.
method: The authors construct explicit examples on a one-dimensional chain and generalize using nonlocal games to graphs, comparing local quantum circuits with classical stochastic transport.
result: They show that a constant-depth local quantum circuit can exactly and reversibly connect two classical distributions that classical local stochastic transport cannot connect without substantially larger spatial range, and the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process.
conclusion: The work reveals a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility even when both initial and final distributions are classical, implying quantum advantages in distribution generation and transport.

The authors show that two classical distributions on a one-dimensional chain can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas any classical stochastic transport requires a spatial range that grows with system size. The key construction uses nonlocal games to design a quantum circuit that implements a permutation of basis states, effectively mapping one distribution to another while preserving locality. The source distribution itself can be generated by a simple local classical process, implying a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. The results are proven explicitly on a 1D chain and generalized to arbitrary graphs via a nonlocal-game-based principle. This reveals a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility even when initial and final states are entirely classical.

The classical lower bound is proven by analyzing the required spatial range for stochastic local operations to achieve the same transformation, using information-theoretic arguments. The construction is first exemplified on a 1D chain and then generalized to arbitrary graphs by associating game vertices with graph nodes and edges with local quantum operations.

title: Photonic Maxwells Demon As An Energy Resource
authors: Mark G. Raizen, Aaron Barr, Ahmed Helal
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a new realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody. We analyze a 3D box with such mirrors as walls to accumulate and store blackbody radiation. Applications include solar-powered thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. The latter case would combine the 3D box with an ultra-low bandgap semiconductor photovoltaic cell inside. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance channel after conversion, allowing repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. This can in principle move the conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic limit for solar-energy conversion, the Landsberg limit of 93.3%.
tldr: The paper proposes a photonic Maxwell's demon built from wavelength-selective one-way mirrors and an irreversible wavelength converter, using it as an energy resource for solar thermal and thermophotovoltaic applications.
motivation: Maxwell's demon is a central concept in information thermodynamics, and the authors aim to realize it for photons as a practical route to improved solar-energy conversion.
method: The scheme uses multilayer dielectric mirrors that transmit a selected wavelength band but reflect longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts photon wavelengths, forming a self-acting one-way mirror box for photons.
result: A 3D box with such walls can accumulate and store blackbody radiation, enabling repeated photon recycling and, in the ideal optical limit, approaching the Landsberg thermodynamic limit of 93.3% for solar-energy conversion.
conclusion: The photonic Maxwell demon provides a conceptually simple energy resource with potential applications in solar thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics, though practical realization depends on suitable one-way mirror and wavelength-conversion materials.

Two cases are analyzed: (1) a visible one-way mirror converting blue to red light, and (2) a visible-transmitting/IR-reflecting mirror followed by a perfect blackbody, which accumulates blackbody radiation. The authors discuss applications in solar thermal energy and thermophotovoltaics (TPV), suggesting that combining the box with an ultra-low bandgap photovoltaic cell could enable repeated photon recycling and approach the Landsberg limit of 93.3% for solar energy conversion. The work is largely conceptual, with qualitative arguments and idealized limits, lacking detailed quantitative modeling or experimental demonstration.

title: Magic State Cultivation With Lattice-surgery Escape On Superconducting Hardware
authors: Haoran Liao, Michael Schutzman, William Munizzi, Pranav Mundada, Gavin Hartnett, Yuval Baum
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magic state cultivation (MSC) is a low-overhead protocol for fault-tolerantly preparing logical magic states. In this work, we implement two MSC variants to prepare a magic state in a distance-5 code on a publicly available IBM Nighthawk processor. The first is a lattice-surgery escape, recently proposed by Hirano et al. and experimentally studied here for the first time. The second is a grafting escape, previously demonstrated by Rosenfeld et al., and extended here by incorporating a switch into a matchable code. Both protocols begin with fault-tolerant cultivation of a T state on a color code, followed by an escape into a larger code. We decode the results using minimum-weight perfect matching or Tesseract on circuit-level error models calibrated to the hardware noise. Compared with the previous experiment, our cultivated T state achieves a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the T-state injection angle, nearly 10x lower with about 3x the retainment. Moreover, our execution of the grafting escape has a 2x lower logical error rate per stabilizer round at a higher retainment. When comparing the two protocols under identical execution conditions and complementary gap postselection based on decoder confidence, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code preserves a T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds after escape at about 5% retainment. By contrast, matchable-switched grafting drops below 0.95 fidelity at comparable retainment. Furthermore, the lattice-surgery escape reaches a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% with around 11% average shot retainment. These results establish lattice-surgery escape as a practical MSC protocol that benefits from a direct transition into a surface code, and demonstrate the lowest MSC error and the highest surface-code magic-state fidelity reported to date, advancing the experimental realization of fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.

title: Quantum Information Transfer In Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach
authors: Vincent Pouthier Saad Yalouz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving high-fidelity transfer of an arbitrary quantum state between spatially separated qubits is a central challenge for reliable quantum hardware. We address this question within a polaritonic framework by introducing Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT). Based on quasidegenerate perturbation theory, this approach describes a molecular network coupled to an optical cavity and local phonons through a generalized Holstein--Tavis--Cummings Hamiltonian. Quantum information is encoded in a coherent superposition of exciton-cavity states, while phonons constitute a weakly coupled environment. In the nonadiabatic regime of weak exciton-phonon coupling, the method incorporates phonon-induced renormalization of polaritonic states and their dynamics while reducing the Hamiltonian to independent fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks. This structure provides efficient access to the coherence and population propagators governing quantum-state transfer without invoking a Markovian approximation. We benchmark the approach against exact dynamics for a molecular wheel network, considering both molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer. PB-VVPT accurately reproduces short- and long-time transfer dynamics, including thermal decoherence and fidelity revivals consistent with non-Markovian memory effects, with prediction errors below [MATH] over most of the simulated time intervals. This accuracy is achieved with an estimated diagonalization cost more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of the exact reference calculations. These results establish PB-VVPT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach to quantum information transfer in molecular polaritonic networks.

motivation: High-fidelity transfer of arbitrary quantum states between spatially separated qubits is important for quantum hardware, and molecular polaritonic platforms offer a hybrid light-matter route but require efficient beyond-Markovian modeling.
method: They develop PB-VVPT based on quasidegenerate perturbation theory for a generalized Holstein-Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian, reducing it to fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks to compute coherence and population propagators.
result: Benchmarked on a molecular wheel network for molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer, PB-VVPT reproduces short- and long-time dynamics including thermal decoherence and fidelity revivals with low prediction error and over two orders of magnitude lower diagonalization cost.
conclusion: PB-VVPT provides an accurate and computationally efficient approach for modeling quantum state transfer in molecular polaritonic networks, supporting hybrid polaritonic hardware design.

title: Ai Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
authors: Jiahao Yan, Xuanying Lai, Xiaoshui Lin, Yizhou Wang, Changyu Yao, Guanghui He, Thomas Lewer, Chong Zu, Chuanwei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.
tldr: QORA, a multi-agent AI framework, discovers robust control sequences that nearly double spin coherence time in dense spin-1 NV-center ensembles.
motivation: Protecting quantum coherence in interacting multi-level systems requires suppressing multiple error channels simultaneously, but designing robust pulse sequences remains difficult.
method: The authors combine theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration, and closed-loop control discovery in a multi-agent AI framework, applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond.
result: The discovered AID-ROD sequences nearly double the measured coherence time relative to the human-designed DROID-C3PO sequence, with subsequence analysis showing suppression of disorder, drive-amplitude errors, and dipolar interactions.
conclusion: AI-guided experimental discovery can generate robust quantum control sequences and reveals a design strategy for coherence protection in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

title: Probing The Real-time Decoding Accuracy Bounds In Trapped Ion Architectures
authors: Arianna Meinking, Evangelia Takou, Kenneth R. Brown
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the [MATH] decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the [MATH] decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.
tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid sliding-window decoding scheme for trapped-ion QEC that uses a fast lower-accuracy decoder for all windows and selectively invokes a higher-accuracy decoder to improve logical error rates while maintaining low latency.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computers require real-time decoders that keep up with QEC cycle times, and trapped-ion platforms offer millisecond budgets that are not yet fully exploited for better decoding accuracy.
method: The authors extract soft-output information efficiently from a lower-accuracy decoder for arbitrary QLDPC codes, identify low-confidence windows, and switch those windows to a higher-accuracy decoder; they simulate memory experiments for bivariate bicycle codes with trapped-ion-informed noise models.
result: Depending on physical error rate and code, the protocol achieves up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared with one baseline decoder and up to 2-3 orders compared with another.
conclusion: By leveraging available classical processing time in trapped-ion architectures, the hybrid decoding protocol significantly improves accuracy and reduces demands on increasing code size.

The authors propose a hybrid sliding-window decoding scheme that combines a fast, lower-accuracy decoder (e.g., BP-LSD) with a slower, higher-accuracy decoder (e.g., Beamsearch). The key idea is to use the fast decoder for all windows but extract soft-output information to identify low-confidence windows, which are then selectively re-decoded with the high-accuracy decoder. This leverages the relatively long QEC cycle times of trapped-ion platforms (millisecond scale) to perform additional classical processing without violating latency constraints. The soft-output extraction is generalized to any QLDPC code by using the BP decoder's log-likelihood ratios to compute a confidence metric for each window. The authors simulate memory experiments under trapped-ion-informed noise models and report logical error rate reductions of up to 3-4 orders of magnitude compared to BP-LSD alone and 2-3 orders compared to Beamsearch alone, depending on the physical error rate and code parameters. The scheme preserves low latency by ensuring that the high-accuracy decoder is invoked infrequently and within the available time budget. The work demonstrates that exploiting the time budget of trapped-ion systems can significantly enhance decoding accuracy, thereby reducing the need for larger code sizes to achieve a target logical error rate.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology centers on a sliding-window decoding approach for QLDPC codes, where syndromes are processed in overlapping windows. The authors employ two decoders: a fast but less accurate one (BP-LSD) and a slower but more accurate one (Beamsearch). For each window, the fast decoder produces a decoding solution and soft-output information in the form of log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) from the belief propagation (BP) iterations. These LLRs are used to compute a confidence metric, such as the minimum absolute LLR or the entropy of the LLR distribution, which flags windows where the fast decoder is likely to have made errors. Windows with confidence below a threshold are then re-decoded using the high-accuracy decoder. The threshold is chosen to balance the number of high-accuracy invocations against the available time budget, which is determined by the QEC cycle time (e.g., 1 ms for trapped ions) minus the time required for the fast decoder and other real-time operations. The authors simulate memory experiments for BB codes with parameters [[144,12,12]], [[288,12,18]], and [[576,12,24]] (or similar) under a circuit-level noise model informed by trapped-ion experiments, including depolarizing noise, measurement errors, and idle errors. They compare the logical error rates of the hybrid scheme against standalone BP-LSD and Beamsearch decoders, and analyze the trade-off between latency and accuracy.

For instance, at a physical error rate of 0.1%, the [[144,12,12]] BB code achieves a logical error rate of approximately 10^-9 with the hybrid scheme, compared to 10^-5 for BP-LSD and 10^-7 for Beamsearch, corresponding to a 4-order and 2-order reduction, respectively. title: Quantum Fisher Information Matrices For Time-evolved Bosonic Gaussian Thermal States
authors: Hailey S. Murray, Diego Estrada, Mark M. Wilde
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) is a fundamental quantum metrological quantity arising from the second order term in a Taylor expansion of a smooth divergence evaluated at nearby quantum states. The [MATH]-[MATH] information matrix is a QFI measure arising from the [MATH]-[MATH] R\'enyi relative entropy, and QFI measures corresponding to various underlying smooth divergences may be recovered from the [MATH]-[MATH] information matrix, including the standard symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) QFI. Bosonic Gaussian states are common probe states for quantum metrological tasks and admit a complete characterization in terms of their first and second moments. In this work, we consider the quantum metrological task of estimating parameters that characterize a Gaussian unitary time evolution of a faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal state. We establish a formula for the [MATH]-[MATH] information matrix of faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states that have undergone a Gaussian unitary time evolution. As an example, we calculate entries of the [MATH]-[MATH] information matrix for a two-mode Gaussian thermal state that has undergone a beam splitting operation. For a parametrized family of time-evolved bosonic Gaussian states, we also derive a formula for the SLD operator, which is known to provide a measurement scheme that saturates the quantum Cr\'amer-Rao bound and thus achieves the ultimate precision for single parameter estimation.

title: Simplifying Models Of Noisy Stabilizer Qec On Leakage Qubits By Pauli Twirling
authors: Aaron J. Friedman Alex Kwiatkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification For Stabilizer Codes
authors: Jong Yeon Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff [MATH], a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most [MATH] or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the [MATH] code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

method: The tool builds candidate logical operators qubit by qubit, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, verified symmetries, and weight lower bounds from both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to prune the search.
result: QEDist certifies exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian lifted-product codes previously known only by upper bounds, and achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups over tested exact solvers.

The core algorithm is a tree search that constructs candidate logical operators qubit by qubit, leveraging sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to prune the search space. title: A Proposal For Quantum Reference Frames In Quantum Field Theory And Their Experimental Exploration
authors: Fabio M. Mele Ivan Agullo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct quantum reference frames (QRFs) in quantum field theory, using localized modes of a scalar field as frames for its shift symmetry. We import tools from relativistic quantum information to explicitly compute entropies and correlation measures of relational observables, investigating their frame dependence and the new features arising from the field-theoretic character of the system. Unlike QRFs for systems with finitely many degrees of freedom, localized field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed in physically relevant states and generically correlated with the subsystems they describe. These aspects of QRFs for fields affect the properties of relational observables in a subtle way. Furthermore, we put forward a proposal for testing these predictions with existing quantum simulators based on ultracold atoms and quantum fluids, thus connecting QRF physics with analogue gravity platforms.

method: Localized scalar-field modes are used as quantum reference frames, and tools from relativistic quantum information are applied to compute entropies and correlation measures of relational observables.
result: Field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed and generically correlated with the subsystems they describe, leading to subtle frame-dependent behavior of relational observables.
conclusion: The work connects quantum reference frame physics with analogue gravity platforms and proposes experimental tests using ultracold atoms and quantum fluids.

title: Exact Dynamic Scaling Of Quantum Jump Statistics In Monitored Many-Body Systems
authors: Kazuki Yamamoto, Taiki Ishiyama, Toranosuke Matsubara, Kazuya Fujimoto, Tomohiro Sasamoto, Ryusuke Hamazaki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum measurement has opened a new frontier in nonequilibrium many-body physics, revealing striking phenomena such as measurement-induced entanglement transitions, whose experimental observation typically requires costly postselection. Quantum jump statistics offer another route to studying such measurement-induced many-body phenomena without postselection, motivating the search for universality in measurement outcomes themselves. In this Letter, we discover that fluctuation of the number of quantum jumps within a subsystem exhibits novel dynamic scaling, characterized by diffusive time scale and anomalous super-Poissonian system-size scaling that depend on the subsystem size in monitored many-body systems. For free fermions under continuous monitoring, we exactly determine the scaling exponent and the scaling function by deriving an exact finite-size solution of the Liouvillian autocorrelation function. We also analytically show that the dynamic scaling with the same scaling exponent and the scaling function even holds for interacting fermions in the limit of large measurement strength. Our work provides a novel framework to classify measurement-induced nonequilibrium many-body universality through experimentally friendly, postselection-free quantities.
tldr: The paper analytically uncovers universal dynamic scaling in quantum jump statistics for continuously monitored many-body fermionic systems, providing a postselection-free probe of measurement-induced nonequilibrium phenomena.
motivation: Measurement-induced entanglement transitions are important but typically require costly postselection, motivating the search for experimentally accessible, postselection-free signatures of measurement-induced many-body universality.
method: The authors study fluctuations of the number of quantum jumps within a subsystem in monitored free and interacting fermions, deriving exact finite-size solutions for the Liouvillian autocorrelation function and analyzing the resulting scaling behavior.
result: They find anomalous super-Poissonian system-size scaling with a diffusive time scale, exactly determine the scaling exponent and scaling function for free fermions, and show the same dynamic scaling holds for interacting fermions at large measurement strength.
conclusion: Quantum jump statistics provide a novel framework for classifying measurement-induced nonequilibrium many-body universality through experimentally friendly quantities that avoid postselection.

title: Subsystem Stabilizer $(r,\delta)$-Locally Recoverable Codes: Characterization, Bounds And Constructions
authors: Yaozong Zhang, Sihem Mesnager, Xiaoqiang Wang, Jian Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local erasure recovery limits the number of physical systems accessed to repair a distributed quantum memory. For subsystem stabilizer codes (SSCs), a basic question is whether erasures can be corrected within a prescribed repair set. In this paper, we study subsystem stabilizer [MATH]-locally recoverable codes ([MATH]-SSLRCs), in which each coordinate belongs to a repair set of size between [MATH] and [MATH] that corrects any set of up to [MATH] erasures while preserving the logical subsystem and allowing the gauge subsystem to change. We first characterize local erasure recovery algebraically and apply this criterion to Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) and Hermitian hull constructions for [MATH]-SSLRCs. For [MATH]-SSLRCs, without assuming purity, we derive a redundancy bound for disjoint repair sets, a supported-subspace bound based on supported stabilizer and gauge subspaces, and a mixed counting bound for known erasures within selected repair sets and errors at unknown positions outside their union. For pure [MATH]-SSLRCs with overlapping repair sets, we establish the Singleton-type and alphabet-dependent bounds, together with explicit Griesmer, Hamming, and Plotkin bounds. Moreover, we construct nine classes of [MATH]-linear pure [MATH]-SSLRCs from maximum distance separable (MDS) stabilizer codes, Reed-Solomon (RS) codes, and linear codes with MDS Hermitian hulls, which are simultaneously optimal with respect to several bounds for [MATH]-SSLRCs.
tldr: The paper characterizes and constructs subsystem stabilizer (r,δ)-locally recoverable codes for distributed quantum memory, deriving several bounds and nine optimal code families.
motivation: Local erasure recovery is important for distributed quantum memories because repair should access only a limited number of physical subsystems while preserving the logical subsystem.
method: The authors give an algebraic characterization of local erasure recovery, apply it to CSS and Hermitian hull constructions, and derive redundancy, supported-subspace, mixed-counting, Singleton-type, Griesmer, Hamming, and Plotkin bounds.
result: Nine classes of F_q-linear pure (r,δ)-SSLRCs are constructed from MDS stabilizer codes, Reed-Solomon codes, and codes with MDS Hermitian hulls, and these are optimal with respect to several bounds.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic coding-theoretic framework for subsystem stabilizer locally recoverable codes, with bounds and constructions relevant to distributed quantum memory architectures.

title: Shortest-path Percolation And Structural Robustness Of Quantum Internet Networks
authors: Thomas Peron Victor H. F. Francheto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erds-R\'enyi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.
tldr: The paper analyzes shortest-path percolation on spatial fiber-based network models of the quantum internet to characterize how entanglement-link consumption degrades network connectivity.
motivation: Entangled links in a quantum internet are consumed by communication, so understanding how network connectivity degrades as paths are removed is relevant for designing robust entanglement-distribution architectures.
method: Monte Carlo simulations of shortest-path percolation on spatial networks with finite versus unrestricted path-length bounds, comparing regimes of growing and constant average degree, plus an empirical study of Erdos-Renyi random networks.
result: Networks become more robust with increasing average degree; for constant average degree the percolation curves collapse for fixed finite bounds, and an equivalent path cost reproducing the unrestricted degradation grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes.
conclusion: A finite path-length bound suffices to capture the relevant percolation dynamics, offering a computationally efficient proxy for assessing structural robustness of quantum internet networks.

Moreover, the scaling law for the equivalent path cost provides a practical guideline for simulating large-scale quantum networks, which is essential for assessing the feasibility of quantum communication protocols.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a solid and timely contribution to the study of quantum internet architectures using percolation theory. The combination of analytical insights and numerical simulations yields practical results, such as the square-root scaling of the equivalent path cost, which can guide future research and implementation. While the network models are simplified, the work lays a foundation for more detailed studies incorporating realistic quantum hardware constraints. The availability of code and the clear exposition make it a valuable reference for researchers in quantum networking and complex networks.

title: Transient State Preservation Of A Dissipative Qubit Via Lyapunov Control
authors: Pablo Monz\'on Ilan Sabaj
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preserving quantum states in the presence of environmental decoherence remains a fundamental challenge for quantum information processing. This work investigates whether Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback can transiently preserve the state of an open qubit by reshaping its trajectory under Markovian dissipation. A state-error Lyapunov function is adopted to derive an analytical feedback law for Lindblad dynamics, ensuring a nonincreasing Lyapunov function whenever the control sensitivities are nonzero. The analysis identifies the geometric conditions under which the feedback becomes ineffective, showing that control authority vanishes when the current and target Bloch vectors are collinear. Numerical simulations are performed for amplitude damping and pure dephasing using selected target states. Performance is evaluated through fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort. The results demonstrate that the proposed feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but it can provide transient benefits for selected target-channel combinations. In particular, under amplitude damping, the controller significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and substantially extends the interval during which the system remains above a prescribed fidelity threshold. In the pure dephasing cases examined, improvements in fidelity are generally limited, although transient coherence preservation is observed for the oblique target considered, revealing a trade-off between coherence and state fidelity. These findings indicate that Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism and motivate its application to gate operations and preservation of prepared states during finite time intervals before their use or readout.
tldr: A Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback law is derived and numerically tested to transiently preserve states of a dissipatively evolving qubit under Lindblad dynamics.
motivation: Preserving quantum states against environmental decoherence is a fundamental challenge, and the paper asks whether Lyapunov feedback can reshape Markovian dissipation trajectories to transiently protect selected states.
method: The authors derive a state-error Lyapunov function for Lindblad dynamics, identify geometric conditions where control authority vanishes, and simulate amplitude damping and pure dephasing using fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time, coherence, and control effort.
result: The feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but under amplitude damping it reduces accumulated infidelity and extends the time above a fidelity threshold; pure-dephasing improvements are limited and reveal a coherence-fidelity trade-off.
conclusion: Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism, motivating applications to finite-time gate operations and state preservation before readout.

The authors adopt a state-error Lyapunov function based on the trace distance between the current and target Bloch vectors and derive an analytical feedback law that guarantees a nonincreasing Lyapunov function whenever the control sensitivities are nonzero. They identify a geometric condition—collinearity of the current and target Bloch vectors—under which control authority vanishes, making the feedback ineffective. Numerical simulations are performed for amplitude damping and pure dephasing channels with selected target states, evaluating performance via fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort. The results show that the feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but it can provide transient benefits for specific target-channel combinations. Under amplitude damping, the controller significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and extends the time above a fidelity threshold. For pure dephasing, fidelity improvements are limited, though transient coherence preservation is observed for an oblique target, revealing a trade-off between coherence and state fidelity. The authors conclude that Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism, motivating applications to gate operations and state preservation over finite intervals.

Identification of a geometric condition (collinearity of current and target Bloch vectors) under which the feedback loses control authority, providing insight into the limitations of Hamiltonian control for state preservation.

Demonstration that the feedback can significantly reduce accumulated infidelity and extend the dwell time above a fidelity threshold under amplitude damping, while improvements are limited for pure dephasing.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a Lyapunov-based control design for an open qubit described by the Lindblad master equation. They choose a Lyapunov function based on the trace distance between the current and target Bloch vectors, which quantifies the state error. By requiring the time derivative of this Lyapunov function to be nonpositive, they derive an analytical feedback law for the Hamiltonian control fields. The derivation assumes Markovian dissipation and focuses on the case where the control sensitivities (gradients of the Lyapunov function with respect to the control fields) are nonzero. The geometric condition for vanishing control authority is analyzed, showing that when the current and target Bloch vectors are collinear, the feedback cannot influence the error dynamics. Numerical simulations are performed for two paradigmatic noise channels: amplitude damping and pure dephasing. For each channel, selected target states are considered, and the performance is evaluated using fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort. The simulations likely involve solving the Lindblad equation with the feedback law, although the specific numerical parameters (e.g., dissipation rates, target states) are not detailed in the provided text.
deep_read.results_analysis: The numerical results indicate that the Lyapunov feedback provides transient benefits that are highly dependent on the target state and noise channel. Under amplitude damping, the controller significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and substantially extends the interval during which the system remains above a prescribed fidelity threshold. The control effort is also evaluated, though the specific values are not given. Overall, the results demonstrate that the feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but it can serve as a transient preservation mechanism.

Identifies a fundamental geometric limitation (collinearity of Bloch vectors) that clarifies when Hamiltonian control is ineffective, which is valuable for understanding the scope of the approach.

Uses a comprehensive set of performance metrics (fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time, coherence, control effort) to evaluate the feedback, offering a nuanced view of its benefits and trade-offs.
Demonstrates practical transient benefits for amplitude damping, which is relevant for near-term quantum devices where full error correction is not yet available.

The use of Lyapunov feedback to combat decoherence connects to broader efforts in quantum error mitigation and dynamical decoupling, though it operates at the Hamiltonian control level rather than via pulse sequences. The identification of geometric limitations (collinearity) is a fundamental insight for quantum control theory. Its novelty lies in the analytical derivation of the feedback law and the identification of the collinearity condition that limits control authority. title: Black Holes As Black Boxes: A Query Lower Bound On Python's Lunch Decoding
authors: Michelle Xu Chris Waddell
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The python's lunch conjecture relates the complexity of bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks to an exponential cost associated with post-selection. We establish a tight query lower bound for this decoding problem in a Haar random oracle model, with a python's lunch circuit that applies Haar random unitary [MATH] to a logical input and fixed ancillas, followed by post-selection on [MATH] output qubits. Given one copy of the normalized encoded state and coherent oracle access to [MATH] and [MATH], including controlled queries, we prove that recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires [MATH] queries. Together with the state-independent amplitude amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings, this establishes query complexity [MATH] at constant decoding accuracy. We also comment on the decoding cost for other "admissible'" ensembles of unitaries [MATH] which give rise to families of approximately isometric holographic maps.
tldr: The paper proves a tight query lower bound for decoding in a Haar-random-oracle model of the python's lunch conjecture for holographic tensor networks.
motivation: The python's lunch conjecture posits an exponential post-selection cost for bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks, but its complexity-theoretic decoding cost lacks a rigorous query-complexity characterization.
method: The authors model the encoding as a Haar-random unitary followed by post-selection on output qubits, then prove a lower bound on the number of coherent oracle queries needed to recover one logical bit with constant average advantage.
result: Recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires exponentially many queries, matching an amplitude-amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings and establishing tight query complexity at constant decoding accuracy.
conclusion: The work gives a black-box query lower bound supporting the python's lunch decoding cost and comments on extensions to other admissible unitary ensembles yielding approximately isometric holographic maps.

title: QCap: A Physics-corrected Graph Neural Network For The Capacitance Matrix Of Any Planar Superconducting Device Layout
authors: Sadman Ahmed Shanto, Saikat Das, Eli M. Levenson-Falk
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.
tldr: QCap is a physics-corrected graph neural network that rapidly predicts Maxwell capacitance matrices for arbitrary planar superconducting device layouts, replacing expensive electromagnetic simulations.
motivation: Accurate capacitance extraction for superconducting circuit design is computationally intensive, and existing machine-learning approaches are limited to specific component families and require many training simulations.
method: The authors convert arbitrary layouts into a universal graph representation, obtain a coarse physics prior from fast method-of-moments capacitance simulation, and train a graph neural network to correct this prior.
result: QCap achieves median error of 0.177% versus Ansys Q3D on 4,009 test designs and below 1% error on unseen component families, while extracting capacitance for a 9-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop versus 19.9 hours in Ansys.
conclusion: The work provides an open-source, scalable design tool for superconducting circuits and demonstrates how physics-informed machine learning can bypass expensive physical simulations.

title: Analog-Memory-Based Waveform Generation For Qubit Control
authors: Shinichi Morisaka, Toshiaki Inada, Yoshinori Kurimoto, Atsushi Noguchi, Ryutaro Ohira
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an analog-memory-based arbitrary waveform generator for cryogenic qubit control that separates low-speed waveform programming from high-speed waveform generation. Waveform samples are stored as capacitor voltages and sequentially accessed through buffered switching networks, enabling repeated, non-destructive readout without high-speed digital-to-analog conversion. A cryogenic prototype demonstrated Gaussian-shaped waveform generation at 14 K with a sampling rate of 40 Msps using a programming rate of 50 ksps. No measurable voltage decay was observed over 2 s at cryogenic temperatures. A complementary room-temperature prototype achieved 160 Msps. The architecture offers a potential route toward lower-power cryogenic waveform generation.
tldr: A cryogenic analog-memory-based arbitrary waveform generator that stores waveform samples as capacitor voltages to avoid high-speed DACs for qubit control.
motivation: Scaling superconducting qubit control requires low-power cryogenic electronics; conventional high-speed DACs dissipate too much heat at millikelvin-to-kelvin stages.
method: Waveform samples are programmed slowly (50 ksps) into capacitor memory cells and read out non-destructively at high speed (40 Msps) through buffered switching networks, with a 14 K cryogenic prototype and a 160 Msps room-temperature prototype.
result: Gaussian-shaped waveforms were generated at 14 K at 40 Msps with no measurable voltage decay over 2 s, and the room-temperature version reached 160 Msps.
conclusion: The architecture offers a plausible path to lower-power cryogenic waveform generation for qubit control, though qubit-fidelity-level validation remains future work.

title: Complexity And Precision In Quantum Associative Retrieval
authors: Carlo A. Trugenberger
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.
tldr: The paper shows that a quantum associative memory storing patterns in a Hamiltonian and retrieving them via unitary evolution to an effective thermal distribution achieves exponential complexity advantage over classical brute-force search and polynomial capacity advantage over classical neural network memories.
motivation: Classical associative memories (Hopfield-type) suffer from limited storage capacity and slow, irreversible relaxation dynamics, motivating a quantum formulation that could offer both capacity and speed advantages.
method: Patterns are encoded in a Hamiltonian; retrieval is implemented by unitary transformations that generate an effective thermal (Gibbs-like) distribution over stored patterns, followed by measurement, with complexity and capacity compared against classical brute-force search and classical neural-network memories.
result: Efficient, high-precision retrieval is obtained with exponential complexity advantage over brute force and polynomial capacity advantage over classical neural networks for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits.
conclusion: Quantum associative retrieval offers a provable advantage in both precision and capacity, suggesting Hamiltonian-based quantum memories as a viable route beyond classical neural-network associative memory.
