title: Parametric And Universal Thouless Invariants In Matrix Product States
authors: Leonardo Goller, Amartya H. Singh, Daniel D. Spiegel, Marco Venuti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the classification of continuous families of translation-invariant injective matrix product states on an infinite chain, parametrized by a paracompact Hausdorff space [MATH] and subject to a compact Hausdorff symmetry [MATH]. We construct an invariant for phases of such families, valued in [MATH], that generalizes the known [MATH] phase invariant for [MATH]-symmetric Thouless pumps. The phase invariant is constructed as the pullback to [MATH] of a single universal ech cohomology class on a classifying space of [MATH]-symmetric translation-invariant injective matrix product states. Several examples are given over various parameter spaces where this invariant is nontrivial.
tldr: The paper constructs a universal Cech cohomology invariant that classifies continuous families of translation-invariant injective matrix product states with a compact symmetry, generalizing Thouless-pump invariants.
motivation: It aims to classify topological phases of parametrized matrix product states and extend the known integer-valued Thouless-pump invariant to families over general parameter spaces.
method: The invariant is defined as the pullback of a universal cohomology class on a classifying space for symmetric translation-invariant injective matrix product states, with several worked examples.
result: The construction yields a cohomology-valued phase invariant and identifies parameter spaces where the invariant is nontrivial.
conclusion: The work provides a general mathematical framework for parametric and universal Thouless invariants in matrix product states, though it is primarily a tensor-network/topological-phase classification result.

title: Masq: Measurement-Adaptive Sampling For Near-Clifford Quantum Error Correction Circuits
authors: Chaebin Jung, Sangmin Jeon, Kyeongwon Lee, Sechan Park, Woojoo Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical sampling of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits supports fault-tolerant protocol evaluation, but estimating rare logical failures requires many independent shots. Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. At each measurement boundary, MASQ materializes only rotations in a measurement-relevant closure capturing direct and indirect non-commuting dependencies, deferring the rest to limit active-state expansion. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. A circuit-dependent schedule is computed once and shared across shots, while adaptive caching of conditional Born probabilities and batched execution reduce repeated sampling work while preserving the measurement-record distribution. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098-fold CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits.
tldr: MASQ is an exact classical sampler for near-Clifford quantum error correction circuits that selectively materializes only measurement-relevant non-Clifford rotations, dramatically speeding up logical failure sampling.
motivation: Evaluating fault-tolerant QEC protocols requires estimating rare logical error events, which demands many circuit samples; dense frame-active-state simulators scale exponentially with active width, making large-scale sampling impractical.
method: At each measurement boundary the sampler computes a measurement-relevant closure of non-commuting non-Clifford rotations, materializes only those, eliminates rotations certified invisible to future measurements via stabilizer arguments, and reuses a circuit-dependent schedule with cached conditional Born probabilities and batched execution.
result: Across 19 QEC benchmarks MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098x CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits while preserving the measurement-record distribution exactly.
conclusion: Selective, measurement-adaptive materialization makes near-Clifford QEC sampling substantially more tractable, enabling faster fault-tolerance protocol evaluation at scale.

title: Commutator-guided Repair And Classical-accessibility Boundaries For Shallow Quantum Circuits
authors: Yifeng Peng, Sunpreet Singh Arora, Harshal Shah, Srinivasan Raghuraman, Kim Wagner, Bin Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trainability does not guarantee low-energy arrival: a shallow quantum circuit can be optimizable yet fail, under fixed depth and evaluation budgets, to reach Hamiltonian-selected states. We introduce a commutator-guided repair for this operational failure mode. Low-order host--Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations, from which a compact completion layer is selected before full reoptimization. Across 189 paired six-qubit trials, unrepaired circuits achieve 0/189 strict successes, a non-deployable per-trial control envelope achieves 109/189, and two predeclared selectors achieve 133/189 and 127/189. The repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS. Under fixed-depth geometric locality, repaired losses and gradients are classically computable, while corresponding ground-state targets admit low-bond-dimension tensor-network approximations through the tested sizes. The method reveals a trainability--arrival--classical-accessibility tradeoff rather than quantum advantage.
tldr: The paper introduces a commutator-guided repair protocol that fixes shallow variational circuits which are trainable but fail to reach Hamiltonian ground states, and shows that under fixed-depth geometric locality the resulting losses become classically computable, exposing a trainability–arrival–classical-accessibility tradeoff.
motivation: Trainability (absence of barren plateaus) is often treated as sufficient for variational quantum algorithms, but a shallow ansatz can be optimizable yet still fail to reach the target Hamiltonian-selected states within a fixed depth and evaluation budget.
method: Low-order host–Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations from which a compact completion layer is selected prior to full reoptimization; the approach is benchmarked in 189 paired six-qubit trials against unrepaired circuits and predeclared selectors, with tensor-network approximations used to probe classical accessibility.
result: Unrepaired circuits achieve 0/189 strict successes, a non-deployable control envelope achieves 109/189, and the two predeclared selectors achieve 133/189 and 127/189; the repair underperforms matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and is size-limited for weighted MIS.
conclusion: Rather than demonstrating quantum advantage, the method reveals a fundamental tradeoff between trainability, target arrival, and classical accessibility of shallow circuits, suggesting the regime studied is classically simulable.

title: Restoring Quantum Neural Network Trainability Through Reusable Calibration
authors: Ruizhe Shen, Xianquan Yan, Kenji Kawaguchi, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) rely on measured quantum observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise can suppress the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning. Here, we develop a structure-preserving error-mitigation framework that improves QNN trainability through reusable calibration of the quantum circuit's effective noise response. By calibrating a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, we construct regularized estimators of local quantum features that remain fixed throughout training. We quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect the recovery of both observables and their derivatives. Numerical simulations demonstrate enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification performance, and an IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under hardware noise. We further demonstrate calibration reuse in a modular QNN comprising 25 independent four-qubit channels, corresponding to 100 qubits in aggregate. Our results establish reusable feature calibration as a practical approach to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated calibration at every training step.
tldr: The paper proposes reusable calibration-based error mitigation to improve trainability and optimization of quantum neural networks under hardware noise.
motivation: Quantum neural networks suffer from hardware noise that suppresses parameter-dependent signals needed for training, motivating practical error-mitigation methods that avoid costly recalibration at every optimization step.
method: The authors calibrate a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit and use it to construct fixed regularized estimators of local quantum features, analyzing calibration-error and response-mismatch effects.
result: Numerical simulations show enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and better classification, while an IBM Quantum experiment and a modular 100-qubit aggregate demonstration confirm improved closed-loop variational optimization and calibration reuse.
conclusion: Reusable feature calibration is presented as a practical route to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated per-step calibration.

title: An Alternate Proof Of The Qma Lower Bound For Set-size Estimation
authors: Chinmay Nirkhe
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the set-size estimation query task, a query algorithm decides whether an [MATH]-bit input has Hamming weight [MATH] or [MATH] (with [MATH] as the yes instances and [MATH] as the no instances). When [MATH], this is sometimes called approximate counting. The query complexity for this problem with a quantum witness (i.e., [MATH] query bounds) was resolved by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler (CCC 2020) and proved using Laurent polynomials. Here we give a morally similar but distinct proof of the lower bound using the polynomial method.
tldr: The paper gives an alternative polynomial-method proof of the QMA lower bound for the set-size estimation query problem.
motivation: Set-size estimation with a quantum witness captures the power of QMA in query complexity, and the known lower bound was previously proved using Laurent polynomials.
method: The author reproves the lower bound using the polynomial method, providing a morally similar but distinct argument to the original Laurent-polynomial proof.
result: The paper establishes the same QMA query lower bound for distinguishing low- and high-Hamming-weight inputs, including the approximate-counting regime.
conclusion: This is a technically focused quantum complexity-theory result that does not directly address the researcher's prioritized topics in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Inapproximability Of L1->l2 Subspace Distortion
authors: Vijay Bhattiprolu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show, assuming NP is not contained in randomized quasipolynomial time, almost polynomial factor inapproximability for maximizing the [MATH] ratio over a real subspace -- a problem also known as subspace distortion. This is a central problem in compressed sensing but also has connections to many areas such as real error correcting codes, dictionary learning, hypercontractive operator norms, small-set expansion, quantum information and random matrix theory. Distortion seems to be at the heart of building inapproximability theory for continuous optimization. Extending our results to the case of [MATH] for all [MATH] would lead to a near characterization of the convex sets over which one can efficiently and approximately maximize an arbitrary quadratic form. A recurring obstruction appears in hardness considerations of distortion -- how does one use a sparsity measure to test proximity to an exponential sized discrete set over the reals? This issue also appears in a host of other problems that involve measures of sparsity, shortness, density or expansion. We believe hardness of distortion is an intermediate step to understanding the complexity of small-set expansion and quantum separability, both of which are important directions of research. The main insight in our hardness reduction is the construction of a randomized affine linear map [MATH] such that the distortion of [MATH] measures proximity to the hypercube [MATH]. Crucial to our construction is subsampling [MATH] at *all* dyadic sample sizes, which gives an inverse polylogarithmic gap. This is a highly non-local tester, and thus departs from the local testing paradigm in PCP theory. Our reduction is also quite succinct, and so it suggests a rather simple distribution of subspaces for which approximately finding a planted sparse vector is intractable.
tldr: The paper proves near-polynomial-factor inapproximability for maximizing the L1-to-L2 ratio over a real subspace (subspace distortion), assuming NP is not in randomized quasipolynomial time.
motivation: Subspace distortion is central to compressed sensing and connects to error-correcting codes, small-set expansion, and quantum separability, but its hardness of approximation was poorly understood; the authors aim to build an inapproximability theory for continuous optimization.
method: A hardness reduction is constructed via a randomized affine linear map whose distortion measures proximity to the hypercube, using subsampling at all dyadic sample sizes to obtain an inverse polylogarithmic gap through a highly non-local tester departing from the local-testing PCP paradigm.
result: Almost polynomial factor inapproximability is established for the L1->L2 subspace distortion problem under the stated complexity assumption, implying a simple distribution of subspaces for which finding a planted sparse vector is intractable.
conclusion: The work positions hardness of distortion as an intermediate step toward understanding the complexity of small-set expansion and quantum separability, with extensions to Lp distortion left as an open direction toward characterizing convex sets with efficiently approximable quadratic form maximization.

title: An Upper Bound On Non-overlapping Codes
authors: Simon R. Blackburn
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-overlapping codes (also known as bifix-free codes or strong comma-free codes) have now been studied for over 60 years as part of information theory, with regular new applications appearing and much recent interest. Let [MATH] be a binary non-overlapping code of length [MATH]. The paper contains a self-contained proof that \[ |X|\leq \left({6e} +O(n^{-1})\right){n} \] as [MATH]. This improves, by a factor of [MATH], the best previously known bound due to Levenshtein (1970). The paper builds on work by Fimmel, Michel, Pirot, Sereni and Str\"ungmann (2019), and by Stanovnik, Mo\v skon and Mraz (2024).
tldr: The paper proves an improved upper bound on the size of binary non-overlapping codes.
motivation: Non-overlapping codes are a classical coding-theoretic object with a long history and recent applications, and the best known upper bound had not been improved for decades.
method: The author gives a self-contained combinatorial proof building on prior work by Fimmel et al. and Stanovnik et al.
result: For a binary non-overlapping code X of length n, the paper establishes |X| <= (6e + O(1/n))^n, improving Levenshtein's 1970 bound by a constant factor.
conclusion: The work sharpens a classical information-theoretic bound but has no direct quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, or hybrid-systems component.

title: Constructions Of Reversible Linear And Dna Codes Through $T_{D,g}^n-$set And $(n_1,c_1|n_2,c_2)-$right Polycyclic Codes
authors: Satyadeep Pandey Avanish Kumar Chaturvedi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we give a construction technique of [MATH]set for reversible linear codes and reversible DNA codes with their code parameters. This technique yields many reversible MDS codes which significantly improves the [MATH]set construction by Oztas et.al. in terms of obtained code parameters. Concatenation-based constructions are presented for reversible linear codes satisfying self-duality and linear complementary dual (LCD) conditions, giving necessary and sufficient condition for desired dual properties. We introduce a new notion of [MATH] right polycyclic codes. Also, a new construction technique is developed to obtain reversible linear [MATH] right polycyclic codes with good parameters (MDS codes) over any finite commutative rings.
tldr: The paper constructs reversible linear codes and reversible DNA codes using T_{D,g}^n-sets and introduces (n1,c1|n2,c2)-right polycyclic codes over finite commutative rings.
motivation: Reversible codes and DNA codes are useful in storage and computing contexts where reversibility and self-dual/LCD properties matter, and the authors aim to improve existing parameter constructions.
method: The authors develop set-based constructions for reversible linear codes and DNA codes, present concatenation-based constructions for self-dual and LCD reversible codes, and define right polycyclic codes over finite commutative rings.
result: The constructions yield reversible MDS codes with improved parameters compared with prior T-set constructions and provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the desired dual properties.
conclusion: The work extends algebraic coding constructions for reversible and DNA codes, but it is a classical coding-theory contribution without a direct quantum information, thermodynamics, network, or hybrid-systems component.

title: A Polynomial-time Decoding Algorithm Up To Half The Square-root Bound For Quadratic Residue And Generalized Quadratic Residue Codes
authors: Philippe Lebacque Phlippe Gaborit
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binary quadratic residue (QR) codes, introduced by Prange in 1958, are cyclic codes of prime length [MATH] and dimension [MATH] whose minimum distance satisfies the square-root bound [MATH]. They include the Hamming code [MATH] and the Golay code [MATH], and were generalized by van Lint and MacWilliams to generalized quadratic residue (GQR) codes of prime-power length [MATH], for which the bound [MATH] still holds and is attained when [MATH] is a square. In coding theory, one usually first finds a lower bound on the minimum distance of a family of codes, and then a polynomial-time algorithm decoding up to half of this bound, as for BCH, Reed--Muller or Gabidulin codes. Until now, GQR codes had resisted this approach: no such algorithm was known, apart from individual short lengths. We give a deterministic algorithm which, for every odd prime power [MATH], corrects every error pattern of weight at most [MATH] in the binary GQR code of length [MATH], in [MATH] operations in [MATH]. We start from a description of QR codes due to Helleseth, which we extend to GQR codes, and in which the syndrome gives the values of the quadratic character of the error-locator polynomial. We then recover this polynomial by adapting to GQR codes the tools that Kopparty developed for recovering polynomials from noisy character values, with the decoding of dual BCH codes as an application. Since the square-root bound is attained when [MATH] is a square, this radius is the largest that can be guaranteed uniformly on the class of GQR codes.
tldr: The paper presents a deterministic polynomial-time decoding algorithm for binary generalized quadratic residue codes up to half the square-root bound.
motivation: Quadratic residue and generalized quadratic residue codes satisfy a square-root minimum-distance bound, but no polynomial-time algorithm was known to decode up to half that bound for general prime-power lengths.
method: The authors extend Helleseth's description of QR codes to GQR codes, use the syndrome to obtain quadratic character values of the error-locator polynomial, and adapt Kopparty's polynomial-recovery techniques for noisy character values.
result: For every odd prime power length, the algorithm corrects all error patterns of weight at most half the square-root bound in polynomial time, which is optimal uniformly over the class of GQR codes.
conclusion: This resolves a long-standing decoding problem in classical coding theory, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Microscopic Revision Of The Rate Equations Of A Heavily Erbium-doped Fiber Laser
authors: Iaroslav L. Pozdniak, Ivan V. Vovchenko, Evgeny S. Andrianov, Alexander V. Dorofeenko
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers can exhibit self-pulsing induced by interacting ion pairs, which was found in numerous experiments and supported by modeling. However, conventional rate-equation models rely on phenomenological parameters with an unclear microscopic origin. We derive a rate-equation model using a Lindblad master equation describing isolated erbium ions and interacting ion pairs coupled to a single cavity mode, with cooperative upconversion represented by an effective dissipative process. In the strong-dephasing limit, adiabatic elimination of coherences and ensemble averaging yield a closed system of equations for the cavity photon number, isolated-ion inversion, and pair populations. We show that in the same limit the pair-cavity coupling constant reduces to that of two independent ions, without superradiant or subradiant contributions. The resulting equations retain spontaneous emission, which provides a photon-number floor between pulses and substantially affects the laser pulsing dynamics. Numerical analysis reveals self-pulsing within finite pump-rate intervals and identifies the region of self-pulsing as a function of the upconversion rate and pair fraction. The model thus establishes a microscopic basis for analyzing self-pulsing in heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers.
tldr: The paper derives a microscopic rate-equation model for heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers using a Lindblad master equation and analyzes self-pulsing induced by interacting ion pairs.
motivation: Conventional rate-equation models for heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers rely on phenomenological parameters with unclear microscopic origins, motivating a more fundamental derivation.
method: The authors model isolated erbium ions and interacting ion pairs coupled to a single cavity mode via a Lindblad master equation, treating cooperative upconversion as an effective dissipative process and performing adiabatic elimination in the strong-dephasing limit.
result: They obtain a closed set of equations for cavity photon number, isolated-ion inversion, and pair populations, showing that pair-cavity coupling reduces to that of two independent ions without superradiant or subradiant contributions; numerical analysis identifies self-pulsing regions.
conclusion: The model provides a microscopic basis for analyzing self-pulsing in heavily erbium-doped fiber lasers and highlights the role of spontaneous emission in pulse dynamics.

title: Generalized Schrieffer-Wolff Transformation
authors: Tie-Cheng Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Schrieffer-Wolff transformation (SWT) is a cornerstone of effective-Hamiltonian theory. However, the SWT is predominantly used for weak-coupling problems, while a systematic counterpart for strongly coupled regimes remains largely unexplored. A general closed-form SWT generator and a clear physical principle for gauge fixing remain elusive, obscuring the transformation's underlying structure. We introduce the dual SWT to deal with the strong-coupling problems. The generalized SWT (gSWT) is formulated for any Hermitian operator and block partition. We establish the geodesic principle for its canonical gauge. Furthermore, we derive an exact closed-form solution of the gSWT generator at every order as a finite nested-commutator sum whose only input is the active gap set. Both the geometric and algebraic aspects of the SWT physics are revealed. The gSWT framework is illustrated in two quantum many-body models, the collective spin model and the transverse-field Ising model.
tldr: The paper introduces a generalized Schrieffer-Wolff transformation (gSWT) for strong-coupling effective-Hamiltonian problems, with a closed-form generator and a geodesic gauge-fixing principle.
motivation: The standard Schrieffer-Wolff transformation is mainly limited to weak coupling, and a systematic strong-coupling counterpart with a clear gauge-fixing principle has been missing.
method: The authors formulate a dual/generalized SWT for arbitrary Hermitian operators and block partitions, establish a geodesic principle for canonical gauge fixing, and derive an exact closed-form nested-commutator expression for the generator at every order.
result: The framework provides both geometric and algebraic structure for the SWT and is illustrated on a collective spin model and the transverse-field Ising model.
conclusion: The gSWT extends effective-Hamiltonian theory to strong-coupling regimes and clarifies the transformation's underlying structure, though it is primarily a quantum many-body method rather than a quantum information or thermodynamics result.

title: Countering Anion Inhibition Of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics On A Superconducting Quantum Processor, And Its Limits
authors: Lucia Malickova
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.
tldr: The paper models laccase anion inhibition using GFN2-xTB cluster models and runs charge-transfer dynamics on an 8-qubit superconducting quantum processor.
motivation: Hydroxide and halide inhibition limit fungal laccases in wastewater treatment, motivating electrostatic design to reduce anion penalties at the trinuclear copper cluster.
method: A four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction is derived from GFN2-xTB models and simulated with Trotterized circuits and Pauli twirling on the Euro-Q-Exa IQM processor, alongside probe and conformer screens.
result: Hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy by 92.0 ± 2.2 meV in the crystal-geometry model and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 ± 1.8 meV; Y116E reduces the hydroxide penalty by 74 ± 7 meV in the probe model, while realistic Glu116 effects are 10–30 meV.
conclusion: The hardware is effectively single-particle on this benchmark and does not resolve electron correlation, requiring contrast loss below 0.13% per CZ gate rather than the measured 0.34–0.54%.

title: Perturbative Recovery Of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations For Quantum Computational Chemistry
authors: Qianjun Yao, Jie Liu, He Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.
tldr: The paper introduces Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover correlation energy missed by stabilizer-based subspace projections in quantum computational chemistry.
motivation: Stabilizer-subspace methods such as CS-VQE reduce qubit requirements for electronic structure calculations, but projecting onto a stabilizer subspace neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace, causing energy errors.
method: SSPT treats Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state, evaluating corrections via Epstein-Nesbet second-order or resolvent-based formulations using Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register.
result: Molecular benchmarks show substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, with chemical precision achieved using fewer contextual qubits in several cases.
conclusion: Stabilizer-guided perturbation theory is proposed as a promising strategy for improving accuracy in resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

title: Quantum Reference Frames, Locality, And Microcausality In Quantum Field Theory
authors: Leon Loveridge Christopher J. Fewster
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a consequence of the relativistic spectrum condition, quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space are never described by projection-valued measures, and in many cases fail a weaker spacetime localisation property known as the norm-[MATH] condition. This has several implications for the local and observable structure of quantum field theories described relative to even the best available frame: for a large class of frame states, strict locality is replaced by almost locality, and microcausality by commutators that decay rapidly with increasing separation, corresponding to an effective smearing of the light cone by the localisation density of the frame state. Operations built from finitely many almost local Kraus operators, for example nonselective measurements of relativised local observables, satisfy an approximate no-signalling bound, with a residue attributable to the localisation uncertainty of the frame. Whether causality in its strongest operational form -- non-disturbance under all physically realisable operations -- survives relativisation is left open. An upshot of our finding is that quantum field theories formulated relative to a quantum reference frame cannot rest on the traditional axioms, and some general relational axiomatisation must replace at least some of them by taking into account physically realistic properties of the frame.
tldr: The paper analyzes how quantum reference frames for spacetime translations in quantum field theory weaken strict locality and microcausality, replacing them with approximate locality and rapidly decaying commutators.
motivation: Quantum reference frames challenge traditional formulations of quantum field theory because relativistic spectrum conditions prevent ideal projection-valued localisation of the frame. The authors ask how observable and causal structure changes when QFT is described relative to such frames.
method: The authors study quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space, using the norm-[MATH] localisation condition and Kraus operators for relativised local observables to derive approximate no-signalling bounds.
result: For a large class of frame states, strict locality becomes almost locality and microcausality is replaced by commutators that decay rapidly with separation, effectively smearing the light cone by the frame localisation density.
conclusion: QFTs formulated relative to quantum reference frames cannot rely on traditional axioms; a relational axiomatisation incorporating realistic frame properties is needed, and operational causality under all physically realisable operations remains open.

title: Charge Self-consistent Dft+qdmft Framework With A Krylov-based Quantum Impurity Solver
authors: M. Karabin, T. Sohail, E. A. Coello P\'erez, S. Ghosh, M. Sajjan, H. Terletska, M. Eisenbach
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We integrate a quantum impurity solver into a charge self-consistent density functional theory (DFT) plus quantum dynamical mean-field theory framework. The solver optimizes adaptive circuits to approximate the ground state of the impurity model and its particle and hole excitations, and reconstructs the impurity Green's function from their Hamiltonian moments. Higher-order moments are predicted from low-order ones using a machine-learning model, while regularized optimization mitigates violations of causality in the resulting self-energy. The latter is used to update the charge density until self-consistency is achieved. We demonstrate the framework through body-centered cubic lithium calculations and compare the results with a reference one using a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo solver. These calculations converge with root-mean-square charge-density residuals below [MATH] and yield a nearly vanishing impurity self-energy, consistent with the noninteracting limit used for weakly correlated lithium.
tldr: The authors embed a variational quantum-circuit impurity solver, accelerated by Krylov-moment reconstruction and machine-learned higher moments, into a charge self-consistent DFT+DMFT workflow and benchmark it on bulk lithium.
motivation: Quantum impurity solvers are the computational bottleneck of DFT+DMFT for strongly correlated materials, and near-term quantum processors may offer a route to treating the impurity model more efficiently than continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo.
method: Adaptive circuits are optimized to approximate the impurity ground state and its particle/hole excitations; the impurity Green's function is reconstructed from Hamiltonian moments, with higher moments predicted from lower ones by a machine-learning model and regularized optimization used to suppress causality violations in the self-energy, which then updates the charge density to self-consistency.
result: For body-centered cubic lithium the scheme converges to root-mean-square charge-density residuals below the stated threshold and yields a nearly vanishing impurity self-energy, reproducing the weakly correlated, essentially noninteracting limit obtained with a reference CT-QMC solver.
conclusion: The work establishes a proof-of-concept for quantum-solver-in-the-loop DFT+DMFT, though validation is limited to a weakly correlated system where quantum advantage is not demonstrated.

title: A Geometric Framework For Local-to-Global Symmetry: Global Constraints On Local Dynamics
authors: Roel Tempelaar Connor Terry Weatherly
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aggregate molecular systems are routinely understood by decomposing them into local structural units, such as monomers in J/H-aggregates, chemical moieties, motifs, and functional groups. Implicit in such decompositions is the assumption that these local structures remain meaningful within the aggregate. Here, we ask how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry, and how this relation determines the constraints that global symmetry imposes on transitions between local symmetry sectors. We construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and show that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. By identifying which global symmetry sectors overlap each local symmetry sector, we resolve symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Through Frobenius reciprocity, these exclusions can be determined from standard character tables of the local and global symmetry groups, with the character values in the inner product paired according to the relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate. Although motivated by molecular aggregates, the construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.
tldr: The authors build a covariant local-to-global representation framework that connects the symmetries of constituent molecular units to aggregate symmetry and derives site-resolved selection rules for transitions between local symmetry sectors.
motivation: Aggregate molecular systems are usually described by decomposing them into local structural units, but it is rarely justified that these local structures remain meaningful inside the aggregate; the paper asks how local and global symmetries relate and what constraints global symmetry places on local dynamics.
method: A covariant local-to-global representation is constructed from framed local symmetry data, and its reconstruction map is shown to intertwine with a global quantum representation; Frobenius reciprocity and standard character tables of local and global groups are used to compute which global sectors overlap each local sector, with character values paired according to relative positions and orientations.
result: Symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions are resolved into site-resolved pathways, and these exclusions can be read off from character tables rather than computed by brute force; the construction is stated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.
conclusion: The framework gives a general group-theoretic way to translate global symmetry constraints into local, site-resolved transition rules in molecular aggregates, with potential extension to any system described by a homogeneous-space geometry.

title: Bandwidth-tunable Thermal Emitter Via Dynamic Resonator Coupling And Loss
authors: Jin-Woo Cho, Tanuj Kumar, Joseph A. Andrade, Shenwei Yin, Samir Rosas, Filiz Yesilk\"oy, Dung T. Quach, Albert G. Wright, Colin M. Hessel, David Woolf, Mikhail A. Kats
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a dynamically tunable omnidirectional thermal emitter that can be switched from a narrowband emission state to a broadband state. The structure is a metal-backed multilayer with subwavelength thickness across the mid-infrared, which forms an angle-insensitive (up to 60{\deg}) optical cavity with one input port. We used an ultrathin VO2 layer to dynamically switch the coupling and loss coefficients of this optical cavity, resulting in narrowband emission from the vibrational mode of a polar dielectric layer that is part of the multilayer stack when the VO2 is in its insulating phase, and broadband emission from a nearly impedance-matched cavity when the VO2 is switched to its lossy metallic phase. We fabricated the structure around a free-standing silicon membrane and integrated it onto a printed circuit board (PCB), which enabled electrical switching of the emitter at the ten-to-hundred millisecond scale, and can be used for free-space identification, tagging, or communication.
tldr: The authors demonstrate a metal-backed multilayer mid-infrared thermal emitter whose emission bandwidth can be electrically switched between narrowband and broadband by driving an ultrathin VO2 layer through its insulator-to-metal transition.
motivation: Tunable thermal emitters are desirable for free-space identification, tagging, and infrared communication, but most designs are passive or require slow, bulky reconfiguration; a fast, electrically switchable, angle-insensitive emitter would enable practical device-level applications.
method: A subwavelength multilayer forming a single-port optical cavity with a polar-dielectric vibrational mode and an ultrathin VO2 layer is fabricated on a free-standing silicon membrane and integrated on a PCB; switching VO2 between insulating and metallic phases tunes cavity coupling and loss coefficients.
result: The device emits narrowband radiation from the polar dielectric vibrational mode in the insulating phase and broadband, near-impedance-matched emission in the metallic phase, with angular insensitivity up to 60 degrees and electrical switching on ten-to-hundred millisecond timescales.
conclusion: Dynamic control of cavity coupling and loss via phase-change materials provides a versatile route to reconfigurable thermal emitters for identification, tagging, and communication applications.

title: Fundamental Physics With Quantum Sensors In Space
authors: Jason Arakawa, Daniel J. Blumenthal, Oliver Buchmueller, Dmitry Budker, Luigi Cacciapuoti, Emily D. Caldwell, Andrei Derevianko, Benjamin P. Dix-Matthews, Michael A. Fedderke, Naceur Gaaloul, Susan Gardner, Jonah Glick, Paul Hamilton, Elena Jordan, Hidetoshi Katori, Peter Kurczynski, David R. Leibrandt, Anna L. Marchant, Indra Periwal, Igor Pikovski, Marianna S. Safronova, Christian Sanner, Sascha W. Schediwy, Volodymyr Takhistov, Yu-Cheng Tien, Yu-Dai Tsai, Jason R. Williams
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.
tldr: These workshop proceedings review how space-based quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can probe fundamental physics beyond the Standard Model.
motivation: Space provides microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, and varying gravitational potentials that may enable sensitive tests of dark matter, general relativity, and gravitational waves.
method: The paper summarizes the scientific case, current quantum-sensor capabilities, and proposed space mission concepts discussed at the Aspen Center for Physics workshop.
result: It identifies opportunities for quantum sensors to search for dark matter, test general relativity, and detect gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from ground-based observatories.
conclusion: Quantum sensors in space offer a promising pathway for fundamental physics discovery, but the work is a community review rather than a technical advance in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum Born Geometries From Modular Quantization
authors: Roberto Conti Paolo Bertozzini
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A structural link between quantization and "thermal-doubled" non-commutative Born geometry (with its split-quaternionic structure) is uncovered via Tomita-Takesaki first-quantized modular theory for complexified and polarized ortho-symplectic spaces. Implications for the modular algebraic quantum gravity program (arXiv:1007.4094) hint at further deep modifications of the notions of space and geometry (thermal quantum space-time hypothesis) waiting to be further explored. Speculative suggestions in the direction of A.Sakharov and L.Boyle-K.Finn-N.Turok CPT-mirror cosmologies will be mentioned, among several others. The present work is based on the manuscript "Modular Quantization and Non-commutative Space-time" (now on alphaXiv) that has been shared, with a selected number of researchers, since end of April 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a structural link between quantization and thermal-doubled noncommutative Born geometry using Tomita-Takesaki modular theory, with speculative implications for modular algebraic quantum gravity and thermal quantum spacetime.
motivation: The authors aim to connect modular operator theory for complexified polarized ortho-symplectic spaces with noncommutative Born geometries and explore possible consequences for quantum gravity and cosmology.
method: The analysis employs Tomita-Takesaki first-quantized modular theory and algebraic structures such as split-quaternionic Born geometry to construct a formal bridge between quantization and thermal-doubled noncommutative spaces.
result: The work uncovers a structural correspondence between modular quantization and noncommutative Born geometry, and suggests speculative links to modular algebraic quantum gravity, Sakharov-style induced gravity, and CPT-mirror cosmologies.
conclusion: The paper is exploratory and highly speculative, proposing a mathematical framework for thermal quantum spacetime rather than delivering concrete quantum-information or thermodynamic results.

title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification Of Term Measurements For Variational Quantum Algorithms
authors: Yifeng Peng, Bin Yan, Harshal Shah, Srinivasan Raghuraman, Kim Wagner, Sunpreet Singh Arora
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.
tldr: The paper proposes a learned controller to sparsify qubit-wise commuting measurement groups in variational quantum algorithms, reducing gradient-measurement shots for molecular VQE.
motivation: Repeated measurements are a bottleneck in VQAs, and the authors identify parameter-specific sparsity in QWC group contributions to parameter-shift gradients, motivating selective measurement.
method: They train a controller on Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features to predict measurement-group relevance and select groups via a coverage threshold, using exact contributions only for offline supervision.
result: Across 15 molecular VQE settings, the method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC; LLMs show promise but are less consistent without physical guidance.
conclusion: The work supports AI-assisted measurement optimization for VQAs and suggests combining general-purpose models with explicit physical representations and domain-grounded validation.

title: Boundedness Of A Schur Multiplier On The Schatten P-class, $1 < P \neq 2 < \infty$, Does Not Imply Complete Boundedness
authors: Jinghao Huang, Anna Tomskova, Fedor Sukochev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the existence of a bounded Schur multiplier on the Schatten class [MATH] which is not completely bounded when [MATH], which confirms Pisier's conjecture (1998).
tldr: The paper proves the existence of a bounded Schur multiplier on the Schatten p-class that is not completely bounded for 1 < p ≠ 2 < ∞, confirming Pisier's 1998 conjecture.
motivation: The work addresses a long-standing problem in operator theory about whether boundedness of Schur multipliers on Schatten classes implies complete boundedness outside the Hilbert-space case.
method: The authors construct a counterexample using techniques from functional analysis and operator space theory to establish the conjecture.
result: They show that for every p in (1, ∞) except p = 2, there exists a bounded Schur multiplier on the Schatten p-class that fails to be completely bounded.
conclusion: This resolves Pisier's conjecture and clarifies the distinction between bounded and completely bounded Schur multipliers on non-Hilbertian Schatten classes.

title: Bourin's Crossed-Heinz Inequality In The Frobenius Norm
authors: Jinli Xu Yulong Tian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For positive semidefinite matrices [MATH] and [MATH], we establish the sharp quantitative Frobenius-norm inequality [MATH] for every dimension [MATH]. In particular, Bourin's crossed-Heinz inequality [MATH] holds with equality if and only if [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves a sharp quantitative Frobenius-norm version of Bourin's crossed-Heinz inequality for positive semidefinite matrices.
motivation: Bourin's crossed-Heinz inequality is a known matrix inequality, and the authors aim to sharpen it quantitatively in the Frobenius norm with equality conditions.
method: The authors establish a dimension-independent sharp inequality for positive semidefinite matrices in the Frobenius norm and characterize the equality case.
result: They obtain a sharp Frobenius-norm inequality for all dimensions, showing that the crossed-Heinz inequality holds with equality under a specific condition.
conclusion: The work is a pure matrix-analysis contribution with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: On The Kissing Number Of Craig's Lattice And Spherical List Decoding
authors: L\'eo Ducas, Julian Nowakowski, Ailsa Robertson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Craig's lattices [MATH] are a family of lattices with large kissing numbers, i.e., relative to their dimension [MATH], they contain a large number of shortest nonzero vectors. Specifically, for small [MATH], a lower bound of Bacher (2015) shows that [MATH] has a super-polynomial kissing number of [MATH]. Craig's lattices are therefore attractive candidates for the construction of spherical codes. In this work, we introduce a polynomial-time list decoder for spherical codes obtained from Craig's lattices for angular distance below [MATH]. Our second main result shows that Bacher's lower bound is asymptotically tight for [MATH]. Finally, we introduce an efficient algorithm for computing the kissing number of [MATH]. Using this algorithm, we compute their kissing number in dimensions up to 521. Based on this data, we pose the open question whether the kissing number of [MATH] with [MATH] grows like [MATH] in dimension [MATH]. Concurrent work by Laarhoven and Kominers as well as Bennett, Hhan, Li and Stephens-Davidowitz proves such a bound for very closely related lattices.
tldr: The paper constructs a polynomial-time list decoder for spherical codes derived from Craig's lattices and computes their kissing numbers up to dimension 521.
motivation: Craig's lattices have super-polynomial kissing numbers and are thus attractive candidates for spherical codes, but their decoding properties and the tightness of Bacher's lower bound were not understood.
method: The authors design a polynomial-time list decoder for angular distance below a certain threshold, prove asymptotic tightness of Bacher's lower bound for a range of parameters, and introduce an efficient algorithm to compute kissing numbers.
result: They compute kissing numbers of Craig's lattices up to dimension 521 and conjecture that the kissing number grows like a specific function of dimension, a bound later proven for closely related lattices in concurrent work.
conclusion: The work advances the classical theory of lattices and spherical codes, with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Refined Upper Bound On The Critical Temperature For Dilute Bose Gases
authors: Phan Th\`anh Nam, Toan T. Nguyen, Izabella Stuhl, Yuri Suhov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an upper bound on the critical temperature shift of three-dimensional Bose gases with general nonnegative finite-range interactions. In the dilute regime [MATH], we prove [MATH], where \[ C_{\rm H}=\sqrt\pi}{3\zeta(3/2)^{2/3}} =3.523992\ldots \] is the coefficient predicted by Huang in 1999. This improves the earlier rigorous upper bound of Seiringer and Ueltschi in 2009. More precisely, we prove the exponential decay of the correlations above the stated temperature through the Feynman--Kac representation, for both integrable and hard-core interactions.
tldr: This paper proves an improved rigorous upper bound on the critical temperature shift of dilute three-dimensional Bose gases with general nonnegative finite-range interactions.
motivation: The critical temperature of interacting Bose gases deviates from the ideal Bose gas prediction, and Huang predicted a coefficient for the leading dilute-limit shift; earlier rigorous upper bounds were weaker than Huang's prediction.
method: The authors use the Feynman--Kac representation and prove exponential decay of correlations above the stated temperature for both integrable and hard-core interactions.
result: They establish the upper bound for the critical temperature shift in the dilute regime with coefficient matching Huang's predicted value C_H = 3.523992..., improving the 2009 Seiringer--Ueltschi bound.
conclusion: The work provides a sharper rigorous justification for Huang's predicted critical-temperature shift in dilute Bose gases, but it is a mathematical statistical mechanics result rather than a quantum information or information thermodynamics contribution.

title: iBraid Group Symmetries Of Iquantum Groups Via Star Product
authors: Xujie Zhou Ming Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish ibraid group symmetries on universal iquantum groups of symmetrizable Kac-Moody type, proving a conjecture of Wang and Zhang. Building on the star product realization of quantum symmetric pairs [MATH], we relate these symmetries to Lusztig's braid group symmetries, extending the compatibility previously obtained via iHopf algebras in the quasi-split setting. Via the Letzter map [MATH] from the iquantum group [MATH] to the horospherical algebra [MATH], we show that the ibraid group symmetry [MATH] of [MATH] transported to [MATH] coincides with Lusztig's braid group symmetry [MATH] on the subalgebra [MATH]. Finally, a mixed product formula, together with a parabolic decomposition, yields an explicit formula for the transported action on the entire horospherical algebra [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves braid group symmetries for universal iquantum groups of symmetrizable Kac-Moody type using star product realizations and relates them to Lusztig's braid group actions via the Letzter map.
motivation: It aims to establish a conjectured symmetry structure for iquantum groups and extend compatibility results from the quasi-split setting to more general symmetrizable Kac-Moody type.
method: The authors use the star product realization of quantum symmetric pairs, the Letzter map from the iquantum group to the horospherical algebra, and a mixed product formula with parabolic decomposition.
result: They show that the transported ibraid group symmetry on the horospherical algebra coincides with Lusztig's braid group symmetry on a subalgebra and obtain an explicit formula for the action on the entire horospherical algebra.
conclusion: The work proves Wang and Zhang's conjecture and clarifies the relationship between ibraid group symmetries and Lusztig's braid group symmetries in this algebraic setting.

title: Renormalization-Group Foundation Of Critical Modes In Correlation Matrices
authors: Yanhua Zhang, Mingmei Xu, Jinghua Fu, Yuanfang Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Based on the relevant scaling operators of renormalization-group theory, we establish a theoretical framework for constructing complete families of critical-sensitive fluctuation observables and their connected correlation matrices. The corresponding eigenstates of the correlation matrices reveal a hierarchy of multiscale critical correlation patterns and the leading normalized eigenvalues and their ratios show the finite-size scaling behavior. Applying this framework to the two-dimensional Ising model, the correlation matrices associated with both spin and energy operators are constructed. The resulting energy-sector eigenstate patterns, together with the scaling behavior of the leading eigenvalues, provide further support for the proposed framework. Finally, we discuss its potential extension to systems with unknown Hamiltonians.
tldr: The paper develops a renormalization-group framework for constructing critical-sensitive correlation matrices and analyzes their eigenstate hierarchy and finite-size scaling in the 2D Ising model.
motivation: The authors aim to identify complete families of fluctuation observables that are sensitive to critical phenomena and to characterize multiscale critical correlations through correlation-matrix eigenstates.
method: Using relevant scaling operators from renormalization-group theory, they construct connected correlation matrices for spin and energy operators and study the eigenstates and leading normalized eigenvalues in the two-dimensional Ising model.
result: The correlation-matrix eigenstates reveal a hierarchy of multiscale critical correlation patterns, and the leading eigenvalues and their ratios exhibit finite-size scaling behavior consistent with the proposed framework.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to extract critical modes from correlation matrices and may be extendable to systems with unknown Hamiltonians.

title: Simultaneous Analysis Of Approximate Leave-one-out Cross-validation And Mean-field Inference Ii: General Convex Penalties
authors: Pierre C Bellec
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For smooth penalties and group Lasso, analyzed approximate leave-one-out (ALO) cross-validation by comparing its weights with the trace correction used in mean-field inference. For a [MATH] penalty [MATH], the matrix entering these corrections is [MATH], where [MATH] is the full-data estimator and [MATH] is the diagonal matrix of fitted loss curvatures; for group Lasso, the penalty and loss curvatures are first restricted to the active support before taking the pseudoinverse. The obstacle to extending this argument to general convex penalties was the lack of an explicit formula for the matrix [MATH] entering these corrections. For every finite-valued strongly convex penalty, we construct such a matrix from ordinary derivatives of the penalty response at the observed subgradient. Its projection--pseudoinverse formula separates the response space and penalty curvature, fixed by conditioning, from the explicit design dependence. This supplies the missing ingredient to extend the probabilistic argument of Part~I. The construction recovers the inverse Hessian for smooth penalties and the active-group inverse for group Lasso, including inactive boundary groups. In the proportional regime, for Gaussian designs with general positive-definite covariance and covariance-scaled strong convexity, we obtain unconditional bounds comparing both ALO and mean-field predictions with exact leave-one-out predictions in regression and single-index models. The expected average squared prediction error is [MATH], and the expected absolute criterion error is [MATH], under bounded, 1-Lipschitz loss scores and suitable test functions. The matrix and ALO weights use only observed data; the mean-field correction additionally uses the design covariance. The construction, recovery identities and statistical guarantees are formalized in Lean~4.
tldr: The paper constructs an explicit projection–pseudoinverse matrix for general strongly convex penalties, enabling a probabilistic comparison of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation with mean-field inference corrections in high-dimensional regression and single-index models.
motivation: Extending the ALO/mean-field comparison of Part I beyond smooth penalties and group Lasso required an explicit formula for the curvature-correction matrix entering both ALO weights and mean-field trace corrections, which was missing for general convex penalties.
method: For any finite-valued strongly convex penalty, a matrix is built from ordinary derivatives of the penalty response at the observed subgradient, with a projection–pseudoinverse formula separating response space from design dependence; the resulting ALO weights and mean-field corrections are then bounded against exact leave-one-out predictions for Gaussian designs in the proportional regime, with all results formalized in Lean 4.
result: The construction recovers the inverse Hessian for smooth penalties and the active-group inverse for group Lasso (including inactive boundary groups), and yields unconditional O(n^{-1}) bounds on expected average squared prediction error and expected absolute criterion error under bounded, 1-Lipschitz loss scores.
conclusion: The missing ingredient for extending the Part I argument to general convex penalties is supplied, giving non-asymptotic guarantees for ALO and mean-field approximations and a formally verified treatment of the underlying linear algebra.

title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization From Two Multiplications And A 64-Byte Table
authors: Muhammed Fatih Bal{\i}n
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.
tldr: CPTC is a low-bit tensor quantization format that uses a tiny 64-byte table indexed by two multiply-and-add operations to approach the information-theoretic rate-distortion limit for LLM weight quantization.
motivation: Per-value rounding formats such as INT4 and FP4 waste bits relative to the information-theoretic ideal, while existing trellis-code decoders either require huge lookup tables or are restricted by hash-based decoding.
method: A trellis decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients, sums the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table, and exploits the non-uniform distribution of that sum so that table extremes cover tail values; one decoder supports 1-6 bit widths.
result: CPTC comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits, matches a random-permutation trellis code with a table thousands of times larger, and achieves the lowest KL divergence versus unquantized Llama 3.1 8B/70B among tested codebooks, with a decoder built into AWS Trainium 4 at native FP4/FP8 throughput.
conclusion: The work delivers a compact, hardware-efficient joint quantization scheme for static tensor storage, but it is a classical source-coding and accelerator-engineering contribution with no quantum information, thermodynamic, network, or hybrid-platform content.

title: Causal Input--Output Modeling With Prior Information
authors: Daran Xu Amirhossein Taghvaei
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of inferring a causal input--output model from unpaired marginal observations and a given prior coupling. We formulate this problem using entropic causal optimal transport, which seeks a coupling that preserves the observed marginals, satisfies a one--sided causality constraint, and remains close to the prior. For Gaussian marginals and general quadratic costs, we prove that the optimal coupling is Gaussian and reduce the problem to a finite--dimensional optimization over covariance matrices. Using a Cholesky transformation to simplify the causality constraint, we derive a Lagrangian dual formulation and develop a block coordinate descent algorithm with explicit update formulas. We establish linear convergence of the algorithm, with explicit convergence rates, and prove stability of the optimal coupling under marginal covariance perturbations and derive a statistical error bound. We further show its equivalence to Sinkhorn iterations. Numerical experiments demonstrate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and illustrate the predictive advantages of causal couplings.
tldr: The paper develops entropic causal optimal transport for inferring causal input-output models from unpaired marginals and a prior coupling, with Gaussian reductions and efficient algorithms.
motivation: The authors aim to infer causal relationships from marginal observations when paired data are unavailable, using a prior coupling to regularize the solution.
method: They formulate entropic causal optimal transport with a one-sided causality constraint, prove Gaussian optimality for Gaussian marginals and quadratic costs, reduce to covariance optimization, and derive a block coordinate descent algorithm with linear convergence.
result: The algorithm has explicit convergence rates, stability under marginal covariance perturbations, a statistical error bound, and is shown equivalent to Sinkhorn iterations; numerical experiments demonstrate efficiency and predictive advantages.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable framework for causal input-output modeling with prior information, but it is a classical optimal transport and causal inference contribution without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Bivariate Renyi Tsallis Divergence
authors: Rajesh G Suramya Surendran
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, a bivariate extension of the differential Renyi Tsallis divergence is introduced for comparing two absolutely continuous bivariate probability distributions. Fundamental properties of the proposed divergence are studied, including non negativity, pseudo additivity under component wise independence, and invariance under monotone and nonsingular linear transformations. Relationships with Renyi, Tsallis, alpha, Bhattacharyya, and Hellinger divergence measures are also established. A sensitivity analysis is performed to compare the Renyi, Tsallis and Renyi Tsallis divergences under the Marshall Olkin and Gumbel type bivariate exponential models, taking the magnitude of Kendall's rank correlation coefficient as a common scale for dependence. The proposed measure is further developed for bivariate order statistics, with particular emphasis on the joint distribution of the minimum and maximum order statistics for several lifetime distributions, including exponential, Weibull, Pareto, and Rayleigh models. When the underlying distributions are unknown, a nonparametric estimator is constructed using bivariate Gaussian kernel density estimators with plug in bandwidth selection. The proposed estimator is applied to a real life dataset and bootstrap resampling is used to assess estimation uncertainty. The results show the applicability of the proposed divergence for comparing bivariate distributions and indicate that its finite sample performance depends on the order parameter and the distributions being compared.
tldr: The paper introduces a bivariate extension of the differential Rényi–Tsallis divergence for comparing two continuous bivariate probability distributions.
motivation: Divergence measures are useful for quantifying differences between distributions, but many existing Rényi/Tsallis divergences are primarily univariate; the authors aim to extend them to bivariate settings with dependence-sensitive comparisons.
method: The authors define a bivariate differential Rényi–Tsallis divergence, establish properties such as non-negativity, pseudo-additivity, and invariance, relate it to existing divergences, and study it under bivariate exponential models and order statistics; a nonparametric kernel-density estimator is also proposed.
result: The proposed divergence satisfies several theoretical properties, is compared with related measures under Marshall–Olkin and Gumbel bivariate exponential models, and is applied to real data with bootstrap uncertainty assessment.
conclusion: The measure provides a practical tool for comparing bivariate distributions, with finite-sample performance depending on the order parameter and the underlying distributions, but it is a classical statistics contribution with no direct quantum information relevance.

title: Path Abstraction For Markov Reward Models: An Isabelle Formalisation In A Free Monoid View
authors: Robert Modderman Arnd Hartmanns
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical definition of discrete-time Markov chains maps pairs of states to transition probabilities. An alternative, proposed in the context of path abstraction in probabilistic counterexample refinement, is to view them as a transition kernel on the free monoid on the state space, mapping paths directly to path probabilities. In this paper, we first extend the free monoid view and path abstraction algorithm to cumulative rewards on Markov reward models. We then use Isabelle/HOL to formalise Markov chains and reward models in this view, exploiting the discrete finite-prefix semantics to work with Isabelle's standard HOL-Analysis library. We mechanise the path abstraction algorithm and its key correctness properties of well-definedness and monotonic absorption, establishing the preservation of reachability probabilities and expected rewards. Proving the convergence of these quantities on relevant path sets is aided by our use of the lightweight free monoid semantics in place of the standard measure-theoretic one used in established Isabelle formalisations of Markov models. We obtain a verified abstract implementation of path abstraction in Isabelle/HOL, providing a foundation for refinement to efficient executable code and integration with probabilistic model checkers.
tldr: The paper extends the free-monoid view of discrete-time Markov chains and path abstraction to cumulative rewards on Markov reward models, and mechanises the theory and its correctness properties in Isabelle/HOL.
motivation: Standard Markov chain semantics maps state pairs to transition probabilities, which makes path-level reasoning and abstraction awkward; a free-monoid transition-kernel view was previously proposed for probabilistic counterexample refinement but had not been extended to rewards or formally verified.
method: The authors generalise path abstraction to cumulative rewards, then formalise Markov chains and Markov reward models in Isabelle/HOL using a discrete finite-prefix free-monoid semantics that plugs into the standard HOL-Analysis library, and mechanise the abstraction algorithm together with proofs of well-definedness and monotonic absorption.
result: They establish preservation of reachability probabilities and expected rewards under path abstraction, with convergence on relevant path sets simplified by the lightweight free-monoid semantics, yielding a verified abstract implementation of path abstraction in Isabelle/HOL.
conclusion: The formalisation provides a verified foundation for refining path abstraction into executable code and integrating it with probabilistic model checkers.

title: Hardness And Inapproximability Of The Covering Radius For Ldpc Codes
authors: Fabrizio Marinelli Massimo Battaglioni
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a binary parity-check matrix [MATH] and an integer [MATH], the covering-radius decision problem asks whether every attainable syndrome can be represented by an error vector of Hamming weight at most [MATH]. We study this problem for sparse parity-check matrices with bounded row and column weights. Using a bounded-occurrence quantified-SAT reduction, we prove that the problem is [MATH]-complete for matrices with maximum row and column weight three, and remains [MATH]-hard under a constant multiplicative gap. Starting from Vertex Cover on 3-regular graphs, we also obtain an explicit NP-hard approximation factor under the same weight constraints. We remark that weight three is the exact threshold for hardness: if either the maximum row weight or the maximum column weight is at most two, the covering radius can be computed in polynomial time.
tldr: The paper proves NP-hardness and inapproximability of the covering-radius decision problem for sparse binary parity-check matrices, with weight three as the sharp hardness threshold.
motivation: The covering radius of a parity-check matrix characterizes the worst-case syndrome decoding weight and is relevant to coding theory and LDPC applications, but its computational complexity for sparse matrices was not fully pinned down.
method: The authors use a bounded-occurrence quantified-SAT reduction to establish NP-completeness and hardness of approximation, and reduce from Vertex Cover on 3-regular graphs to obtain explicit inapproximability factors.
result: They show the problem is NP-complete for matrices with maximum row and column weight three, remains NP-hard under a constant multiplicative gap, and becomes polynomial-time computable when either maximum row weight or maximum column weight is at most two.
conclusion: Weight three is the exact threshold separating tractable and hard instances for covering-radius computation in sparse parity-check matrices, with strong inapproximability consequences.

title: Inverse Design For Nonplanar Conformal Layers
authors: Arjun Khurana, Michael J. Probst, Stephen E. Ralph
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conformal layering, where a deposited layer follows the nonplanar topography beneath it, arises from both deliberate passivation overlays and imperfect planarization between depositions. However, inverse design methods typically model planar, vertically extruded layers, resulting in geometric discrepancies between the modeled and fabricated structure. To address these discrepancies, we present differentiable mapping functions that incorporate both uniform conformal overlays and partially conformal interlayer dips into a standard inverse design paradigm, requiring no additional design parameters over planar structures. Using these mappings, we design (1) mode-selective GaAs grating reflectors with uniform conformal SiN passivation for high-aspect-ratio VCSELs, reaching differential modal reflectivities of 33.1% (single-etch) and 63.4% (dual-etch), and (2) a dual-layer silicon grating coupler whose upper layer dips up to 40 nm into the lower layer, reaching -0.75 dB coupling efficiency. Modeling conformal layering during optimization, rather than treating it as post-hoc fabrication error, permits direct exploitation of the conformal layering, yielding inherently fabricable and performant designs.
tldr: The paper introduces differentiable conformal-layer mapping functions into inverse design workflows to make photonic device designs (GaAs grating reflectors, silicon grating couplers) inherently fabricable.
motivation: Inverse design typically assumes planar, vertically extruded layers, causing geometric mismatch between modeled and fabricated nonplanar structures such as passivation overlays and imperfectly planarized interlayer dips.
