method: The authors derive differentiable mapping functions capturing uniform conformal overlays and partially conformal interlayer dips, embedding them in a standard adjoint-based inverse design paradigm without adding design parameters.
result: They design mode-selective GaAs grating reflectors with conformal SiN passivation achieving 33.1% (single-etch) and 63.4% (dual-etch) differential modal reflectivities, and a dual-layer silicon grating coupler with 40 nm interlayer dip reaching -0.75 dB coupling efficiency.
conclusion: Treating conformal layering inside optimization rather than as post-hoc fabrication error enables direct exploitation of nonplanar topography, yielding fabricable and performant photonic designs.

title: Existence Of A Third Self-similar Solution Of The Yang--Mills Equation In High Even Dimensions
authors: Piotr Bizo\'n
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the spherically symmetric [MATH] Yang--Mills equation admits a third smooth self-similar profile, in addition to the two known explicit profiles, in every even dimension [MATH]. This complements the analogous existence theorem in odd dimensions [MATH] (arXiv:2610.36784). In contrast to the odd-dimensional case, where the classification of smooth self-similar profiles reduces to counting roots of an explicit resonance polynomial [Phys. Rev. D 114, 064021 (2026)], the even-dimensional proof requires solving a nonlinear connection problem. In [MATH], where one explicit profile degenerates to the zero solution, we give a formal argument for the existence of a second nontrivial smooth profile in addition to the single nontrivial explicit one.
tldr: The paper proves the existence of a third smooth spherically symmetric self-similar profile for the Yang--Mills equation in every even dimension.
motivation: The work extends prior classification and existence results for self-similar Yang--Mills profiles from odd to even dimensions, where the proof requires a nonlinear connection problem.
method: The author uses analytical PDE methods to solve a nonlinear connection problem for spherically symmetric self-similar Yang--Mills configurations in even dimensions.
result: A third smooth self-similar profile is shown to exist in every even dimension, complementing the two known explicit profiles and the odd-dimensional existence theorem.
conclusion: The paper completes the even-dimensional analogue of the odd-dimensional classification and provides a formal argument for an additional nontrivial profile in a degenerate case.

title: Approximation Numbers Of Hankel Operators On Weighted Fock Spaces And The Berger--Coburn Phenomenon
authors: Guijun Liu, Xiaofeng Wang, Jin Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a real-valued weight whose real Hessian is uniformly positive definite and bounded. For [MATH], [MATH], and possibly unbounded symbols [MATH], we give necessary and sufficient conditions for prescribed decay of the approximation numbers of Hankel operators [MATH] from weighted Fock spaces [MATH] to weighted Lebesgue spaces [MATH] in terms of the non-increasing rearrangement of the IDA function of [MATH]. We also characterize membership in the approximation ideals [MATH] and their weak counterparts [MATH] for [MATH]. The symbol criteria involve Lorentz, Lorentz--Zygmund, and Copson--Lorentz spaces. Our approach also yields the converse to the sufficient condition in [15], thereby completing the characterization of prescribed singular value decay for Hankel operators on a broad class of weighted Bergman spaces. For the pair [MATH] and [MATH] on weighted Fock spaces, we characterize simultaneous decay of their approximation numbers and simultaneous membership in these ideals in terms of the mean oscillation function of [MATH]. For bounded symbols, we establish the Berger--Coburn phenomenon for both ideals in sharp exponent ranges. A new feature in the case [MATH], where the sharp threshold [MATH] is strictly less than [MATH].
tldr: This paper characterizes approximation-number decay and ideal membership for Hankel operators on weighted Fock and Bergman spaces, including a Berger--Coburn phenomenon for approximation ideals.
motivation: The authors aim to give sharp symbol criteria for prescribed singular-value decay of Hankel operators in weighted function spaces and to complete converse characterizations for weighted Bergman spaces.
method: They use non-increasing rearrangements of the IDA function, mean oscillation functions, and Lorentz, Lorentz--Zygmund, and Copson--Lorentz space criteria to obtain necessary and sufficient conditions.
result: The paper establishes characterizations of approximation ideals and their weak counterparts, simultaneous decay for paired Hankel operators on weighted Fock spaces, and the Berger--Coburn phenomenon in sharp exponent ranges.
conclusion: The work extends and completes singular-value decay characterizations for Hankel operators on broad weighted Bergman and Fock spaces, but it is a pure functional-analysis result with no direct connection to the listed quantum information research directions.

title: Noise Characterization And Robust Signal Detection In Yeast Pheromone Molecular Communication
authors: Nikolaos Ntetsikas, Styliana Kyriakoudi, Antonis Kirmizis, Ioannis Krikidis, Ian F. Akyildiz, Marios Lestas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A critical aspect of Molecular Communications (MC) is the implementation of signal detection policies amidst noise. To date, noise characterizations within the MC field have predominantly drawn from methodologies found in wireless communications literature. In this study, we diverge from existing MC research by utilizing a newly developed experimental platform that employs yeast, allowing us to consider more realistic noise characterizations based on the relevant signaling pathways. We propose suitable signal detection mechanisms tailored to this experimental setup, which focuses on yeast cell-to-cell communications. Our analysis identifies gene transcription as the primary source of noise, and we utilize a Markov birth-death process model with Poisson arrivals and departures to characterize it. The noisy expression of the FUS1 gene is best represented using a mixed Gaussian distribution model. This model serves as a foundation for evaluating the performance of Maximum Likelihood Detection mechanisms in terms of Bit Error Rate (BER) for both symbol-by-symbol and sequence transmission schemes. Error analysis indicates that appropriate adjustments to the signal threshold can reduce errors to as low as 10%, which is not negligible. In contrast, the detection of symbol sequences demonstrates enhanced error performance, achieving error rates as low as 0.4%, albeit at the cost of increased computational complexity.
tldr: The paper characterizes gene-transcription noise in yeast pheromone molecular communication and evaluates maximum-likelihood signal detection schemes.
motivation: Molecular communication signal detection has relied heavily on noise models imported from wireless communications, which may not capture biological signaling noise realistically.
method: Using an experimental yeast cell-to-cell communication platform, the authors model FUS1 gene expression noise with a Markov birth-death process and a mixed Gaussian distribution, then analyze ML detection for symbol-by-symbol and sequence transmission.
result: Threshold adjustments reduce symbol-by-symbol error rates to about 10%, while sequence detection achieves error rates as low as 0.4% at higher computational cost.
conclusion: Realistic biological noise characterization improves detection design in yeast-based molecular communication, though sequence detection trades complexity for lower error rates.

title: Threat Landscape Of Vibe Coding And The Road To Secure Autonomy
authors: Devki Nandan Jha, Shubh Anand, Karthick Keeranagere Krishnaiah, Roman Ahearn, Suhas Nale
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.
tldr: This paper surveys security threats in vibe coding, where AI agents write, test, and deploy software, and proposes a reference architecture, autonomy levels, threat model, taxonomy, and research challenges.
motivation: AI coding agents are becoming autonomous and can execute commands, manage dependencies, and access cloud resources, creating security risks beyond insecure code generation.
method: The authors consolidate fragmented research by defining a vibe-coding reference architecture, characterizing six agent autonomy levels, and building a threat model with five trust boundaries and a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes.
result: They review evidence and defenses for each threat, finding that risk grows with agent operational authority and that most defenses rely on model judgment and address only isolated threats.
conclusion: The paper identifies eleven open research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks for assessing vibe-coding security.

title: New Gate, Weight And Wire Complexity Bounds For Sigmoid Neural Networks
authors: Jiatu Li, Daniel Reichman, Ryan Williams, Tony Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feedforward neural networks with sigmoid activations are of fundamental importance in neural computation. However, our understanding of the circuit complexity of such networks for implementing Boolean functions remains limited. The analog output of the sigmoid, along with its transcendental nature, leads to unique mathematical challenges for proving lower bounds. Introducing new techniques, we establish new upper and lower bounds on the complexity of sigmoidal networks computing Boolean functions: We prove nearly tight bounds for the wire complexity of computing PARITY with such networks of constant depth and polynomial-bounded weights. We extend the size lower bound of Kane and Williams [STOC'16] against depth-[MATH] threshold circuits, to depth-3 sigmoidal networks with polynomial weights, proving a [MATH] size lower bound for computing an explicit function in [MATH]. We prove that every symmetric function on [MATH] bits can be computed by a depth-[MATH] sigmoidal network with [MATH] wires and polynomial weights. This stands in stark contrast with threshold circuits of [MATH] depth, where [MATH]-wire lower bounds are known for [MATH]. We also answer a few fundamental problems related to sigmoidal networks, including proving new simulations and separations between threshold circuits and sigmoidal networks. We establish these results using a variety of techniques, including random restrictions for sigmoid gates, analyzing the average sensitivity of networks with sigmoids, simulation arguments, and using tools from approximation theory, complex analysis, and algebraic geometry.
tldr: The paper proves new gate, weight, and wire complexity bounds for sigmoid-activated neural networks computing Boolean functions.
motivation: Understanding circuit complexity of sigmoid neural networks is limited due to their analog, transcendental outputs, motivating new lower-bound techniques.
method: The authors use random restrictions for sigmoid gates, average sensitivity analysis, simulation arguments, and tools from approximation theory, complex analysis, and algebraic geometry.
result: They obtain nearly tight wire-complexity bounds for PARITY, extend a size lower bound to depth-3 sigmoidal networks, and show every symmetric function is computable by depth-2 sigmoidal networks with few wires.
conclusion: The work establishes new separations and simulations between threshold circuits and sigmoidal networks, advancing classical circuit complexity for neural networks.

title: Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning For Fine-Grained Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Class Analysis In Heterogeneous Attack Environments
authors: Travis Atkison Abul Kalam Azad
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a vital role in protecting modern network infrastructures. Although Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw network traffic, global models struggle with non-IID attack distributions. Moreover, practical security operations require fine-grained attack classification for targeted threat responses. To address these challenges, this paper investigates the convergence dynamics and performance of Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning (HPFL), which combines multi-tier aggregation with client-level personalization, for 8-class, 6-class, and 4-class intrusion detection using Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) models implemented in NVIDIA FLARE on the CICIDS2017 dataset. Experimental results show that personalized HPFL models achieve micro F1-scores up to 0.9911 in the 6-class task, while the overall local accuracy reaches 0.9975 in the 8-class task. On 8-class local test sets, HPFL achieves a micro F1-score of 0.9901 and a macro F1-score of 0.8324, outperforming FedAvg (0.7176) and FedProx (0.5624) in macro F1. Cross-client evaluations demonstrate out-of-distribution generalization, with HPFL achieving a 4-class micro F1-score of 0.9294 compared with 0.9140 for standalone local models. Furthermore, distance-weighted network analysis estimates a 48.9% reduction in transmission overhead compared with conventional FL (194.4 MB vs. 380.3 MB for the 8-class task). These findings demonstrate HPFLs potential as an accurate, privacy-preserving, and communication-efficient approach to fine-grained intrusion detection in heterogeneous networks.
tldr: This paper evaluates Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning (HPFL) with MLP models on the CICIDS2017 dataset for fine-grained (4/6/8-class) intrusion detection in heterogeneous, non-IID attack environments.
motivation: Federated learning enables collaborative intrusion detection without sharing raw network traffic, but global models degrade under non-IID attack distributions and practical security operations demand fine-grained attack classification for targeted responses.
method: HPFL combines multi-tier aggregation with client-level personalization, implemented in NVIDIA FLARE with MLP models, and is benchmarked against FedAvg and FedProx across 8-class, 6-class, and 4-class intrusion detection tasks including cross-client out-of-distribution evaluation and a distance-weighted communication overhead analysis.
result: Personalized HPFL reaches micro F1 up to 0.9911 (6-class) and local accuracy 0.9975 (8-class), with macro F1 of 0.8324 versus 0.7176 (FedAvg) and 0.5624 (FedProx); cross-client 4-class micro F1 is 0.9294, and transmission overhead is estimated to drop by 48.9% (194.4 MB vs. 380.3 MB).
conclusion: HPFL is presented as an accurate, privacy-preserving, and communication-efficient approach for fine-grained intrusion detection in heterogeneous networks.

title: Flexibility Has A Price: Quantifying Modality Policies In Maliciously Secure Multi-Biometric Authentication
authors: Fuyi Wang, Wang Zhang, Neo Xu, Chao Chen, Kok-Leong Ong, Jianying Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-biometric authentication improves robustness and accessibility by combining information from multiple biometric modalities. Existing research has primarily focused on secure multimodal authentication, feature fusion, and recognition performance, while paying comparatively little attention to the security implications of modality-flexible authentication policies. At the same time, most systems provide limited cryptographic protection for biometric data during authentication. This paper addresses both challenges. We first study modality flexibility as a security decision rather than merely a usability feature. Each accepted modality subset creates an authentication entry point, and the resulting risk depends on the joint behavior of all accepted subsets and the attempt budget. We introduce a framework for quantifying this security cost and develop a policy-selection procedure that identifies policies satisfying a target risk level while supporting users who can present only a subset of modalities. We then present SUPERMBA, a two-server privacy-preserving authentication system that enforces the selected policy without revealing biometric templates or the modality subset used in an authentication attempt. The protocol provides verifiable policy enforcement even when one server is malicious and executes the same computation irrespective of the chosen policy or modality subset. Experiments on the three-modality MULB+ dataset show that allowing all modality subsets increases impostor risk from 1.21% for the weakest entry to 4.42% for the union of entries. On VidTIMIT, the increase is substantially smaller and is not statistically resolved with the available identities. SUPERMBA completes an authentication attempt in only 6.42 ms on MULB+ and 6.03 ms on VidTIMIT.
tldr: The paper formalizes the security cost of modality-flexible multi-biometric authentication policies and introduces SUPERMBA, a two-server privacy-preserving protocol that enforces such policies without revealing templates or the chosen modality subset.
motivation: Multi-biometric systems treat modality flexibility as a usability feature while neglecting its security implications, and most deployments give weak cryptographic protection to biometric data during authentication.
method: The authors model each accepted modality subset as an authentication entry point and quantify joint impostor risk under an attempt budget, yielding a policy-selection procedure; they then build a two-server privacy-preserving protocol with verifiable policy enforcement secure against one malicious server and with data-independent computation.
result: On MULB+, allowing all modality subsets raises impostor risk from 1.21% to 4.42% across entries, while VidTIMIT shows a smaller, statistically unresolved increase; authentication takes 6.42 ms (MULB+) and 6.03 ms (VidTIMIT).
conclusion: Modality flexibility carries a measurable security price that can be quantified and bounded by policy selection, and privacy-preserving enforcement is practical at few-millisecond latency.

title: Primal--Dual Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox For Dynamic Mean Field Games
authors: Erhan Bayraktar, Ibrahim Ekren, Lu Vy, Ziqing Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compute finite-horizon dynamic mean field equilibria using a primal--dual Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox algorithm. Each iteration updates occupation measures by exponential tilting and computes the dual correction by solving a linear PDE, without solving a nonlinear Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or a best-response control problem. Under assumptions and Lasry--Lions monotonicity, we prove an [MATH] ergodic Minty bound after [MATH] iterations and an [MATH] approximate-equilibrium bound for the corrected average. We obtain convergence rates for the population flow under strong monotonicity, and for smooth diffusions with uniformly convex control costs under ordinary monotonicity. We also prove convergence of continuous-time Markov chain approximations to diffusion equilibria and, under additional smoothness and convexity assumptions, bound the error in terms of the spatial mesh size and the number of iterations. Galerkin approximations preserve the [MATH] estimates under suitable bounds on the correction errors. Numerical experiments illustrate the method and its convergence.
tldr: The authors introduce a primal-dual Kullback-Leibler Mirror-Prox algorithm for computing finite-horizon dynamic mean field game equilibria without solving nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations.
motivation: Solving dynamic mean field games typically requires handling coupled HJB-Fokker-Planck systems or best-response control problems, which are computationally demanding; the paper seeks an efficient saddle-point iteration scheme.
method: Each Mirror-Prox iteration updates occupation measures via exponential tilting and computes dual corrections by solving a linear PDE, with convergence analysis under Lasry-Lions monotonicity, strong monotonicity, and convexity assumptions, plus continuous-time Markov chain approximations and Galerkin discretizations.
result: The authors prove an ergodic Minty bound after N iterations and approximate-equilibrium error bounds, obtain convergence rates for the population flow, and bound discretization error in terms of spatial mesh size and iteration count, supported by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The primal-dual KL Mirror-Prox approach provides a tractable and provably convergent method for dynamic mean field equilibria, avoiding nonlinear HJB solves while retaining theoretical guarantees.

title: Exact Solution Of The Two-dimensional One-component Plasma On The Truncated Beltrami Pseudosphere
authors: Josep Batle
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve exactly the two-dimensional one-component plasma at coupling [MATH] on the truncated Beltrami pseudosphere, a surface of constant negative curvature bounded by two parallels. A conformal map onto a flat cylinder leaves the particles interacting through the flat-cylinder potential, with the curvature entering only through the area element. The partition function becomes a product of incomplete gamma functions, the density is explicit, and all correlations are determinantal. Since the area is bounded, the large-N limit is taken at fixed shape. The free energy, obtained through the constant term with every coefficient in closed form, contains a bulk term (1/2)N ln N, a term linear in N, the flat hard-wall surface tension times the total boundary length, and a shape-dependent constant, with no ln N term. This is the conformal-anomaly prediction for Euler characteristic zero, tested here on a surface where the integrated Gaussian and boundary curvatures are separately nonzero and cancel. The expansion coincides term by term with the cylinder result of Shen and Forrester, whose universal constants are quadratures of the two boundary layers. At both walls the density tends to the flat contact value [MATH] ln 2, from opposite sides, although the circumferences differ by a factor cosh u_max. We compare the asymptotics with the exact solution up to N=4096, and Monte Carlo simulations at [MATH]1, 4 and 6, validated against the exact [MATH] 2 density, show how the boundary layers evolve with coupling.
tldr: The paper exactly solves the two-dimensional one-component plasma on a truncated Beltrami pseudosphere and analyzes its free energy, density, and boundary-layer behavior.
motivation: It aims to test conformal-anomaly predictions and boundary effects for a Coulomb plasma on a constant-negative-curvature surface with boundaries.
method: A conformal map to a flat cylinder reduces the problem to the flat-cylinder potential with curvature entering via the area element; the partition function is expressed through incomplete gamma functions and correlations are determinantal.
result: The free-energy expansion contains bulk, linear, boundary-tension, and shape-dependent constant terms with no ln N term, matching the Euler-characteristic-zero conformal-anomaly prediction and cylinder results.
conclusion: The exact solution and Monte Carlo checks clarify how boundary layers evolve with coupling on a curved bounded surface.

title: Cycles Of Arbitrary Period In Multidimensional Heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause Dynamics
authors: Iryna Zabarianska Anton V. Proskurnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study periodic behavior in heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics with multidimensional opinions and norm-defined confidence neighborhoods. We prove that, for every dimension [MATH], every [MATH] norm with [MATH], and every integer [MATH], a system of five agents admits a periodic trajectory of minimal period [MATH]; moreover, different periods can coexist for fixed confidence radii. Four agents remain stationary, while the fifth moves along a line segment contained in their convex hull. The stationary agents may share a common strictly positive confidence radius, and all confidence inequalities are strict. A geometric criterion underlying the construction extends these results to further classes of norms. However, this criterion cannot be satisfied in dimensions one and two, regardless of the confidence norm. We also prove that no heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause system with less than five agents admits a nonconstant periodic trajectory, under any norm and in any dimension; every trajectory with at most three agents converges exponentially.
tldr: The paper proves the existence of periodic trajectories of arbitrary minimal period in heterogeneous multidimensional Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics, with a minimum of five agents required for nonconstant periodic behavior.
motivation: The work studies periodic behavior in a well-known bounded-confidence opinion dynamics model, extending prior results to heterogeneous agents, multidimensional opinions, and general norms.
method: The authors construct explicit five-agent configurations in which four agents are stationary and one moves along a line segment in their convex hull, and they establish geometric criteria for periodic trajectories under arbitrary norms and dimensions.
result: They show that for every dimension, norm, and integer period, a five-agent system admits a periodic trajectory of that minimal period, with different periods coexisting; fewer than five agents cannot produce nonconstant periodic trajectories, and trajectories with at most three agents converge exponentially.
conclusion: The findings characterize the minimal system size and geometric conditions for periodic behavior in heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause dynamics, while showing that the construction is impossible in one and two dimensions.

title: Structural Balance In Complex Networks: From Measurement To Dynamics, Emergence And Implications
authors: Giacomo Vaccario, Piotr J. G\'orski, Georges Andres, Manuel S. Mariani, Janusz A. Ho{\l}yst
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural balance theory, introduced in social psychology to describe how friendly and hostile ties organize into consistent patterns, has been reinterpreted through statistical physics and complex networks. In the classical formulation, a triad with positive or negative links, representing friendship and hostility, is balanced when the product of its signs is positive; a balanced network splits into at most two internally friendly, mutually hostile groups. This review synthesizes how the triadic formulation has been extended to a statistical-ensemble perspective in which balance is encoded by immanent three-body interactions described by a proper Hamiltonian, balanced configurations correspond to low-energy states, and balance measures serve as order parameters for transitions between consensus, polarization, and disorder. We organize the field into three sections: Measurement, Dynamics and Emergence, and Implications. In Measurement, we compare measures of structural balance and null models, and show that conclusions for a given system depend on the chosen measure and null model. In Dynamics and Emergence, we review deterministic and stochastic systems, including the gradient, Hamiltonian, and local triad models, and examine how noise, topology, and competing mechanisms determine whether balance emerges. In Implications, we survey consequences for belief formation, opinion contagion dynamics, polarization, international relations, and markets. Across domains, the evidence is strongest for local triadic stability and weakest for system-wide balance. Balance is not synonymous with harmony: balanced structures can reflect cohesion, polarization, or persistent conflict. Its empirical relevance is well supported in some reciprocal social systems, but remains less settled in biological and other complex networks.
tldr: A review of structural balance theory in complex networks, synthesizing measurement, dynamical emergence, and implications of signed triadic interactions across social, political, and economic systems.
motivation: Structural balance theory from social psychology has been reinterpreted via statistical physics and complex networks, but the field lacks a unified account of how balance measures, null models, and dynamical models relate and where empirical evidence is strongest.
method: Review organized into three parts -- Measurement (comparison of balance measures and null models), Dynamics and Emergence (gradient, Hamiltonian, and local triad models with noise and topology), and Implications (belief formation, polarization, international relations, markets).
result: Conclusions about a given system depend sensitively on the chosen balance measure and null model; evidence is strongest for local triadic stability and weakest for system-wide balance, and balanced structures can correspond to cohesion, polarization, or persistent conflict.
conclusion: Balance is not synonymous with harmony, and its empirical relevance is well supported in reciprocal social systems but remains unsettled in biological and other complex networks.

title: Asymptotic Analysis Of Sample Average Approximations For Optimal Control Problems With Uncertain Dynamics
authors: Maria Soledad Aronna, Jo\~ao Miguel Machado, Oscar Sierra Fonseca
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study sample average approximations (SAA) of optimal control problems with control-affine dynamics depending on an uncertain parameter. The objective is an expected terminal cost plus a Tikhonov regularization term, and the controls are square-integrable functions subject to pointwise convex constraints. We show that the reduced objective is twice continuously differentiable in the square-integrable topology, so that no two-norm discrepancy arises, and that its Hessian is a Hilbert--Schmidt perturbation of a multiple of the identity. This yields Lipschitz regularity of stationary controls and second-order conditions without gap for polyhedral constraints. For the SAA scheme with sample size [MATH], we prove almost sure uniform consistency of the empirical minimizers, convergence rates of order [MATH] for the optimal values, independent of the dimension of the parameter space. We then derive the asymptotic distributions. The optimal values satisfy a central limit theorem, obtained from a functional central limit theorem for the SAA objective. The empirical minimizers are asymptotically Gaussian when the constraints are inactive; under polyhedral constraints, their limit solves a quadratic problem on the critical cone with a Gaussian linear term. We also derive confidence intervals for linear functionals of the optimal control and illustrate the results on two numerical examples.
tldr: The paper develops a rigorous asymptotic theory for sample average approximations of optimal control problems with control-affine dynamics depending on an uncertain parameter, including consistency, convergence rates, and central limit theorems.
motivation: Sample average approximation is a standard computational approach for stochastic optimization, but its asymptotic statistical properties have not been fully established for control-affine optimal control problems with pointwise convex control constraints and Tikhonov regularization.
method: The authors prove twice continuous differentiability of the reduced objective in the square-integrable topology, show the Hessian is a Hilbert-Schmidt perturbation of a multiple of the identity, and then derive uniform consistency, rates of order 1/sqrt(M), and asymptotic distributions for empirical minimizers under inactive and polyhedral constraints.
result: Empirical minimizers converge almost surely and uniformly, optimal values satisfy a central limit theorem with dimension-independent rates, and the limiting distribution of minimizers is Gaussian or a quadratic-program solution on the critical cone with Gaussian linear term.
conclusion: The results provide a complete asymptotic inferential framework for SAA in uncertain optimal control, enabling confidence intervals for linear functionals of the optimal control, illustrated numerically.

title: Forests Of Omnitrees: Analysis And Applications To Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements
authors: Nils Margenberg
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests, which bisect cells along selected axes. A canonical descriptor characterizes representable partitions independently of split order. Complete one-level cycles, including coarsening, face balance and selected coarse meshes, take sequential work proportional to stored input and output at fixed dimension and key width, with polynomial depth dependence even for unbalanced input. From balanced input, refinement-only balance stays within each request's coordinate slab; this bound is attained. Polynomial trace equations characterize conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions. Reconstruction moments bound interpolation errors and capture the logarithmic loss that bilinear nodal interpolation can suffer on balanced meshes. Elements of degree up to four resolve moving heat layers on unstructured 4D space-time and 5D space-time-parameter meshes. Multigrid uses the generated hierarchies.
tldr: The paper proves output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests used in anisotropic space-time finite element meshing and applies them to high-order discretizations and multigrid solvers.
motivation: Adaptive mesh refinement in higher-dimensional space-time settings requires data structures whose computational cost scales with input and output size rather than with the full ambient mesh, motivating a rigorous complexity analysis of omnitree-based partitioning.
method: The author introduces a canonical descriptor for representable partitions, analyzes complete one-level cycles (refinement, coarsening, face balance), derives polynomial trace equations for conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions, and bounds interpolation error via reconstruction moments.
result: Sequential work for one-level cycles is shown proportional to stored input plus output at fixed dimension and key width with polynomial depth dependence, balanced-input refinement stays within each request's coordinate slab, and degree-four elements resolve moving heat layers on 4D and 5D space-time meshes.
conclusion: Omnitree forests provide provably efficient, order-independent adaptive meshing suitable for high-order space-time finite element and multigrid computations, with controlled interpolation error including logarithmic losses on balanced meshes.

title: Bias-Reduced And Parallel Heavy-Tailed Stochastic Convex Optimization In $\ell_p$ Geometries
authors: Zhengyun Nie, Anant Shyam, Brian Bullins
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the fundamental problem of parallel stochastic convex optimization (SCO), whose aim is to approximately minimize a convex objective when given the ability to query a moment-bounded stochastic gradient oracle multiple times in parallel per round. Whereas most previous results have focused on the variance-bounded Euclidean ([MATH]-norm) setting, meaning the objective is Lipschitz with respect to the [MATH]-norm over an [MATH]-bounded feasible set in [MATH], in this work we study parallel SCO in [MATH] settings for [MATH] under a heavy-tailed noise model. We begin by introducing a new class of [MATH]-optimal-distance-convergence (ODC[MATH]) algorithms, drawing on prior stochastic bias-reduced techniques [ACJ+21], which combine with multilevel Monte Carlo methods to efficiently estimate the optimum of uniformly convex objectives. As a consequence of our ODC[MATH] algorithms, we first establish rates for projection-efficient [MATH]-Lipschitz optimization, composite convex minimization, and efficient [MATH]-proximal point estimation. Combining our ODC[MATH] algorithms with a new [MATH]-generalized Gaussian-based stochastic gradient estimator ([MATH]-GREG), we provide two efficient [MATH] parallel algorithms, EpochDA and [MATH]-AC-SA, which achieve optimization error [MATH] with at most [MATH] query depth, improving upon the sequential heavy-tailed stochastic query depth of [MATH] for [MATH]. We also establish dimension-dependent lower bounds of [MATH] adaptive rounds for nonsmooth convex optimization over a subset of the unit [MATH] ball. Our results improve upon the [MATH] bounds of [DG19], when adapted to the same feasible set.
tldr: The paper develops bias-reduced, parallel stochastic convex optimization algorithms for ℓ_p geometries under heavy-tailed gradient noise, achieving improved query-depth rates and dimension-dependent lower bounds.
motivation: Prior parallel SCO work is largely confined to the variance-bounded Euclidean setting; the authors aim to extend efficient parallel optimization to general ℓ_p geometries with only moment-bounded (heavy-tailed) stochastic gradients.
method: They introduce a class of optimal-distance-convergence (ODC_p) algorithms built on stochastic bias-reduction combined with multilevel Monte Carlo, and pair these with a new p-generalized Gaussian-based stochastic gradient estimator (p-GREG) to construct the EpochDA and p-AC-SA parallel algorithms.
result: The parallel algorithms attain the target optimization error with substantially reduced query depth, beating the sequential heavy-tailed query depth scaling, and the authors prove dimension-dependent lower bounds on the number of adaptive rounds for nonsmooth convex optimization over a subset of the unit ℓ_p ball.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for projection-efficient, heavy-tailed parallel SCO in ℓ_p spaces with near-optimal depth guarantees, sharpening earlier bounds when restricted to the same feasible set.

title: When Is Membership Graded? Identifiability And Resolution Limits Of A Graded Gaussian Mixture Model
authors: Peter Chin Sie Hendrata Dharmawan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed-membership models describe each unit as a graded blend of latent types. Before the blend is interpreted, the data should be able to rule out the simpler story in which every unit belongs to a single type. We ask when they can, in a scalar graded Gaussian mixture model, in which each observation is a Beta-weighted convex combination of independent Gaussian draws from two types, the mechanism behind functional mixed-membership models and the normal compositional model. The model is identifiable, unequal variances included, but the identifying information sits in the far tails of the marginal. For the symmetric model we give a closed-form hard-membership mixture that matches the graded marginal in five cumulants, and a Le Cam bound turns it into a certified sample size below which no test separates graded from hard membership with summed error under one half. The threshold is governed by the concentration [MATH] relative to [MATH], where [MATH] is the type half-separation in within-type standard deviations. At [MATH] it is about 2,600 observations at [MATH] and 77,000 at [MATH]. Most of the difficulty comes from learning [MATH]. On 100 simulated datasets with graded membership, a correctly specified posterior under the default priors of a published Bayesian sampler for this model class reports hard membership every time, a weak prior gives intervals for the concentration spanning orders of magnitude, and the sampler's own answers depend on where it starts.
tldr: The paper establishes identifiability and Le Cam-type sample-size lower bounds for a Beta-weighted graded Gaussian mixture model, showing that distinguishing graded from hard membership requires enormous sample sizes concentrated in the distribution tails.
motivation: Mixed-membership models are ubiquitous, but before interpreting graded blends one should be able to reject the simpler hard-membership explanation; the authors ask when data can actually do so in a minimal scalar model.
method: They construct a closed-form hard-membership mixture matching five cumulants of the symmetric graded marginal and apply a Le Cam bound to obtain certified sample-size thresholds; they also probe a published Bayesian sampler on 100 simulated datasets.
result: Thresholds scale with the concentration parameter relative to type separation, reaching roughly 2,600 observations at one setting and 77,000 at another, with most difficulty attributable to learning the concentration; the Bayesian sampler reports hard membership every time and is sensitive to initialization and priors.
conclusion: Graded membership is only detectable at very large sample sizes, and standard Bayesian inference for such models can be misleadingly confident, so identifiability alone does not guarantee practical resolution.

title: Beyond The Error Horizon: Averaged Quantile Kaczmarz Methods For Corrupted And Noisy Linear Systems
authors: Elizaveta Rebrova Sofiia Shvaiko
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear systems and least-squares problems can contain measurement errors of different scales: a few measurements may be highly unreliable, while small noise affects every measurement. Residual-based iterative filtering can remove the influence of sparse corruption, but its accuracy is limited by a noise-dependent error horizon. We study how averaging and relaxation reduce this horizon in averaged quantile randomized Kaczmarz (AQRK), which filters equations by residual quantiles and averages a batch of single-row updates. Filtering, however, introduces an update bias that averaging alone cannot remove. We show that re-querying the accepted equations can remove this bias, and when the corruption is sparse enough relative to the conditioning of the matrix and large enough relative to the noise, we prove that AQRK with re-queried residuals reduces the horizon as averaging does without the corruption: its error decays to a horizon proportional to [MATH], where [MATH] is the stepsize and [MATH] the update batch size. Further, decreasing stepsizes or increasing batches gives convergence to the solution of the clean system. Numerical experiments support the theory and examine settings beyond it, including noise that cannot be re-queried and the corrupted low-rank tensor fitting problem. In the latter, AQRK inner solves succeed where standard alternating least-squares solvers and single-row robust updates fail.
tldr: Averaged quantile randomized Kaczmarz methods are analyzed to show how averaging, relaxation, and re-querying reduce the noise-induced error horizon in corrupted and noisy linear systems.
motivation: Iterative residual-based filtering can remove sparse measurement corruption but its accuracy is capped by a noise-dependent error horizon, which the authors aim to shrink.
method: The authors study averaged quantile randomized Kaczmarz (AQRK), which filters rows by residual quantiles and averages batched single-row updates, and introduce re-querying of accepted equations to eliminate the filtering-induced update bias, supported by convergence proofs.
result: Under conditions on corruption sparsity relative to conditioning and noise, AQRK with re-queried residuals reduces the error horizon to one proportional to stepsize times batch size, and decreasing stepsizes or increasing batch sizes yields convergence to the clean solution; experiments confirm the theory and show gains on corrupted low-rank tensor fitting.
conclusion: AQRK with re-queried residuals provides a provably improved robustness-accuracy tradeoff for solving corrupted and noisy linear systems, outperforming standard ALS and single-row robust updates in tested settings.

title: Projector-Based Conic Formulations And Exact Decompositions For Continuous Multifacility Location
authors: V\'ictor Blanco, Diego Laborda-Guti\'errez, Miguel Mart\'inez-Ant\'on
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the continuous multisource facility location problem, where facility locations and the assignment of demand points must be determined simultaneously. We show that the assignment structure can be represented by orthogonal projection matrices. This observation leads to new mixed-projection conic formulations that avoid the big-M envelopes used in standard mixed-integer models. Based on these formulations, we develop exact decomposition algorithms that separate the discrete selection of the assignment projectors from location convex conic subproblems. We also derive semidefinite relaxation bounds and primal procedures that provide warm starts for the exact methods. The proposed approach draws new connections between continuous multifacility location, orthogonal projectors, and low-rank semidefinite optimization, and applies to general conic-representable distances.
tldr: The paper develops projector-based conic formulations and exact decomposition algorithms for continuous multifacility location problems.
motivation: Standard mixed-integer models for simultaneous facility location and demand assignment rely on big-M envelopes, which can be inefficient and numerically challenging.
method: The authors represent assignment structure using orthogonal projection matrices, derive mixed-projection conic formulations, and design exact decomposition algorithms separating discrete projector selection from convex conic location subproblems.
result: They obtain new conic formulations, semidefinite relaxation bounds, and primal warm-start procedures that avoid big-M envelopes and connect the problem to low-rank semidefinite optimization.
conclusion: The work provides an exact optimization framework for continuous multifacility location with general conic-representable distances, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Residual-driven Lattice Boltzmann Equation. Part I: Framework And Nonlinear Solution Methods
authors: Li-Shi Luo Xingzhou Ji
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We developed a residual-driven framework of the lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE) to integrate general nonlinear iterative methods. The nonlinear residual is constructed directly from the complete LBE collision-streaming update, allowing general nonlinear solvers to be integrated without modifying the original LBE algorithmic structure, i.e., the kernel consisting of collision-streaming, boundary conditions, and various forcing and interaction effects. Sophisticated techniques, such as weighted fixed-point iteration, full approximation scheme (FAS) multigrid, and Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov methods are integrated into the LBE via this framework, and preconditioned LBE is further incorporated as a nonlinear smoother to demonstrate solver composability. Numerical tests validate that FAS and Newton methods do converge to the same discrete steady fixed-point obtained with the primitive LBE iteration. For the 2D lid-driven cavity flow, the FAS scheme reduces the measured solution time by a factor of approximately 44 at Re = 1000 and more than 224 at Re = 5000. Accurate results are also obtained for the steady flows past a cylinder at Re = 20 and the NACA0012 airfoil at Re = 1000. The low Mach-number tests for the flow past a NACA0012 airfoil further show that both the FAS scheme and preconditioning can not only substantially reduce the work required to reach steady solutions, but also mitigate the zero Mach-number crisis.
tldr: This paper introduces a residual-driven framework for the lattice Boltzmann equation that enables integration of general nonlinear iterative solvers (FAS multigrid, Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov) without altering the core collision-streaming kernel.
motivation: Steady-state lattice Boltzmann simulations converge slowly with primitive fixed-point iteration, so the authors seek a way to plug sophisticated nonlinear solvers into existing LBE codes without rewriting their algorithmic structure.
method: A nonlinear residual is constructed directly from the full LBE collision-streaming update, and weighted fixed-point iteration, FAS multigrid, and Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov methods are integrated through this residual formulation, with preconditioned LBE used as a nonlinear smoother.
result: FAS and Newton methods converge to the same discrete fixed point as primitive iteration, with FAS reducing solution time by ~44x at Re=1000 and >224x at Re=5000 for 2D lid-driven cavity flow, while also mitigating the zero Mach-number crisis in low-Mach NACA0012 tests.
conclusion: The residual-driven framework offers solver composability and large speedups for steady LBE simulations, providing a general-purpose numerical infrastructure for computational fluid dynamics.

title: Flocking Time And Graph Volume In Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models With Dynamic Networks
authors: Jea-Hyun Park Sooyeon Song
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete [MATH]-Laplacian ([MATH]) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.
tldr: The paper analyzes flocking time versus graph volume in a nonlinear Cucker-Smale model with dynamic networks and discrete p-Laplacian coupling, supported by transformer-based PPO experiments on network selection.
motivation: The authors aim to quantify how time constraints on consensus/ flocking force an increase in network connectivity, formalizing the intuition that faster agreement demands denser interaction graphs.
method: They prove finite-time flocking for a Cucker-Smale system with dynamic networks governed by the discrete p-Laplacian, derive a lower bound relating flocking time to graph volume, and run reinforcement-learning experiments where a transformer-based PPO policy selects network structures at each step.
result: They establish a quantitative inverse relation between flocking time and graph volume, and experiments confirm a threshold effect where the most stringent time constraints sharply increase the average number of connections, with larger initial velocity variance requiring greater volume.
conclusion: Time constraints induce 'connection mobilization' in self-organizing networks, and the theoretical time-volume bound is reflected in learned network-selection policies.

title: Nonlocal Regularization Of Sharp-crack Energetics: A Variational Bridge From Griffith Geometry To Emergent Constitutive Degradation
authors: Qing Cheng, Yuqi Sun, Xuejun Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.
tldr: The paper develops a variational diffuse-crack model that bridges sharp-crack Griffith energetics and nonlocal strain-energy regularization.
motivation: The authors aim to formulate fracture degradation without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law.
method: They use nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy with a bounded saturation potential, derive the constitutive stress via first variation, and implement a structure-preserving SAV scheme compared with velocity-Verlet solutions.
result: The model recovers classical elasticity in the vanishing averaging-radius limit and the Griffith surface-energy coefficient for planar opening transitions, while maintaining an exact discrete energy balance.
conclusion: The approach provides a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation and is demonstrated on dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff-Winkler impact.

title: Waist Inequality And A Hurewicz-type Theorem For Mean Dimension
authors: Qiang Huo, Kangbo Ouyang, Ruxi Shi, Masaki Tsukamoto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a Hurewicz-type inequality relating mean dimension and conditional metric mean dimension. For every equivariant continuous map between dynamical systems, the mean dimension of the domain is bounded above by the sum of the mean dimension of the target and the conditional metric mean dimension of the map. In particular, any equivariant continuous map that decreases mean dimension must have infinite topological conditional entropy. The key ingredient is a new waist inequality, which we believe is of independent geometric interest beyond its application to dynamical systems. Compared with Gromov's original waist inequality, a distinctive feature of this inequality is that it applies to finite simplicial complexes of arbitrary topology, subject only to dimensional restrictions.
tldr: The paper proves a Hurewicz-type inequality relating mean dimension and conditional metric mean dimension via a new waist inequality for finite simplicial complexes.
motivation: The authors aim to establish dimension-theoretic bounds for equivariant continuous maps between dynamical systems and to generalize waist inequalities beyond Gromov's original setting.
method: They develop a new waist inequality applicable to finite simplicial complexes of arbitrary topology under dimensional restrictions, then use it to derive a Hurewicz-type inequality for mean dimension.
result: They show that the mean dimension of the domain is bounded by the sum of the target's mean dimension and the map's conditional metric mean dimension, implying that any equivariant map decreasing mean dimension has infinite topological conditional entropy.
conclusion: The work advances pure dynamical systems and geometric topology, with the new waist inequality potentially of independent geometric interest.

title: Watermark Evidence Under Open-Weight Llm Modification: Exact Bounds For Low-Rank Output Watermarks
authors: Prashant Shekhar, Dumindu Samaraweera, Caroline Howard
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.
tldr: The paper derives exact bounds on watermark evidence for open-weight LLM output watermarks under model modification such as quantization, pruning, and LoRA fine-tuning.
motivation: Open-weight language models can be modified after release, yet watermark verifiers still score outputs against the original models; the authors study how such modifications affect the reliability of OpenStamp-style detection.
method: They model modifications as residuals in next-token logits at shared prefixes and derive finite-vocabulary lower bounds, deviation bounds, covariance-based first-order evidence shifts, sequence-level conditional exponential-moment bounds, and a supermartingale plus order-statistic certification argument.
result: Experiments on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 show that INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain 85.6-94.8% true-positive rates, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning reduces them to 28.8% and 11.6%; covariance predictions track measured LoRA evidence drift with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 prefixes and zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical and empirical characterization of watermark robustness to model-editing attacks, yielding certified high-confidence bounds on miss probability after attack selection.

title: LLMs As Validators For Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level And Transaction-Level Attack Detection On Solana
authors: Yasir Rahman, Ishraq Samiha, Shahnewaz Karim Sakib, Anindya Bijoy Das
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.
tldr: This paper evaluates whether open-weight LLMs can diagnose vulnerabilities in Solana cross-chain bridge programs from source code and transaction records, distinguishing correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms.
motivation: Cross-chain bridges have lost substantial assets due to missing validation checks in on-chain programs, and it is unclear whether LLMs can genuinely diagnose such flaws rather than merely raise generic alarms.
method: The authors build a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants (two modeled on Cashio and Wormhole incidents, two from audit-documented vulnerability classes), pair vulnerable and secure programs with attack, benign, and blocked sessions, and evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses with two blinded LLM graders.
result: Without comments, models diagnose only 24% of vulnerable source inputs while often flagging the secure bridge; original comments raise source diagnosis to 60%, and transaction-level diagnosis is high only for the missing-signer scenario (averaging 6% for the other three).
conclusion: LLM-based bridge security review shows large condition-dependent variation, underscoring the need to separate correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms before such tools can be trusted as validators.

title: Eight In Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, An Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
authors: Ana Clara Zoppi Serpa, Anderson Rocha, H\'elio Pedrini
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.
tldr: A red-team study shows that most tested LLMs can be induced to leak a secret flag embedded in their system prompts.
motivation: The authors aim to audit how well instruction hierarchies are enforced across a large set of commercial text-in/text-out models and to identify which models disclose protected system-prompt secrets.
method: An AI agent steered by a human researcher attempts prompt-injection and persuasion attacks against 363 models, each guarding a 16-character secret flag; successful exfiltration techniques and language pivots are recorded.
result: The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of 363 initially tested models, plus four later-released models, yielding 300 captures; 170 captures involved a non-English language pivot, most often French.
conclusion: Practitioners should avoid storing secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model, and avoid relying solely on an LLM judge for consequential decisions.

title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise To A Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts With Matched Perturbations
authors: Ege Kaya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
tldr: A pre-registered study shows that 4-bit quantization can shift chat-model refusal behavior, but the direction and magnitude depend on the specific rounding error rather than bit-width or likelihood.
motivation: Chat models are often deployed as 4-bit quantized copies, and audits disagree about whether quantization affects safety refusal; the authors ask whether observed behavioral shifts are due to the specific rounding error or any perturbation of similar size.
method: The study evaluates three 3–4B chat models using paired tests, blind human labels, an 8-bit null condition, and matched perturbations including shuffled, Gaussian, mirrored, scaled, and llama.cpp Q4_K_M variants.
result: Two opposite-sign 4-bit shifts are found: Qwen2.5-3B more often continues harmful content under compliant prefill, while Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often on held-out jailbreaks; matched perturbations average near zero and scaled real error changes behavior near-linearly.
conclusion: Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not bits per weight or likelihood, so each quantized build must be compared with its original model.

title: Settling The Time And Structural Complexity Of Bertrand Networks
authors: Suho Shin Mohammadtaghi Hajiaghayi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the seminal Bertrand network game introduced by Babaioff et al. (2013), each seller posts a single price to captive buyers and to the markets it shares with neighboring sellers, where sellers cannot price discriminate across the markets. Although the existence of equilibria and polynomial-time algorithms to compute them in trees (Babaioff et al. (2013)) have been known, it has been a major open problem whether there exist efficient algorithms to compute them for general graphs. In this paper, we resolve this open question negatively by proving that computing any constant-error approximate Nash equilibrium in a Bertrand network is [MATH]-complete. This hardness holds even on sparse bipartite graphs of maximum degree five with constant integer market weights. Complementing our hardness result, we design an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) when both the maximum degree and the number of sellers with captive buyers are bounded. Beyond time complexity, since exact equilibria require randomizing prices over continuous intervals, another fundamental question left open by Babaioff et al. (2013) is whether an exact equilibrium can always be represented with a finite number of price intervals, \ie whether its structural complexity is finite. We resolve this question affirmatively by proving that every achievable equilibrium revenue profile can be realized by an equilibrium with structural complexity [MATH], which leads to an exact algorithm running in doubly exponential time. We further show that this bound is tight: there exist instances for which the unique equilibrium realizing target revenue profiles has structural complexity [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies the computational and structural complexity of equilibria in Bertrand network games, showing approximate equilibrium computation is hard and exact equilibria have finite interval complexity.
motivation: Bertrand networks model price competition among sellers in shared markets, and while equilibria are known for trees, efficient computation on general graphs and finite representation of exact equilibria were open problems.
method: The authors prove NP-hardness of computing constant-error approximate Nash equilibria on sparse bounded-degree bipartite graphs and design an EPTAS under bounded degree and captive-buyer sellers; they also bound the structural complexity of exact equilibria via price intervals.
result: Computing approximate equilibria is NP-hard in general, but tractable under additional restrictions; every achievable equilibrium revenue profile has finite structural complexity, with matching worst-case doubly exponential bounds.
conclusion: The paper resolves open questions on the time and structural complexity of Bertrand network equilibria, but it is an algorithmic game theory result with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation
authors: Jin Wei, Rundong Li, Li Ma, Yikai Wang, Ruihao Yang, Jianxiong Wu, Xiaoyuan Duan, Yanbo Wang, Runyu Mao, Chen Fang, Chang Xu, Ping Chen, Jun Dai, Xiaoyan Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.
tldr: TetherMark is a post-hoc image watermarking scheme that binds watermark evidence to a specific registered visual instance, preventing cross-instance transplantation attacks.
motivation: Existing watermark verification only checks message decodability or content consistency, so an attacker can transplant valid watermark evidence from one registered image to another of the same category.
method: The scheme combines a message check (edit-robust payload) with a relation check built on secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization; acceptance requires both checks.
result: Across 240 test subjects TetherMark reaches 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, giving the best instance-binding balanced accuracy.
conclusion: Instance-level relational checks close the cross-instance transplantation gap in robust watermarking, though the work is entirely in computer-vision security and unrelated to quantum information science.

title: From Constraints To Causality: Petri Net Encodings For Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
authors: Alex Chan (newcastle University), Mohamed Tarraf (newcastle University), Alex Yakovlev (newcastle University), Rishad Shafik
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained hardware and on-device components in autonomous systems. However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. Finally, we outline two directions this opens: a correctness-of-translation theorem, and a causal-trace analysis of where two trained BNNs diverge in their decisions, a structural question that constraint-based verifiers cannot express.
tldr: The paper encodes trained binary neural network inference as a 1-safe Petri net to produce causal firing-sequence traces explaining how decisions are reached.
motivation: Binary neural networks are hard to analyze and trust in safety-relevant settings, and existing SAT/SMT verification only says whether a property holds rather than how the computation reaches its result.
method: The authors give a compositional translation from BNN inference semantics to a 1-safe Petri net where each computation step is an explicit transition, and validate it on a worked example by exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation.
result: The Petri-net encoding is faithful in the worked example, and contrasting firing sequences localize where a single-feature change alters the prediction.
conclusion: The work proposes a discrete-event causal-trace view of BNN inference and outlines future directions for a correctness-of-translation theorem and divergence analysis between trained BNNs.

title: How Well Is My Artwork Protected? Predicting And Tailoring Protection Against Style Mimicry By Personalization
authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Sungwoo Hwang, Namhyuk Ahn
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protection tools add an imperceptible perturbation to each artwork so that a model personalized on it fails to imitate its style, and they apply one recipe, a protection method at a fixed strength, to every artwork. We find that the same recipe protects artworks very differently, well beyond the noise of personalization seeds, and that cheap signals predict this protection before any personalization. Because protection rises and falls together across recipes, our method, Patina, predicts the protection of every recipe from one short trial protection and gives each artwork the weakest recipe whose predicted protection reaches a chosen level. At the same level of visibility, Patina lets more artworks pass the protection threshold than any single recipe and warns the artist about artworks for which no recipe is predicted to pass it.
tldr: Patina predicts how well an adversarial style-protection perturbation will defend a given artwork against personalized style mimicry, and assigns each artwork the weakest recipe that still reaches a chosen protection level.
motivation: Existing protection tools apply a single fixed-strength recipe to every artwork, yet the same recipe protects different artworks very unevenly; artists need per-artwork prediction and tailoring of protection.
method: The authors show that cheap pre-personalization signals predict protection outcomes, and that protection levels rise and fall together across recipes, letting one short trial protection predict the protection of all recipes; Patina then picks the weakest recipe meeting a target protection level.
result: At equal visibility, Patina lets more artworks pass the protection threshold than any single recipe, and it flags artworks for which no recipe is predicted to succeed.
conclusion: Per-artwork prediction and recipe tailoring substantially improve the efficiency and reliability of style-mimicry protection for artists.

title: Provable Mixing Properties Of Parallel Mixnets Revisited
authors: Pierfrancesco Ingo, Peter Druschel, Deepak Garg
