abstract: ArXiv:2611.22732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A mix-network (mixnet) is a routing network that breaks source-to-destination message trackability by indistinguishably mixing the routes of concurrently transmitted messages, thus providing anonymity to senders, receivers and sender-receiver pairs. Given their potential use in high-stakes scenarios like protecting whistleblowers, one would like to prove formally that sender anonymity holds in a mixnet, even against strong adversaries that can compromise subsets of mixnet servers. However, existing work on anonymity in mixnets is either limited to linear mixnets (which do not scale horizontally), relies on special provisions such as additional noise or chaff messages, or is empirical -- typically based on entropy, which does not provide strong guarantees if the adversary has auxiliary information. In this paper, we present a new analysis of parallel mixnets which scale horizontally, showing that these networks can provide strong indistinguishability for messages even without additional noise messages. Our analysis works by bounding the statistical variance of the adversary's posterior likelihood of where a message of interest is at a given point in time. Using concentration bounds on this distribution, we show that parallel mixnets satisfy [MATH]-differential indistinguishability for messages routed through the mixnet (similar to [MATH]-differential privacy) with very small failure probabilities [MATH] and small privacy parameters [MATH] under reasonable operating conditions. Our model also enables an examination of the quantitative trade-off between anonymity, latency and per-router bandwidth in parallel mixnets.
tldr: The paper provides a new statistical analysis of parallel mixnets, showing they can achieve strong differential-indistinguishability guarantees for message anonymity without extra noise messages.
motivation: Mixnets are important for anonymity in high-stakes communication, but existing formal anonymity analyses are often limited to non-scalable linear mixnets, rely on additional noise/chaff, or use entropy-based empirical arguments that are weak under adversarial auxiliary information.
method: The authors bound the statistical variance of an adversary's posterior likelihood for a target message's location over time and apply concentration inequalities to derive differential-indistinguishability-style anonymity guarantees for parallel mixnets.
result: They show that parallel mixnets satisfy differential indistinguishability with very small failure probabilities and small privacy parameters under reasonable operating conditions, and analyze trade-offs among anonymity, latency, and per-router bandwidth.
conclusion: Parallel mixnets can provide provable strong anonymity without additional noise messages, and the proposed framework enables quantitative design trade-off analysis for scalable mixnet architectures.

title: Backward-scattering Photoelectron Holography Of A Polar Molecule Driven By A Sub-cycle Laser Pulse
authors: Eiji J. Takahashi Rambabu Rajpoot
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate photoelectron holographic interference in the polar CO molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse using time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation simulations and a classical-trajectory-based analysis. The sub-cycle temporal confinement of the driving field enables the forward-scattering holographic (FSH) and backward-scattering holographic (BSH) interference structures in the photoelectron momentum distributions (PMDs) to be clearly distinguished. The FSH fringes exhibit a strong dependence on molecular orientation, which is associated with the orientation-dependent transverse displacement of the ionizing electron wave packet (EWP). Furthermore, the heteronuclear nature of CO results in different FSH fringe shifts for ionization occurring predominantly from the C and O sides of the molecule. In contrast, the curved interference structures in the negative parallel-momentum region are identified as BSH interference arising from the coherent superposition of direct and backward-scattered EWPs. The BSH fringe positions show weak dependence on molecular orientation and remain clearly visible after orientation averaging. We further show that BSH visibility depends on the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) and that the fringes remain discernible after CEP averaging. Moreover, the BSH interference pattern exhibits a systematic dependence on the internuclear separation, demonstrating its sensitivity to molecular geometry. These results highlight the potential of sub-cycle pulse enabled backward-scattering photoelectron holography for probing molecular structure and demonstrate its robustness against molecularorientation and CEP averaging.
tldr: Time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulations and classical-trajectory analysis show that sub-cycle laser pulses allow forward- and backward-scattering photoelectron holography to be separated, with the backward-scattering fringes being robust against molecular-orientation and CEP averaging.
motivation: Photoelectron holography encodes molecular structure in interference fringes, but overlapping forward- and backward-scattering contributions and orientation/CEP averaging typically wash out the signal; the authors aim to isolate backward-scattering holography using few-cycle temporal confinement.
method: Numerical TDSE simulations of the polar CO molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser field, complemented by a classical-trajectory-based analysis of direct and rescattered electron wave packets.
result: Forward-scattering fringes depend strongly on molecular orientation and on which atomic centre ionizes, whereas backward-scattering interference in the negative parallel-momentum region is weakly orientation-dependent, survives orientation and CEP averaging, and varies systematically with internuclear separation.
conclusion: Sub-cycle-pulse backward-scattering photoelectron holography is a robust route to probing molecular geometry, resilient to experimental averaging effects.

title: Finite Volume Neural Networks For Singularly Perturbed Boundary Value Problems
authors: Junghwa Kim Gung-Min Gie
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a singular-layer enhanced Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) methodology for solving singularly perturbed boundary value problems. The proposed framework combines flux-conserving finite volume residuals with analytically derived boundary layer correctors, enabling stable and efficient approximation of sharp boundary variations induced by small perturbation parameters. Numerical experiments over a broad range of small perturbation parameters ([MATH] to [MATH]), demonstrate that the sl-FVNN yields uniformly accurate predicted solutions and significantly improved convergence behavior compared to conventional FVNN methods. Further comparisons with sl-PINNs from (Gie, Hong, Jung, Appl. Anal. 2024) show that our sl-FVNNs attain comparable accuracy for reaction--diffusion and Burgers equations, while achieving significantly improved convergence for convection-dominated nonlinear problems. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating asymptotic layer structures into finite volume based neural networks, offering a practical and scalable framework for multiscale PDE learning in stiff regimes.
tldr: The paper introduces singular-layer enhanced Finite Volume Neural Networks (sl-FVNNs) for solving singularly perturbed boundary value problems with sharp boundary layers.
motivation: Standard neural network PDE solvers struggle with stiff multiscale problems where small perturbation parameters create thin boundary layers, so the authors aim to incorporate asymptotic layer structure directly into the solver.
method: The approach combines flux-conserving finite volume residuals with analytically derived boundary layer correctors in a neural network framework, and compares against conventional FVNNs and singularly perturbed PINNs.
result: Numerical experiments across a broad range of small perturbation parameters show uniformly accurate solutions and improved convergence, especially for convection-dominated nonlinear problems.
conclusion: Embedding asymptotic layer structures into finite volume neural networks provides a practical and scalable framework for multiscale PDE learning in stiff regimes.

title: Weak Error Estimates Of A Spectral Galerkin Approximation To The Stochastic Burgers Equation Driven By Rough White Noise
authors: Minxing Zhang, Yongkui Zou, Yanzhao Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate weak error estimates for a spectral Galerkin approximation to a stochastic Burgers equation driven by rough space-time white noise. The roughness of the driving noise results that the mild solution possesses only [MATH]-regularity rather than any positive-order differentiability order regularity. The theory of classical numerical analysis reveals that the convergence rate of numerical solution is determined by the smoothness of the exact solution, and hence [MATH]-regularity is insufficient to yield any positive convergence rate. Indeed, De Vecchi et al.\ studied a spectral Galerkin approximation to such equation and only proved pathwise convergence. However, we aim to derive positive weak convergence rate for the spectral Galerkin approximation, which is determined by the roughness order of noise. To overcome the difficulty caused by the absence of smoothness of the exact solution, we turn to study the differentiability regularity of the first and second order Fr\'echet derivatives of the solution to a Kolmogorov equation associated with the spectral Galerkin approximation. We manage to prove that they possess nearly second order smoothness, enabling us to derive a positive weak convergence rate for the spectral Galerkin approximation. Finally, we conduct a numerical experiment to illustrate the theortical analysis.
tldr: The paper derives weak error estimates for a spectral Galerkin approximation of the stochastic Burgers equation driven by rough space-time white noise.
motivation: Classical numerical analysis yields no positive convergence rate when the solution has only negative-order regularity due to rough noise, so the authors seek positive weak convergence rates.
method: They analyze Fréchet derivatives of the solution to an associated Kolmogorov equation for the spectral Galerkin approximation, establishing nearly second-order smoothness.
result: They prove a positive weak convergence rate determined by the roughness order of the noise and support it with a numerical experiment.
conclusion: The work extends numerical analysis for rough stochastic PDEs by overcoming regularity obstructions through Kolmogorov-equation differentiability estimates.

title: A Locking-free Enriched Linearized Neural Network For Linear Elasticity
authors: Young Ju Lee Bonyong Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural-network Galerkin methods suffer from volumetric locking in nearly incompressible elasticity. We propose the locking-free enriched linearized neural network (LF-ENN), to the best of our knowledge, the first neural-network Galerkin method proved to be locking-free. Following the enriched Galerkin (EG) method of Yi, Lee and Zikatanov (2022), for finite [MATH] it admits a displacement-only formulation whose trial space is a linearized neural network enriched by one dilation field per element of an auxiliary mesh. The parameter [MATH] enters only through a piecewise constant discrete divergence, whose action on the dilation fields is the graph Laplacian of the dual graph of the mesh. Hence any conforming field can be made discretely divergence-free, and the error is bounded independently of [MATH]. The network needs no boundary factor: the Dirichlet condition is imposed weakly by Nitsche's method, and a Galerkin least-squares term on the shear part, as in ENN, together with a Hessian penalty on the elements along the traction boundary, replaces the trace inequality that networks lack. Under the stated approximation and quasi-uniformity assumptions, the discrete stability and error-estimate constants are independent of network width, mesh size, and [MATH], for both clamped and mixed boundary conditions. For solutions with reduced regularity, we establish an error estimate of order [MATH] under the assumptions [MATH] and [MATH], with [MATH]. Numerical experiments, including Cook's membrane, demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in the presence of boundary singularities.
tldr: The paper proposes a locking-free enriched linearized neural network Galerkin method for linear elasticity, with error bounds independent of the incompressibility parameter.
motivation: Neural-network Galerkin methods suffer from volumetric locking in nearly incompressible elasticity, motivating a method that avoids locking while retaining neural-network trial spaces.
method: The authors construct a displacement-only enriched neural-network formulation using a piecewise constant discrete divergence on an auxiliary mesh, weak Nitsche boundary conditions, and Galerkin least-squares stabilization.
result: They prove stability and error estimates independent of network width, mesh size, and the incompressibility parameter, and demonstrate effectiveness numerically including Cook's membrane.
conclusion: The LF-ENN provides a locking-free neural-network Galerkin approach for linear elasticity, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Forensic Analysis Of Metadata And Information Leakage In Swedish Public Documents
authors: Noor Abo Hasan, Kajsa Linderoth, Monia L\"onn
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates metadata and structural content leakage in publicly available PDF documents from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities. Using an automated collection pipeline and ExifTool-based extraction, 2,876 documents were analyzed and classified using an R0-R3 risk taxonomy. Results reveal that 48.4% of documents exhibit significant metadata exposure (R2 or R3), with significant variation across institutional tiers (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis across three legislative periods reveals a statistically significant reduction in metadata exposure between the baseline and post-enactment periods, yet 44.9% of documents published after the enactment of the Swedish Cybers\"akerhetslagen continue to leak sensitive metadata. Furthermore, 41.6% of documents contain incremental update layers; forensic analysis recovered verifiable text alterations, including deleted personal data and internal identifiers, from 228 of these cases. These findings highlight persistent regulatory lag and a systemic reliance on default, unsanitized document publication workflows within the Swedish public sector.
tldr: The paper analyzes metadata and structural information leakage in 2,876 Swedish public-sector PDF documents, finding widespread unsanitized metadata and recoverable incremental update content despite regulatory efforts.
motivation: Public documents may unintentionally expose sensitive metadata or hidden text through default publication workflows, creating privacy and security risks. The authors aim to quantify this leakage across Swedish authorities and assess the impact of cybersecurity legislation.
method: They built an automated collection pipeline and used ExifTool-based extraction to analyze PDFs from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities, classifying exposure with an R0-R3 risk taxonomy and performing forensic recovery of incremental update layers.
result: 48.4% of documents showed significant metadata exposure, with variation across institutional tiers; 44.9% of post-enactment documents still leaked sensitive metadata, and 41.6% contained incremental update layers, with 228 cases yielding recoverable deleted text or internal identifiers.
conclusion: The findings indicate persistent regulatory lag and systemic reliance on default document publication workflows, highlighting the need for better metadata sanitization in public-sector document handling.

title: Exploiting Aggregate Feedback For Decentralized Equilibrium Learning In Markov Games: A Smart Grid Application
authors: Siying Huang, Yifen Mu, Ge Chen, Qingshan Jia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many multi-agent systems, an agent's payoff depends on its own action and an aggregate of other agents' actions, rather than their individual decisions. This paper investigates decentralized equilibrium learning in Markov games (MGs) with such aggregative reward structures. However, existing decentralized learning algorithms for general MGs typically rely on bandit feedback, without exploiting the additional information available from aggregate observations. To exploit this information, we develop an aggregation-predictive stage-based V-learning algorithm with hybrid-feedback Exp3-IX. Using known local reward functions and observed aggregate quantities, each agent evaluates the immediate rewards of all candidate actions and predicts their immediate losses from historical aggregate feedback, while continuation values are learned from selected-action state transitions. The algorithm requires neither opponents' individual information nor knowledge of the transition kernel. We establish a high-probability regret bound that explicitly depends on aggregate prediction errors and retains the standard worst-case order. Under a regularity condition on adaptive stage lengths, the algorithm learns an [MATH]-approximate coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) within [MATH] episodes and extends to correlated equilibrium (CE) learning. We further apply the algorithm to a renewable-rich microgrid with strategic prosumers and shared energy storage. Numerical results show smaller deviation gaps and lower gap-AUC than three learning baselines. Compared with representative demand-response rules, the learned policies exhibit weaker incentives for unilateral deviations while maintaining favorable user rewards, high renewable utilization, and relatively stable electricity prices.
tldr: The paper develops a decentralized equilibrium-learning algorithm for Markov games with aggregative rewards and applies it to a smart-grid energy-management setting.
motivation: Multi-agent systems often have payoffs that depend on aggregate behavior rather than individual opponent actions, but existing decentralized Markov-game learning algorithms typically ignore useful aggregate feedback.
method: The authors propose an aggregation-predictive stage-based V-learning algorithm with hybrid-feedback Exp3-IX, using local rewards and aggregate observations to predict immediate losses while learning continuation values from selected-action transitions.
result: They derive a high-probability regret bound depending on aggregate prediction error and show learning of approximate coarse correlated equilibrium, with numerical improvements over baselines in a renewable-rich microgrid application.
conclusion: Aggregate feedback can be exploited to improve decentralized equilibrium learning in aggregative Markov games, with a demonstrated application to strategic prosumers and shared energy storage.

title: Convergence Of Discrete Exterior Calculus For The Hodge-Dirac And Hodge-Laplace Problems On Surfaces
authors: Thomas A. Wasserman
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that discrete exterior calculus converges for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on every closed oriented Riemannian surface. The proof applies the error bounds of a companion paper on finite element exterior calculus. We prove and use that every closed oriented surface, with any metric, carries uniformly regular families of triangulations that are acute with a uniform margin.
tldr: The paper proves convergence of discrete exterior calculus for Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on closed oriented Riemannian surfaces.
motivation: Discrete exterior calculus is a numerical framework for geometric PDEs, but convergence guarantees for Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on general surfaces have been lacking.
method: The author applies error bounds from finite element exterior calculus and constructs uniformly regular acute triangulations for any closed oriented surface with any metric.
result: Convergence is established for both the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on every closed oriented Riemannian surface.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous convergence foundation for discrete exterior calculus on surfaces, supported by the existence of suitably regular acute triangulations.

title: Finite Sample Guarantees Of Mppi: Suboptimality, Sample Complexity And Closed-loop Guarantees
authors: Changyi Lei, Dragan Nesic, Ye Pu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers model predictive path integral (MPPI) control for nonlinear finite-horizon optimal control problems with bounded inputs, allowing nonconvex and nonsmooth costs. We prove theoretical guarantees that quantify the suboptimality caused by positive temperature and finite sampling on MPPI and establish their implications for closed-loop guarantees. Specifically, we derive a suboptimality bound for infinite-sample MPPI that characterizes the effects of temperature and prior coverage, followed by a high-probability finite-sample approximation error bound that reveals the dependence on sample size, temperature, and cost variability. By incorporating these bounds into a terminal-constraint-free MPC framework, we further establish semi-global practical recurrence of the closed-loop system. Numerical examples involving a four-link planar manipulator illustrate the temperature-sampling tradeoff and the influence of prior quality on approximation accuracy and closed-loop performance.
tldr: The paper derives suboptimality and finite-sample approximation-error bounds for model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, and uses them to establish semi-global practical recurrence of the closed-loop system.
motivation: MPPI is widely used for nonlinear, nonconvex optimal control with bounded inputs, but its performance guarantees under finite sampling and nonzero temperature were largely heuristic rather than theoretically characterized.
method: The authors prove an infinite-sample suboptimality bound capturing temperature and prior-coverage effects, then a high-probability finite-sample error bound depending on sample size, temperature, and cost variability, which is embedded in a terminal-constraint-free MPC framework.
result: The bounds yield semi-global practical recurrence for the closed loop, and four-link planar manipulator simulations illustrate the temperature–sampling tradeoff and the impact of prior quality on accuracy.
conclusion: MPPI's stochastic sampling and temperature can be traded off with quantified performance losses, providing rigorous closed-loop guarantees for a practical sampling-based control scheme.

title: An Explicit Parallelizable Robin-Robin Splitting Scheme For Navier-Stokes-Naghdi Shell Interaction
authors: Yifan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a novel explicit Robin-Robin splitting scheme for the system of an incompressible viscous fluid coupled to a time dependent Naghdi shell model. The shell model includes three displacement components and three independent rotation components, accounting for membrane, bending, and transverse-shear deformations. Both Robin conditions depend only on interface data from the previous time step, allowing the fluid and shell subproblems to be solved independently without coupling subiterations. For the fixed-domain Stokes-Naghdi problem, we derive a discrete energy identity that incorporates shell rotational inertia, interface velocities, and interface loads. We prove that the scheme is unconditionally stable for any fixed positive common Robin coefficient under homogeneous external data. Under suitable regularity and initialization assumptions, we establish first-order consistency and an [MATH] temporal error bound in the mechanical energy norm. Numerical experiments with a moving-domain pressure pulse compare the proposed scheme with the kinematically coupled [MATH]-scheme and a monolithic solver. To demonstrate its applicability to a more realistic vascular configuration, we simulate a stented artery using a bonded layered shell with stiff strut bands, capturing spatial variations in the arterial wall response.
tldr: The paper proposes an explicit, parallelizable Robin-Robin splitting scheme for coupling an incompressible viscous fluid to a time-dependent Naghdi shell, with proven unconditional stability and first-order temporal accuracy.
motivation: Fluid-structure interaction with thin shell models is computationally demanding because monolithic solvers require expensive coupling iterations; the authors seek a decoupled, easily parallelized scheme with rigorous stability guarantees.
method: Both fluid and shell subproblems are equipped with Robin interface conditions built only from previous-time-step interface data, enabling independent solves; a discrete energy identity is derived and stability, consistency, and error bounds are proven for the fixed-domain Stokes-Naghdi case.
result: The scheme is unconditionally stable for any fixed positive common Robin coefficient under homogeneous data, achieves first-order consistency and an O(dt) temporal error bound in the mechanical energy norm; numerical tests on a moving-domain pressure pulse and a stented artery validate the approach against the kinematically coupled scheme and a monolithic solver.
conclusion: The explicit Robin-Robin splitting provides a stable, accurate, and parallel-friendly alternative for realistic vascular fluid-shell simulations.

title: The Critical Time For Local Controllability Of A Water Tank
authors: Zhaobo Liu Feizheng Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the critical time for local controllability near equilibrium of a water tank governed by the one-dimensional Saint-Venant equations and controlled by its horizontal acceleration. With [MATH] fluid trajectories and continuous controls, local controllability holds exactly for [MATH]. In normalized units, [MATH], where [MATH] is determined by two transcendental equations. In particular, local controllability fails for [MATH]. For times just above [MATH], we construct a control that cancels the linear and quadratic terms of the endpoint expansion and apply a fixed point argument. At [MATH], a weighted comparison with a critical plane curve, combined with estimates along the nonlinear characteristics, gives the obstruction.
tldr: The paper determines the exact critical time threshold for local controllability of a one-dimensional water tank described by the Saint-Venant equations under horizontal acceleration control.
motivation: Local controllability of nonlinear hyperbolic systems near equilibrium depends sensitively on the control time horizon, and precise critical-time characterizations are rare; the authors aim to pin down this threshold for a shallow-water tank model.
method: Using fluid trajectories and continuous controls, the authors construct controls that cancel linear and quadratic terms in the endpoint expansion and apply a fixed-point argument just above the critical time, while at the critical time a weighted comparison with a critical plane curve plus estimates along nonlinear characteristics yields an obstruction.
result: Local controllability holds exactly for times above a critical value T* given in normalized units by two transcendental equations, and fails at and below T*.
conclusion: The critical time for local controllability of the water-tank system is fully characterized, providing a sharp threshold separating controllable from non-controllable regimes.

title: Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing For Micropayments
authors: Guru-Vamsi Policharla Patrick O'grady
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.
tldr: Bajillion is a cryptographic clearing protocol for scalable micropayments using signed payment requests, operator preconfirmations, and periodic on-chain net settlement.
motivation: Web funding via advertising may decline as AI agents browse on behalf of humans, motivating agent-to-service micropayments at potentially hundreds of millions of payments per second.
method: A sender signs a payment request and an untrusted operator returns a preconfirmation; epochs are closed on chain by posting only net balances, with accountability enforced cryptographically.
result: The protocol ensures a malicious operator can only omit payments, cannot over-debit senders or misdirect transfers, and enables immediate finalization and withdrawal of posted balances.
conclusion: Bajillion provides an accountable clearing design for high-throughput micropayments, but it is a classical cryptographic/payment-systems contribution unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become A Privacy Risk
authors: Chaklam Cheong, Tiancong Cao, Qi Li, Zelin Zhang, Jianbing Ni, Rongxing Lu, Mohammad Zulkernine
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.
tldr: GapLeak identifies and mitigates a privacy vulnerability in LLM-based web agents where agents escalate to reachable but unauthorized higher-sensitivity data sources to fill information gaps in legitimate web forms.
motivation: Existing privacy safeguards for LLM web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege, which constrain authorized sources but not other reachable high-sensitivity sources, leaving a gap an adversary can exploit without prompt injection.
method: The authors formalize the GapLeak vulnerability, evaluate it across three web-agent frameworks and six commercial LLMs in recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare domains, and propose submission-time verification that filters unauthorized content before form submission.
result: GapLeak induces roughly 37% average unauthorized disclosure, with the information gap as the primary driver (eliminating it cuts disclosure by over 50%); submission-time verification removes over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.
conclusion: Least-privilege instruction-level defenses are insufficient for LLM web-agent privacy; architectural submission-time verification offers a robust mitigation without sacrificing utility.

title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks On LLM-Controlled Social Robots
authors: Stanley Akingbola, Ugbede Ibrahim, Yan Lin Aung, Quang Dan Le, Hong Qing Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper demonstrates network-exposed configuration attacks against an LLM-controlled social robot (Reachy Mini Lite), showing that unauthenticated attackers can replace personality settings and system prompts without any adversarial conversational input.
motivation: Embodied LLM robots introduce security dependencies beyond inference, and the authors investigate whether inference-layer refusal alone can protect against unauthorized modification of model instructions through management interfaces.
method: They perform hands-on testing on physical Reachy Mini Lite hardware, attempting eleven prompt injections across five categories alongside configuration-layer attacks via local and network-adjacent access, map weaknesses to CWE-306, CWE-1327, and CWE-352, and conduct a source review of 59 public repositories.
result: Prompt-injection attempts were reportedly resisted, but both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioral changes on hardware, with missing authentication found in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications (11 of 11 including a framework-default case).
conclusion: The authors characterize a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security, warning of surveillance and social-engineering risks, but noting the findings indicate recurrence in sampled repositories rather than commercial prevalence.

title: Hill's Lunar Equation As A Leaf: Riccati Reduction And Frobenius Theory For Second-Order PDEs
authors: Bruno Sc\'ardua V\'ictor Le\'on
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The equations of Hill and Adams for the lunar perigee and node, Mathieu's equation and Lam\'e's equation arise as leafwise restrictions of one class of linear partial differential equations, the [MATH], where [MATH] is an analytic vector field and [MATH] are analytic functions. Such an equation has a regular singularity exactly when the foliation defined by [MATH] is analytically linearizable. At rational saddles, where every point of the indicial conic is resonant, we obtain convergent solutions whose exponents are holomorphic functions of a first integral; their variation describes the monodromy along the leaves and decides when classical Frobenius solutions exist. For a Hill equation, the characteristic exponent becomes the value of such a holomorphic function, given by a convergent series. This yields rigorous computer-assisted proofs of Hill's constant for the motion of the lunar perigee and of Adams' constant for the motion of the node: Hill's value is confirmed within his own error estimate and its fifteenth decimal is determined, his value of the motion of the perigee is shown to be correct in all its digits, and Adams' value is confirmed to twelve decimals. For Mathieu's equation, the curves of constant characteristic exponent that govern ion trapping appear as classical Frobenius loci. For Lam\'e's equation, we prove a product formula for the logarithmic obstructions, which coincide with the leading coefficients of the eigenvalue splittings computed by Volkmer and whose vanishing reflects the finite-gap property.
tldr: The paper studies Hill's lunar equation, Adams' node equation, Mathieu's equation, and Lamé's equation as leafwise restrictions of a class of second-order linear PDEs, using Riccati reduction and Frobenius theory to obtain rigorous constants and monodromy results.
motivation: The authors aim to unify several classical second-order differential equations under a common analytic foliation framework and to provide rigorous computer-assisted proofs of historical lunar constants.
method: They analyze a linear PDE defined by an analytic vector field, characterize regular singularities through analytic linearizability of the foliation, and use resonant rational saddles, holomorphic first integrals, and monodromy to determine Frobenius solutions.
result: The framework yields rigorous proofs of Hill's constant for lunar perigee motion, Adams' constant for lunar node motion, and Frobenius-locus interpretations for Mathieu and Lamé equations.
conclusion: The paper demonstrates that classical equations such as Hill's, Mathieu's, and Lamé's arise naturally as leafwise restrictions and that their special solutions and constants can be understood via foliation, monodromy, and Frobenius theory.

title: Polylogarithmic Regret Via Certainty Equivalence In Degenerate Lqr
authors: Luca Vignola, Melanie Zeilinger, Bruce D. Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves [MATH] expected regret over [MATH] interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an [MATH] minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.
tldr: This paper studies online linear quadratic control with singular input penalties and shows that certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret under weaker identifiability conditions.
motivation: Positive definite input penalties impose restrictive identifiability requirements for certainty-equivalence algorithms in online LQR, so the authors seek relaxed conditions via singular input penalties.
method: They analyze a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase and prove expected regret bounds, complemented by a minimax lower bound for a case where controller identifiability fails.
result: The main result is polylogarithmic expected regret whenever controller identifiability holds; for minimum variance control, knowing only the range of the input matrix suffices, covering underactuated systems.
conclusion: Singular input penalties broaden the class of online LQR problems where certainty equivalence attains polylogarithmic regret, including underactuated examples such as cart-pole.

title: B-Series Theory For Continuous Time Integration Methods
authors: Adrian Sandu Reid J. Gomillion
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: B-Series are a common tool for constructing numerical integration methods and partitioned variations. In this paper, we expand the operations of B-Series to describe the formal expansion of modified differential equations found in multirate ODE solvers. Typically, such modified differential equations have time dependent approximations using summed fixed constant states. To create the B-Series we introduce a new operation called replacement to induce the constant states and add a time parameterization to the labels of the B-Series. By doing so we introduce new analysis via the permanent and block matrices which provide alternative formulations to composition and substitution. To support the time dependent labels properties are provided, the exact solution is described in Tree Iterated Integrals, and the underlying approximate representations are analyzed.
tldr: The paper extends B-series algebra with a 'replacement' operation and time-dependent labels to formally analyze modified differential equations arising in multirate ODE solvers.
motivation: Multirate ODE solvers generate modified differential equations with time-dependent approximations built from summed constant states, which existing B-series formalisms cannot describe directly.
method: The authors introduce a replacement operation to induce constant states, add time parameterization to B-series labels, and develop new analysis tools via permanent and block matrices giving alternative formulations of composition and substitution.
result: Time-dependent label properties are established, the exact solution is expressed in terms of Tree Iterated Integrals, and the underlying approximate representations are analyzed.
conclusion: The extended B-series framework provides a rigorous algebraic foundation for analyzing modified equations in multirate numerical integration, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Ocp: A Greedy Projection Method For Row-sparse Representations Of Minimum-norm Solutions
authors: Tao Li, Deanna Needell, Qing-Wen Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a greedy projection method, termed orthogonal constraint pursuit (OCP), for identifying a small set of rows of a consistent linear system [MATH] whose span contains the minimum-norm solution [MATH], along with the coefficients of that representation. The method successively activates the most violated constraint, and then projects the iterate onto the intersection of all activated constraints. We prove that OCP is equivalent to OMP applied to the dictionary [MATH] and the signal [MATH], and that it terminates in at most rank(A) iterations. When [MATH] is a linear combination of [MATH] rows of a matrix whose rows are independent and uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, OCP identifies those rows in exactly [MATH] iterations with probability [MATH], provided that [MATH] for a sufficiently large constant [MATH]. We also derive a variant of OCP with constraint removal for hard-margin support vector machines with regularized bias, which returns the support vectors, along with the multipliers that satisfy the KKT conditions. Numerical results on both real and synthetic problems demonstrate the identification of representing rows and the regime in which it is competitive with Krylov subspace methods.
tldr: The paper introduces orthogonal constraint pursuit (OCP), a greedy projection algorithm for finding row-sparse representations of minimum-norm solutions to consistent linear systems.
motivation: The authors aim to efficiently identify a small subset of rows whose span contains the minimum-norm solution of a linear system, with applications to support vector machines and sparse recovery.
method: OCP successively activates the most violated constraint and projects onto the intersection of activated constraints; it is shown equivalent to OMP on a derived dictionary and signal, and a constraint-removal variant is developed for hard-margin SVMs with regularized bias.
result: OCP terminates in at most rank(A) iterations and, under random row models, identifies the representing rows in exactly the target number of iterations with high probability given sufficient samples; numerical experiments demonstrate competitiveness with Krylov methods.
conclusion: OCP provides a greedy projection framework for row-sparse minimum-norm representations and extends to SVM support-vector identification via KKT conditions.

title: Anytime-valid Inference For Conditional Hazard And Survival Functions With Streaming Data
authors: Valentin Patilea Eni Musta
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the nonparametric estimation of the conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions of a time-to-event variable from streaming data subject to censoring, truncation, or a cure fraction. A time-to-event model is a map from the distribution of the latent variables to that of the observed ones. For a large class of models this map has an explicit inverse, and the conditional hazard is the ratio of the density of the exactly observed durations to an at-risk function. Both are estimated by one-pass learners, in which each observation contributes once and is never revised, such as recursive kernel, series and histogram estimators. Our main result is an asymptotic confidence band sequence for the conditional hazard at a fixed covariate value, uniform in time and in the sample size, which allows monitoring after a burn-in, and stopping at a data-dependent time. The band can shrink at the optimal uniform rate up to a logarithmic factor. Bands for the cumulative hazard and the survival function follow. In simulations, a fixed-sample band inspected repeatedly fails in about half of the streams, while the miscoverage of the recommended bands stays below, or close to, the nominal level.
tldr: The paper develops anytime-valid, nonparametric confidence band sequences for conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions estimated from censored/truncated streaming data.
motivation: Classical fixed-sample survival-analysis confidence bands lose validity when data arrive as a stream and are inspected repeatedly, so a sequential, uniform-in-time inference framework is needed.
method: The conditional hazard is expressed as the ratio of the density of exactly observed durations to an at-risk function, both estimated by one-pass recursive kernel, series or histogram learners; an asymptotic confidence band sequence uniform in time and sample size is derived.
result: The proposed bands attain the optimal uniform rate up to a logarithmic factor, support data-dependent stopping after a burn-in, and in simulations keep miscoverage near nominal levels while repeated inspection of fixed-sample bands fails in roughly half the streams.
conclusion: Anytime-valid inference provides a principled and practical alternative to fixed-sample survival bands for streaming time-to-event data.

title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition For Power System Fault And Attack Diagnosis
authors: S M Zia Ur Rashid, Sazidul Islam Hira, Rupesh Sah, Suman Rath
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.
tldr: ActiGrid benchmarks active evidence acquisition for cyber-physical power system fault and attack diagnosis, finding that learned DQN policies do not outperform simpler stopping rules or compact subset classifiers.
motivation: Diagnostic models often inspect all telemetry sources even when only a subset is needed, so the paper asks whether a learned policy for selectively acquiring evidence is worth the added complexity.
method: The authors introduce ActiGrid, combining a classifier tolerant to missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network that decides whether to request another telemetry source or stop and diagnose, and compare it against fixed subsets/orders, entropy stopping, greedy value-of-information, and per-subset tree ensembles on two public benchmarks.
result: The learned policy adapts to observations but is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL; entropy stopping over compact subset classifiers achieves the best mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of sources) but no saving over a static three-source subset on MSU/ORNL.
conclusion: Selective acquisition can help, but on these benchmarks a learned policy is unnecessary; simpler subset classifiers and entropy stopping are preferable to the DQN approach.

title: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots Vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception?
authors: Pedro Beltr\'an-L\'opez, Raul Gonzalez Jimenez, Dario Maddaloni, Manuel Gil P\'erez, Pantaleone Nespoli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable honeypots to generate responses and deceptive artefacts on demand, yet existing approaches evaluate generated content one reply at a time and leave open whether artefacts that jointly describe a coherent event retain an attacker better than unrelated ones. This question becomes pressing as autonomous LLM-driven offensive agents emerge as realistic adversaries. This paper proposes narrative deception, a reactive strategy in which the defender maps each observed attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, selects a compatible scenario from a curated catalogue based on MITRE Engage, and deploys mutually referential artefacts (files, processes, services, and logs) on an emulated Ubuntu host while the intrusion is under way. An LLM-powered defender and an autonomous LLM attacker interact through a real SSH session, and the attacker's termination policy distinguishes abandonment due to suspected deception from abandonment due to loss of interest. A campaign of 1,150 sessions compares four conditions of increasing sophistication (Static, Same-TTP, Multi-TTP, and Chain) across four open-weight attacker models, four defender models, and three attacker skill levels. Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.
tldr: The paper studies whether narrative-coherent LLM-generated honeypot artefacts improve attacker engagement compared with unrelated artefacts.
motivation: LLM-driven honeypots and autonomous LLM attackers are emerging, but prior evaluations focus on single responses rather than coherent multi-artefact deception campaigns.
method: The authors implement a reactive defender that maps SSH attacker commands to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, selects MITRE Engage scenarios, and deploys mutually referential artefacts during an intrusion; they compare four deception conditions over 1,150 sessions with multiple attacker and defender models.
result: Coherent scenarios significantly increase engagement, raising median session length for advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reducing abandonment from 86% to 52%, with effects consistent across model pairs and skill levels.
conclusion: Narrative coherence materially improves LLM-driven honeypot deception, and most sessions end through loss of interest rather than deception detection, suggesting defenders should sustain plausible findings rather than only emulator fidelity.

title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
authors: Steven Yu Tung, Shubham Vaijanath Phoolari, Christoph Lauer, Abhinav Valada, Steven Peters
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.
tldr: The paper introduces CaFe, a causally faithful conditional traffic scenario generator that prevents private language instructions from leaking to surrounding agents in closed-loop traffic simulation.
motivation: Language-conditioned traffic simulation can leak private intent across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react prematurely and undermining the intended test scenario, but existing benchmarks do not measure what uninstructed agents could have known.
method: The authors formalize intent leakage, propose a paired intervention test holding an instructed agent's trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, build the WOMD-PACT dataset with timed behavior tags and counterfactual ghost tests, and develop CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop to restrict inter-agent interactions to public beliefs.
result: Existing conditioning designs displace 23–83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage even when the instructed agent's motion is fixed, while CaFe eliminates measurable leakage and maintains comparable WOSAC realism at 0.763.
conclusion: Causal faithfulness can be enforced in language-conditioned traffic simulation without sacrificing measured realism, providing a new evaluation, dataset, and modeling approach for leakage-free scenario generation.

title: Different Stories: European Astronomy As A Tool Of Colonization In The Americas And Hawai'i
authors: D. Lussier Gregg A. Wade
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The history of Western astronomy is frequently told as a story of discovery, technological innovation, and human progress. Yet the astronomical knowledge, instruments, and techniques associated with these achievements also contributed to European colonial expansion. Through four material and visual examples - a marine chronometer, an astronomical surveying quadrant, the Nautical Almanac, and contemporary observatories on Maunakea - we invite reconsideration of astronomy's relationships with navigation, territorial mapping, colonial authority, and Indigenous lands. How might these histories be told differently when considered through Indigenous Knowledges and Perspectives? What might such reconsideration reveal about the continuing relationships between astronomy, colonialism, and place?
tldr: A history-of-science essay arguing that European astronomy and its instruments functioned as tools of colonial expansion in the Americas and Hawai'i.
motivation: The authors challenge the standard narrative of astronomy as pure discovery and progress, aiming to surface its entanglement with navigation, territorial mapping, colonial authority, and Indigenous lands.
method: Humanities/scholarship approach: close reading of four material and visual case studies (a marine chronometer, an astronomical surveying quadrant, the Nautical Almanac, and observatories on Maunakea), framed through Indigenous Knowledges and Perspectives.
result: The examples are shown to link astronomical practice to navigation, land survey, and the occupation of Indigenous sites, prompting alternative tellings of astronomy's history.
conclusion: The paper calls for reckoning with astronomy's colonial legacies, including ongoing relationships between observatories, colonialism, and place such as Maunakea.

title: Decision-Weighted Limit Theorems: Less Conservative Robust Optimization
authors: Dimitris Bertsimas, Danique de Moor, Dick Den Hertog, Federica Donnini
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Limit theorems provide a natural way to construct tractable models for optimization under uncertainty. Existing approaches typically apply them to unweighted sums of uncertain parameters and use the resulting bounds to construct uncertainty sets. We show that sharper formulations are obtained by applying limit theorems directly to the uncertain linear expressions in the optimization problem, with the decision variables as weights. For independent random variables with finite variance, the weighted central limit theorem yields a second-order cone constraint with a decision-dependent protection term, and for heavy-tailed random variables governed by stable limit laws, the weighted approach yields power-cone constraints. Using norm duality, we show that, under a condition on the individual bounds, the feasible region of the unweighted formulation is contained in that of the weighted one. In 16,000 knapsack instances with a prescribed violation probability of 5%, the weighted formulation improves the optimal objective value by 20.9% on average, with overall average violation probabilities between 3.45% and 4.95%, whereas those of the unweighted formulation are near zero.
tldr: The paper introduces decision-weighted limit theorems that yield tighter second-order cone and power-cone uncertainty sets for robust optimization under uncertainty.
motivation: Standard robust optimization applies limit theorems to unweighted sums of uncertain parameters, producing uncertainty sets that are needlessly conservative.
method: Limit theorems (weighted central limit theorem for finite-variance variables, stable limit laws for heavy-tailed variables) are applied directly to uncertain linear expressions with decision variables as weights, with a norm-duality argument proving containment of the unweighted feasible region.
result: Across 16,000 knapsack instances at a 5% target violation probability, the weighted formulation improves the optimal objective by 20.9% on average while keeping empirical violation probabilities between 3.45% and 4.95%.
conclusion: Decision-weighted limit theorems give sharper, less conservative robust optimization models with better-controlled violation probabilities than unweighted approaches.

title: Structural Functional Identifiability Of Unknown Differential Equation Observation Maps
authors: Torkel E Loman, Alexander P Browning, Ruth E Baker
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many differential equation models of real-world systems, the mechanistic structure of the dynamics is known, but the map from the dynamics to the observations is not. This is potentially problematic, as it can prevent us from e.g. learning model parameter values from data. Examples where this occurs include measuring a fluorescent marker as a proxy for the dynamics of a cellular circuit, and using wastewater measurements to follow the development of an epidemic. The nascent field of hybrid modelling, in which machine learning components (like neural networks) are embedded within mechanistic models, provides the tools to learn such maps. Here, the system's dynamics keep their mechanistic form, while a neural network represents the unknown observation map and is trained alongside any unknown core system parameters. This raises a question of identifiability: when can the true observation map be learnt, and when does one simply learn some map that transforms the dynamics into the available data? Building on previous work, we show how structural functional identifiability analysis can establish whether a model's unknown observation maps and core system parameters are identifiable, i.e. can be uniquely learnt from data. We both prove general results on when models with unknown observation maps are, and are not, identifiable, and demonstrate a general methodology (based on differential algebra) for assessing the identifiability of such models. This paves the way for applying classic differential equation workflows to the many real-world systems that contain such unknown maps.
tldr: The paper develops a structural functional identifiability framework, based on differential algebra, for hybrid differential-equation models in which the observation map is unknown and represented by a neural network.
motivation: In many mechanistic models the dynamics are known but the map from state variables to observations is not, which obstructs parameter learning; hybrid modelling addresses this, but it is unclear whether the true observation map and core parameters can be uniquely recovered from data.
method: Building on prior identifiability work, the authors prove general results characterizing when models with unknown observation maps are or are not identifiable, and present a differential-algebra-based methodology for testing identifiability of both the map and the core system parameters.
result: They establish conditions under which the true observation map and core parameters are uniquely learnable versus cases where only some indistinguishable map consistent with the data can be recovered, and provide a practical assessment procedure.
conclusion: The framework enables classical differential-equation identifiability workflows to be applied to real-world systems with unknown observation maps, such as fluorescence-proxy cellular circuits and wastewater epidemic monitoring.

title: A Nonlinear Multigrid Method For The Preconditioned Lattice Boltzmann Equation
authors: Li-Shi Luo Xingzhou Ji
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work developed a preconditioned lattice Boltzmann equation (PLBE) smoother for the residual-driven full approximation scheme (FAS) multigrid to accelerate steady-state LBE calculations. To overcome the deterioration of LBE smoothing at low viscosity, we used a two- relaxation-time (TRT) collision model together with characteristic-velocity and kinetic precondition- ing to keep the relaxation frequency for the even-order moments within a favorable range, while independently selecting the relaxation frequency for the odd-order moments to reduce their local amplification factor. We further investigated F-, W-, and hybrid V/W-cycles to address residual stagnation observed with V-cycles at high Reynolds numbers. The 2D lid-driven cavity flow was used as a test case. At Re = 5000, TRT-PLBE-FAS achieves an approximately 27-fold speedup over single-grid TRT-PLBE. At Re = 20000 on a 20482 grid, the hybrid V/W-cycle reduces solution time by 14% compared with the W-cycle.
tldr: The paper develops a preconditioned lattice Boltzmann equation smoother combined with FAS multigrid cycles to accelerate steady-state CFD simulations of lid-driven cavity flow.
motivation: Lattice Boltzmann solvers lose smoothing efficiency at low viscosity (high Reynolds number), causing slow convergence or residual stagnation in multigrid steady-state calculations.
method: A two-relaxation-time collision model with characteristic-velocity and kinetic preconditioning is used as a smoother for residual-driven FAS multigrid, with F-, W-, and hybrid V/W-cycles tested on 2D lid-driven cavity flow.
result: At Re = 5000 the TRT-PLBE-FAS scheme achieves roughly a 27-fold speedup over single-grid TRT-PLBE, and at Re = 20000 on a 2048^2 grid the hybrid V/W-cycle reduces solution time by 14% versus the W-cycle.
conclusion: Preconditioned TRT-LBE smoothers with appropriate multigrid cycling substantially accelerate steady-state LBE computations at high Reynolds numbers.

title: Training Neural Networks To Be Locally Adaptive
authors: Soham Sarkar Bilol Banerjee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function [MATH] is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point [MATH], a is trained on the [MATH] nearest-neighbours of [MATH] alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of [MATH] attains the rate [MATH], up to logarithmic factors, when [MATH] is locally [MATH]-H\"older with [MATH] and the covariates are supported on a [MATH]-dimensional manifold embedded in [MATH]. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires [MATH] to be calibrated to the smoothness of [MATH], which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of [MATH] that makes the neural network adapt to the local H\"older exponent of [MATH] and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.
tldr: The paper proposes training a separate neural network on the k nearest neighbours of each query point, yielding a locally adaptive estimator whose pointwise risk is minimax optimal under local Hölder smoothness on a low-dimensional manifold.
motivation: Globally trained networks commit to one model over the whole covariate space and therefore fit poorly when the regression function varies rapidly in some regions and is nearly flat in others.
method: For each query point a network is fit only on its k nearest neighbours, and the estimator is analysed via a localization argument; a data-driven choice of k is given that adapts simultaneously to the local Hölder exponent and the intrinsic dimension.
result: The pointwise risk attains the optimal rate up to logarithmic factors for locally Hölder regression on a d-dimensional manifold embedded in high dimension, and a matching Le Cam lower bound establishes pointwise minimax optimality; simulations show gains over global training and state-of-the-art baselines.
conclusion: Local, query-dependent training with an adaptively calibrated neighbourhood size makes neural networks locally adaptive, though the work is purely classical statistical learning with no quantum information, thermodynamic, or network content.

title: A Critical Appraisal And Motivated Intruder Test Of A Search Dataset Anonymised For The Purposes Of The Eu Digital Markets Act
authors: Ghislain D'entremont, Lisa Pilgram, Sophie Stalla-Bourdillon, Renee Gil, Lucy Mosquera, Olga Vovk, Khaled El Emam
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study evaluated the European Commission's anonymisation measures for Alphabet's search-data sharing under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act against European Data Protection Board guidance and contemporary practice, and assessed re-identification through motivated intruder testing. The measures focus on search end-users, leaving other individuals mentioned in queries insufficiently protected, and do not explicitly address inference. The accompanying controls and safeguards reflect good practice for managing residual risk. Motivated intruder testing targeted 98,501 individuals across six countries using publicly available profiles. Google-verified matches yielded a re-identification rate of 0.094%, below the study's 0.47% per-team threshold. Each verified match required about three hours (Euro 105), excluding Google verification and Gemini costs, suggesting limited cost deterrence. All country-level rates were below the threshold, but one region exceeded it. The threshold drew on conservative precedents, adjusted for data quality, verification, controls and safeguards, assuming five independent attack teams. Some sensitivity scenarios exceeded the threshold, but relied on strong assumptions, such as treating all uncertain matches as correct. Results may not generalise beyond the targeted population, and ethics requirements constrained the attacks. Personal data detection recall was assumed rather than tested: the minimum defensible recall was 0.88, with 0.976 recommended. However, missed identifiers outside the allow-list would remain in the dataset. Under the study's contextual framework, assumptions and testing limitations, identity-disclosure risk was considered insignificant. This finding does not resolve the gaps concerning inference and other individuals' information; safeguards remain necessary.
tldr: A privacy/legal-technical appraisal of the European Commission's anonymisation measures for Alphabet's search-data sharing under the EU Digital Markets Act, including motivated-intruder re-identification testing.
motivation: Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act requires data sharing, and the authors assess whether the accompanying anonymisation and safeguards genuinely prevent re-identification of search users and individuals appearing in queries.
method: The anonymisation measures are compared against EDPB guidance and current practice, followed by motivated-intruder testing targeting 98,501 individuals across six countries using publicly available profiles, with verification of candidate matches and cost/time accounting.
result: Google-verified re-identification reached 0.094%, below the study's 0.47% per-team threshold, with each verified match costing roughly three hours (EUR 105); one region exceeded the threshold and some sensitivity scenarios also did so under strong assumptions.
conclusion: Under the study's contextual framework and assumptions identity-disclosure risk is judged insignificant, but gaps regarding inference and protection of non-user individuals remain unresolved, so safeguards remain necessary.

title: From Apology To Action: Apologies, Compensation, And Cooperation In Llm Agents
authors: Grace Ibukunoluwa Ufeoshi, Alessandro Di Stefano, Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, The Anh Han, Zhao Song
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make decisions that affect other agents, but what happens after a harmful or unsuccessful interaction remains poorly understood. We investigate whether apologies by LLM agents are associated with subsequent cooperative behaviour, using controlled Prisoner's Dilemma experiments with four commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Mistral Large 3). Across payoff conditions, we examine when agents apologise, the reasons they provide, and the actions that follow. We also examine how access to one round of interaction history affects behaviour and, in a second experiment, whether and how agents offer compensation alongside their apologies. Apology behaviour differed substantially across models and preceding interaction outcomes, and verbal expressions of cooperation did not always align with subsequent actions. Notably, Claude Opus 4.8 apologised even after mutual cooperation, while Mistral Large 3 apologised after being exploited but continued to defect even when its opponent cooperated. After unilateral defection, positively compensated apologies from GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro were followed by mutual cooperation, unlike those from Claude and Mistral. Our findings suggest that apologies, compensation, and strategic behaviour are distinct: conciliatory messages may precede continued defection, while costly apologies may go unanswered. This has important implications for the study of machine behaviour and human-AI interactions, as verbal signals alone may not reliably reflect an AI system's subsequent actions.
tldr: Commercial LLM agents are tested in iterated Prisoner's Dilemma games to see whether their apologies and offers of compensation predict subsequent cooperative behaviour.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly make decisions affecting other agents, yet little is known about the post-conflict dynamics of their conciliatory language and whether it matches their later actions.
method: Controlled Prisoner's Dilemma experiments with four commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Mistral Large 3) across payoff conditions, with and without one round of interaction history, plus a second experiment on compensation offers accompanying apologies.
result: Apology behaviour varied strongly across models and prior outcomes; verbal cooperation signals often diverged from later actions, with some models apologising after mutual cooperation or continuing to defect after being exploited, and only some compensated apologies were followed by mutual cooperation.
conclusion: Apologies, compensation, and strategic behaviour are distinct phenomena in LLM agents, so verbal signals alone cannot be trusted as indicators of future action, which matters for machine behaviour and human-AI interaction research.

title: From Token Changes To Task Failures: Bit Flips In A Shared KV-Cache Block
authors: Satoshi Matsuura Yuji Yamamoto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In LLM serving systems with prefix caching, each KV block of a shared system prompt is held in GPU memory as a single physical copy, which every request with that prompt reads. Our earlier work measured change and showed that one bit flip in such a block changes many later responses without making them visibly degenerate. This paper extends that work by measuring how often the changed responses are wrong. Using software fault injection into vLLM serving Qwen3-8B, we flip the most significant mantissa bit or the sign bit of a value in such a block. We score responses on four tasks: code generation, short-answer questions, multiple-choice reasoning, and refusal under a policy. The fraction of changes that turned a correct response wrong depended strongly on the task: 0.023 on MBPP+ and 0.59 on held-out TriviaQA at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 and 0.60 at the sign bit. Harm fell on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong, so the damage of a flip depends on how common such requests are. Harmed responses looked like ordinary errors, so a flip should be detected by checking cached blocks rather than by monitoring outputs.
tldr: The paper quantifies how often single bit flips in a shared KV-cache block of an LLM serving system (vLLM with Qwen3-8B) turn correct responses into incorrect ones across four task types.
motivation: Prefix caching stores one physical copy of each KV block shared across requests, so a hardware fault in that block can silently corrupt many downstream outputs; earlier work showed changes but not whether they are harmful.
