method: Software fault injection is used to flip the most significant mantissa bit or sign bit of a value in a shared KV-cache block, and the resulting responses on code generation, short-answer QA, multiple-choice reasoning, and policy-refusal tasks are scored for correctness.
result: The fraction of changes that converted correct answers into wrong ones ranged from 0.023 (MBPP+) to 0.59 (held-out TriviaQA) at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 to 0.60 at the sign bit; harm concentrated on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong and corrupted outputs resembled ordinary errors.
conclusion: Bit-flip damage is task- and query-dependent and invisible in outputs, so detection should rely on checking cached blocks rather than monitoring response quality.

title: Dressed In Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking Of MLLMs Via Visual Trust Bias
authors: Weihang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Yangbangyan Jiang, Zitai Wang, Zhipeng Yu, Qingming Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing, yet their safety remains a critical concern, especially under jailbreak attempts. Existing MLLM jailbreaks either inject fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesize toxic visual cues to achieve text-driven attack intents. In contrast, a more practical MLLM jailbreak emphasizes enhancing attack efficacy directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs. We address this problem by proposing Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a new jailbreak framework that exploits a previously overlooked attack surface: MLLMs exhibit an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, which enables transferable and stealthy jailbreaks. VTBA constructs a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input pair to the most relevant one, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, thereby leveraging credible visual cues to override safety refusals while preserving naturalness. We further construct a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs to evaluate jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong MLLMs, revealing a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. Warning: This paper may contain sensitive content.
tldr: The paper introduces Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a black-box jailbreak framework that exploits MLLMs' trust in authoritative-looking visual layouts to elicit harmful outputs from naturally occurring image-text pairs.
motivation: Existing MLLM jailbreaks rely on fragile adversarial perturbations or synthesized toxic imagery, which are impractical; the authors instead target realistic harmful image-text pairs and an overlooked surface: the model's inherent trust bias toward credible, authority-styled visual cues.
method: VTBA builds a bank of authoritative visual templates, retrieves the template most relevant to each input pair, and embeds the harmful intent into that layout so credible visual framing overrides safety refusals while keeping the image natural; a 2,500-pair dataset of naturally occurring image-text pairs is constructed for evaluation.
result: Experiments report consistently high attack success rates across several strong MLLMs, demonstrating that the trust-bias surface transfers and remains stealthy.
conclusion: Multimodal safety alignment has a severe, previously underexplored vulnerability to authority-styled visual framing, motivating more robust alignment and defense strategies.

title: Computing Ef1 Allocations With Few Value Queries
authors: Ayumi Igarashi Max Dupr\'e la Tour
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that allocates [MATH] indivisible goods among [MATH] agents with nonnegative additive valuations using [MATH] value queries and guarantees envy-freeness up to one good (EF1). Concurrent work of Lin, Liu, Tao, and Zhou achieves [MATH] comparison queries, attaining the optimal [MATH] dependence on [MATH] for fixed [MATH]. Each comparison query can be simulated using two value queries, so their bound also holds for value queries. Our contributions are a much simpler algorithm and proofs, and polynomial-time computation.
tldr: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm computes EF1 allocations of indivisible goods with few value queries.
motivation: Fair division of indivisible goods with EF1 guarantees is central to computational social choice, and query complexity matters when valuations are accessed via oracles.
method: The authors design a simpler deterministic polynomial-time algorithm using a sublinear-in-m value-query scheme, contrasting with concurrent comparison-query approaches.
result: The algorithm achieves EF1 with few value queries and much simpler proofs, matching the asymptotic query dependence of concurrent work up to constants.
conclusion: The work simplifies and clarifies query-efficient EF1 allocation, but lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Plenty To Fret About: From Hazard Analysis To Formal Requirements For Robot-Assisted Dressing
authors: Gunjari Chakraborty (university Of Manchester), Yasmin Rafiq (university Of Manchester), Hazel M. Taylor (university Of Manchester), Marie Farrell
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding requirements for systems involving humans and robots is essential for providing robust evidence that such systems behave correctly. Requirements formalisation approaches such as the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET) can support the transition from unstructured natural language to formal representations suitable for verification. In this paper, we formalise 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing (RAD) case study, previously classified using a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements. Through an iterative process involving domain-expert clarification, these were represented by 117 unique FRETISH requirements. Formalisation exposed ambiguities, temporal and probabilistic assumptions, and cases where source requirements needed to be decomposed or could be consolidated because they expressed the same formal behaviour. Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. We report practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements and identify directions for further work.
tldr: This paper formalises 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing case study into 117 FRETISH requirements and analyses their temporal semantics and realisability.
motivation: Human-robot systems need robust evidence of correct behaviour, and formalising informal requirements can expose ambiguities and hidden temporal or probabilistic assumptions.
method: The authors iteratively translate hazard-derived requirements, previously classified with a Human-Robot Teamwork taxonomy, into FRETISH using the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool with domain-expert clarification, then analyse temporal patterns and realisability.
result: Formalisation exposed ambiguities, decomposed or consolidated requirements, and showed 70.1% of unique FRETISH requirements use immediate-response or ordering constraints, revealing cross-category relationships in the HRT taxonomy.
conclusion: HRT classification and formalisation give complementary views, with the taxonomy capturing teamwork concerns and FRETISH making required behaviour explicit; practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements are reported.

title: Let's Talk This Out: Towards Explanation-based Distributed Goal Satisfaction
authors: Anton Reinecke (hamburg University Of Technology Hamburg, Germany), Sibylle Schupp
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital systems are embedded in a modular environment of different components with individual goals and settings, which are often installed without central oversight. In this research preview paper we present a framework for communication between components to facilitate compositional problem solving based on explanation patterns and A/G-contracts, without the need for an oracle. Our approach uses partial MaxSMT solving and quantifier elimination to compute counterfactual explanation messages. We illustrate the feasibility of the approach with a proof-of-concept chain topology example, and discuss future challenges when expanding the protocol to more complex topologies.
tldr: The paper proposes a communication framework for distributed components to solve goal-satisfaction problems compositionally using explanation patterns and A/G-contracts without an oracle.
motivation: Digital systems are often composed of independently installed components with individual goals, making centralized oversight impractical and requiring decentralized problem-solving mechanisms.
method: The framework uses partial MaxSMT solving and quantifier elimination to generate counterfactual explanation messages between components, illustrated with a proof-of-concept chain topology example.
result: The approach is shown to be feasible in a simple chain topology, and the authors discuss challenges for extending the protocol to more complex topologies.
conclusion: Explanation-based distributed goal satisfaction offers a promising direction for compositional problem solving, but further work is needed to scale the protocol beyond proof-of-concept examples.

title: From Attack Tree To Model Checker: Binding Capec Patterns To Verify Robotic System Security
authors: Juel Hussain (department Of Computer Science, University Of Manchester, UK), Louise A. Dennis (department Of Computer Science, University Of Manchester, UK), Clare Dixon (department Of Computer Science, University Of Manchester, UK), Marie Farrell
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security-minded verification of autonomous and robotic systems presupposes an attacker, yet the path from a threat catalogue to a checkable attacker model is still traversed by hand. This research preview presents the theory and construction of a pipeline that mechanises it. Each leaf of an attack tree is mapped to a CAPEC attack pattern and written in first-order logic as a rule: the attacker's prerequisites imply the attack's effect. Casting the pattern as such a rule is what makes it operational - its variables can be bound to a specific system's parts, and its prerequisites can then be tested against that system under a chosen configuration of security controls. Binding is our means of verifying whether a system is vulnerable to a given attack: from a bound pattern we derive an attacker model, turn its effect into a temporal-logic property, and check that property against the system with and without a countermeasure, reporting the control that defeats the attack. We describe the signature, schemas, profiles for approach, and explore how CAPEC can support reasoning about robotics security.
tldr: This research preview describes a pipeline that maps attack-tree leaves to CAPEC attack patterns, encodes them as first-order logic rules, and derives checkable attacker models for verifying robotic system security with model checking.
motivation: Security verification of autonomous and robotic systems requires an explicit attacker model, but translating threat catalogues into checkable attacker models is currently done manually.
method: Each attack-tree leaf is bound to a CAPEC pattern expressed as a first-order rule (prerequisites imply effect); binding the rule to system parts yields an attacker model whose effect is turned into a temporal-logic property and checked against the system with and without countermeasures.
result: The paper outlines the signature, schemas, and approach profiles of the pipeline and discusses how CAPEC can support reasoning about robotics security, reporting which control defeats a given attack.
conclusion: The work mechanises the path from threat catalogues to verifiable attacker models for robotic systems, though it remains a research preview with theory and construction rather than full empirical evaluation.

title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines From Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
authors: Alexandre Dulaunoy C\'edric Bonhomme
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: -05-X-03), Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, and exploitation sightings. We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources. Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes. Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings. Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. We identify the additional disclosure, exploitation observation, and patch availability timestamps needed to improve vulnerability lifecycle measurements.
tldr: The paper builds a provenance-aware evidence model in Vulnerability-Lookup to measure exploitation-to-patch intervals across 3,758 vulnerability identifiers using CVE, KEV, and exploitation-sighting records.
motivation: Vulnerability lifecycle metrics such as exploitation-to-patch time are widely cited but rarely grounded in verifiable, machine-readable evidence with clear provenance and date precision.
method: The authors introduce an evidence model that selects the earliest record per lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific from bulk-catalog entries, preserves date precision, and traces each date to its original source, then applies it to aggregated public vulnerability data.
result: 98% of the 3,758 identifiers have disclosure dates but only 15.7% have patch evidence; after filtering bulk imports and ambiguous same-day cases, 59 vulnerabilities show patch-after-exploitation with a median interval of 7.6 days, and collector misclassification was found to distort up to 40% of initial exploitation dates.
conclusion: Exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable but their reliability hinges on evidence availability, precision, and provenance; the authors specify the additional timestamps needed for sound lifecycle measurement.

title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses With Adaptive Injection Stressors
authors: Yujun Wang, Yilun Liu, Jinhe Bi, Krishna Kanth Nakka, Xuebing Zhou, Hinrich Sch{\"u}tze, Yunpu Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.
tldr: The paper proposes 'Evolution Under Fire', a staged framework that co-evolves executable safety harnesses and adaptive injection stressors to defend tool-using LLM agents against prompt-injection attacks.
motivation: Tool-using language-model agents ingest untrusted emails, webpages and documents, so malicious instructions and legitimate directives share the same channel; existing defenses are hand-designed and static, requiring repeated manual redesign to improve.
method: Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping model, benchmark, tools and evaluator fixed; adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that drive a further round of harness evolution.
result: On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini attack success drops from 50.4% to 3.0% with improved clean and attacked utility; on Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it falls from 82.6% to 62.0% with helpfulness retained, and evolved harnesses transfer to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9%.
conclusion: Automated co-evolution of harnesses and stressors yields a better security-utility trade-off than reproduced static defenses and transfers across models without further evolution.

title: Guarded Swarms In The Loop: A Ros 2/px4 Digital Twin For Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination Of Uav/ugv Swarms
authors: Uwe M. Borghoff, Paolo Bottoni, Luca D'aurizio, Remo Pareschi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.
tldr: Presents the first executable ROS 2/PX4/Gazebo digital twin of the 'Guarded Swarms' architecture, pairing a TB-CSPN-based digital coordination layer with an independent analog safety veto layer for UAV/UGV swarms in contested environments.
motivation: Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles in adversarial settings cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are themselves part of the attack surface.
method: The TB-CSPN transition chain from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, with the analog layer modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board gating every command, evaluated over 60 counterfactual runs and fault-injection experiments.
result: The three negative guarantees hold at three stages across all 60 runs, threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality, and the independent veto prevents all collisions from forged missions or compromised workers while a worker-held veto prevents none.
conclusion: The digital twin validates the architectural guarantees while exposing implementation-level hazards, and delineates which properties simulation can verify versus those requiring hardware.

title: A Riemann-invariant Contact-capturing Scheme With Weno Reconstruction And RH-motivated Dual-speed Dissipation For Compressible Two-phase Mixture Flows
authors: Ankit Ruhi, Ramesh Kolluru, Shrinath KS
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work develops and benchmarks centred (Riemann-solver-free) finite-volume fluxes for a hyperbolic two-phase mixture model with velocity non-equilibrium. The baseline method combines a Riemann-invariant contact-capturing algorithm (RICCA) with dual-speed dissipation and primitive-variable WENO3/WENO5 reconstruction, avoiding full eigen-decomposition while retaining a conservative update. An RH-motivated companion flux (RICCA--RH) is introduced, in which the acoustic weight in [MATH] is controlled by a binary pressure/Rankine--Hugoniot switch. On one-dimensional gas--magma Riemann suite, RICCA--RH tracks legacy RICCA and is sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax--Friedrichs at material contacts; a linearised spectral study clarifies how its dual-speed dissipation differs from FORCE. With WENO5, RICCA, RICCA--RH and FORCE produce essentially identical smooth profiles, indicating that most differences are confined to first-order contact metrics. In two dimensions (gas--liquid benchmarks), the production flux implemented on CPU and Apple Metal reproduces expansion-tube, collision and forward-facing-step patterns and yields intermediate cut-based roughness between RICCA and FORCE. High order is obtained using an approximate face-normal acoustic characteristic reconstruction, a pragmatic multi-variable hybrid sensor, and a Zhang--Shu-style invariant-domain face limiter on [MATH]. An under-dissipative soft-switch variant that rings severely is also documented, and a resident 2D Metal kernel on Apple Silicon is reported to deliver up to [MATH] wall-clock speedup on completed CPU/Metal comparisons (peak on the [MATH] expansion tube).
tldr: The paper develops and benchmarks Riemann-solver-free finite-volume fluxes (RICCA and a Rankine-Hugoniot-motivated variant RICCA-RH) with WENO reconstruction for compressible two-phase mixture flows with velocity non-equilibrium.
motivation: Centred finite-volume schemes avoid expensive full eigen-decomposition while still capturing material contacts sharply in hyperbolic two-phase mixture models, motivating improved dual-speed dissipation formulations.
method: The baseline combines a Riemann-invariant contact-capturing algorithm (RICCA) with dual-speed dissipation and primitive-variable WENO3/WENO5 reconstruction; a companion RICCA-RH flux uses a binary pressure/Rankine-Hugoniot switch to control the acoustic weight, with a Zhang-Shu-style invariant-domain face limiter and hybrid sensor for high order.
result: On 1D gas-magma Riemann tests RICCA-RH tracks legacy RICCA and is sharper than first-order FORCE/Lax-Friedrichs at contacts, while with WENO5 all schemes give nearly identical smooth profiles; 2D gas-liquid benchmarks reproduce expansion-tube, collision, and forward-facing-step patterns, with a resident Apple Metal kernel giving wall-clock speedups.
conclusion: The scheme offers a practical, eigen-decomposition-free approach whose gains are largely confined to first-order contact resolution, with GPU acceleration demonstrated on Apple Silicon.

title: Direct Element-Level Mass Matrix Inversion
authors: Eli Hanukah
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explicit finite element methods for transient solid dynamics commonly use lumped mass matrices to avoid solving systems of equations for nodal accelerations at each time step. However, diagonal mass matrices may inadequately represent inertia, particularly for higher-order elements and coarse or distorted meshes. This has limited the use of higher-order elements in explicit dynamic analyses. This paper presents a systematic method for directly evaluating the inverse of non-diagonal element-level mass matrices for solid isoparametric elements of arbitrary interpolation order. The method applies to mixed mass matrices defined as linear combinations of lumped and consistent mass matrices, with a weighting parameter controlling the transition between diagonal, consistent, and intermediate formulations. It therefore provides a framework for incorporating non-diagonal mass formulations, including those for quadratic elements, into explicit finite element algorithms. The approach is demonstrated by deriving an explicit inverse formula for the mixed mass matrix of the eight-node hexahedral element. This formula enables efficient element-level inversion without solving a global system. The proposed method can improve inertial representation in transient dynamic analyses while retaining the computational advantages of explicit time integration and is suitable for element-by-element implementations.
tldr: The paper presents a systematic method for directly inverting non-diagonal element-level mass matrices for solid isoparametric finite elements of arbitrary interpolation order, enabling non-diagonal mass formulations in explicit transient dynamics.
motivation: Explicit finite element solvers typically rely on lumped (diagonal) mass matrices to avoid solving systems at each timestep, but lumping poorly represents inertia for higher-order elements and coarse or distorted meshes, limiting the use of such elements.
method: The authors develop a direct element-level inversion procedure for mixed mass matrices expressed as linear combinations of lumped and consistent mass matrices, and derive an explicit closed-form inverse for the eight-node hexahedral element.
result: An explicit inverse formula for the mixed mass matrix of the eight-node hexahedral element is obtained, permitting efficient element-by-element inversion without assembling or solving a global system.
conclusion: The approach improves inertial representation in explicit transient solid dynamics while preserving the computational advantages of explicit time integration and element-by-element implementation.

title: Banach-Mazur Distance And Related Methods Of Comparing Convex Bodies
authors: Stanislaw J. Szarek Marek Lassak
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Banach-Mazur distance is one of the standard tools used in the study of mathematical objects such as convex bodies or normed spaces, and it becomes indispensable when investigating properties that are invariant under linear isomorphisms. It appears in convex geometry and convex analysis as a way to quantify the approximation of convex bodies. In functional analysis, it plays a basic role in the study of local properties of Banach spaces. The goal of this survey is to present a cohesive picture of these two perspectives. We supply an extensive collection of known results for reference and list open problems of varying difficulty, which could stimulate further research. We include in our discussion several distinct variations on the concept of the Banach-Mazur distance, some of them exploratory, that haven't received much attention to date in the literature. We follow the trend - which emerged in recent decades - of considering arbitrary convex bodies, and not just those that are centrally symmetric. Finally, we include a comprehensive list of references on the Banach-Mazur distance.
tldr: This is a survey of the Banach-Mazur distance and related methods for comparing convex bodies and normed spaces.
motivation: The Banach-Mazur distance is a central tool in convex geometry and functional analysis, and the authors aim to unify perspectives from both fields.
method: The paper surveys known results, variations on the Banach-Mazur distance, open problems, and an extensive reference list, including non-centrally symmetric convex bodies.
result: It provides a cohesive overview of the topic, catalogs existing results, and highlights exploratory variants and open problems.
conclusion: The survey is intended as a reference and stimulus for further research in convex geometry and Banach space theory.

title: High-Order Regularization For Singular And Nearly Singular Laplace And Stokes Layer Potentials In Two Dimensions
authors: Han Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layer potentials represent the solutions of many elliptic boundary value problems, but their kernels have the singularity of the fundamental solution, so standard quadrature loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel gives a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral [MATH], but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius [MATH]. We construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials that achieve regularization error [MATH], [MATH], uniformly for targets on and near the curve. The resulting method is both high-order accurate and easy to implement: the integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. Choosing [MATH] with [MATH], where [MATH] is the node spacing, keeps the discretization error smaller than the regularization error as [MATH], and numerical experiments confirm the predicted [MATH] convergence. Finally, we combine the near-curve evaluation with a fast Poisson solver to compute the potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.
tldr: The paper constructs high-order regularized kernels for singular and nearly singular 2D Laplace and Stokes layer potentials, evaluated accurately with a fixed-node periodic trapezoidal rule.
motivation: Standard quadrature for layer potentials loses accuracy near the boundary because the kernels inherit the singularity of the fundamental solution, and existing Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel achieves only first-order regularization error for the single layer.
method: Modified single- and double-layer kernels for 2D Laplace and Stokes problems are constructed to attain higher-order regularization error uniformly for on- and near-curve targets, with integrals evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes; the smoothing radius is scaled with node spacing.
result: The scheme achieves the predicted high-order convergence numerically, with discretization error kept below regularization error, and is combined with a fast Poisson solver to compute potentials on an entire Cartesian grid.
conclusion: The approach yields a high-order accurate yet simple-to-implement boundary integral method for singular and nearly singular layer potentials, extendable to full-grid evaluation via fast Poisson solvers.

title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity
authors: Ketan Mittal, Julian Andrej, John Camier, Veselin Dobrev, Tzanio Kolev, Leonardo Molinari, Vladimir Tomov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-order mesh r-adaptivity typically entails minimizing a nonlinear functional using its gradients and, for Newton-based methods, its Hessian. These derivatives can be expensive to derive, must be updated with any changes to the functional, and errors in the derivatives directly impact the convergence of r-adaptivity. Additionally, derivatives of the r-adaptivity operator are required for consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse problems. This work develops a framework for differentiable r-adaptivity based on the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm. Given a pointwise functional defining the local mesh-adaptation objective, the proposed framework uses [MATH]FEM to automatically generate pointwise first- and second-order derivatives. These local derivatives are then assembled into a global gradient vector and a Hessian operator through the finite element operator decomposition. The derivative kernels support portable CPU and GPU execution, with partial assembly and tensor sum factorization enabling matrix-free application of the Hessian operator. The framework also provides consistent sensitivities of the r-adaptivity operator through automatically generated mixed derivatives and implicit differentiation of the mesh stationarity equations. Numerical experiments show GPU solve times comparable to those of hand-derived TMOP implementations on a benchmark problem, improvement in r-adaptivity convergence due to accurate computation of the derivatives, and demonstrate the use of mesh sensitivities for material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.
tldr: The paper presents a differentiable framework for high-order mesh r-adaptivity built on the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm, using automatic differentiation to generate gradient and Hessian kernels for CPU/GPU execution.
motivation: Mesh r-adaptivity requires expensive-to-derive nonlinear functional derivatives that must be re-derived when the objective changes, and consistent sensitivities are needed for inverse problems.
method: Uses automatic differentiation (FEM) to generate pointwise first- and second-order derivatives, assembles them into global gradient/Hessian operators via finite element operator decomposition, and applies implicit differentiation for mesh sensitivities.
result: GPU solve times are comparable to hand-derived TMOP implementations, r-adaptivity convergence improves from accurate derivatives, and mesh sensitivities enable material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.
conclusion: Differentiable r-adaptivity offers a practical, portable alternative to hand-coded derivatives while improving robustness and enabling sensitivity-based inverse problem workflows.

title: Decision Stability And Model Reduction For Hamilton--Jacobi Navigation In Multiscale Flows
authors: Ruimeng Hu, Byungdoo Kong, Xu Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous vehicles plan time-optimal routes through flow fields that are known only through reduced, finite-resolution models of an underlying multiscale flow. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi homogenization concerns convergence of the value function as the fine scale vanishes; but what a vehicle commits to is a route, and value accuracy need not imply route accuracy. We study this gap for a fixed-resolution reduction rather than in the homogenization limit. The committed route's dependence on the model-reduction error splits into two regimes. When the optimal route is a unique, nondegenerate minimizer with a regular value-function neighborhood, it depends Lipschitz-continuously on the reduction error, while the extra travel time from acting on the reduced model grows only quadratically with that error. When two routes are tied on the cut locus of the value function, the value remains stable, but an arbitrarily small change in the flow can switch the selected route, making route selection discontinuous in the reduction error. This dichotomy identifies where a reduced model must be accurate: not where the flow error is largest, but where the route choice is fragile. In the regular regime it yields a resolution-allocation principle, while an oracle marginal-regret benchmark illustrates the potential benefit of decision-aware resolution allocation relative to refinement based on flow-error magnitude.
tldr: The paper analyzes how errors in reduced multiscale flow models affect route selection in Hamilton-Jacobi navigation, showing a stability/instability dichotomy for committed routes.
motivation: Autonomous vehicles plan routes using finite-resolution reduced models of multiscale flows, but value-function convergence does not guarantee that the selected route remains stable under model-reduction error.
method: The authors study route dependence on reduction error at fixed resolution, separating regular unique-minimizer regimes from cut-locus tie regimes using Hamilton-Jacobi value functions and stability arguments.
result: In the regular regime, routes depend Lipschitz-continuously on reduction error and excess travel time grows quadratically; near cut loci, arbitrarily small flow changes can switch the selected route despite stable value.
conclusion: Reduced models should allocate resolution where route decisions are fragile rather than merely where flow error is largest, motivating decision-aware resolution allocation.

title: Doing Well By Doing Good: Alignment Of Revenue And Welfare In Robust Product Line Design Through Data-Driven Optimization
authors: Maoqi Liu, Liangjie Li, Yun Hui Lin, Xiuli Chao, Jiajie Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Product line design (PLD) selects product variants for a firm to maximize expected revenue. Candidate assortments are usually evaluated under random utility maximization (RUM), in which choice probabilities stem from the joint distribution of latent consumer utilities. As this utility distribution cannot be directly observed and is estimated from choice data, distributional uncertainty inevitably arises. This paper studies how to hedge PLD decisions against such ambiguity. We construct a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model that maximizes worst-case expected revenue over an l1-Wasserstein ball around a nominal utility distribution. We derive a dual reformulation for general nominal distributions and then specialize to two cases. With independent Gumbel utility shocks, the dual simplifies to a closed-form robust multinomial logit. We derive revenue gap bounds for parameters estimated from finite full-assortment choice data. When the true model structure is unknown beforehand, we adopt a data-driven scheme using the empirical distribution of sampled utility vectors and extend optimality-gap analysis to a general RUM oracle. For the NP-hard empirical problem, we propose Adaptive Parametric Search (APS), an algorithm with certified relative optimality guarantees. Numerical experiments show fast computation and better out-of-sample performance.Dual analysis shows that robustness to preference uncertainty endogenously encourages the firm to raise buyer welfare. This incentive takes distinct forms: robustness supports larger assortments in the unconstrained logit setting, whereas under the empirical nominal, it favors products with lower prices and higher utility relative to the outside option. Numerically, we identify a "doing well by doing good" effect: product lines with higher in-sample buyer welfare attain higher out-of-sample revenue and buyer welfare.
tldr: This paper develops a distributionally robust optimization framework for product line design under uncertain consumer utility distributions, showing that robustness to preference uncertainty can simultaneously raise firm revenue and buyer welfare.
motivation: Firms selecting product assortments rely on choice models estimated from limited data, so the latent utility distribution is uncertain; the authors ask how to hedge product-line decisions against this distributional ambiguity.
method: They formulate a DRO model maximizing worst-case expected revenue over an l1-Wasserstein ball around a nominal utility distribution, derive a dual reformulation, specialize to a closed-form robust multinomial logit under independent Gumbel shocks, and propose an Adaptive Parametric Search algorithm with optimality guarantees for the empirical problem.
result: They obtain revenue-gap bounds for parameters estimated from finite choice data, extend optimality-gap analysis to a general RUM oracle, and numerically find fast computation, better out-of-sample performance, and a 'doing well by doing good' effect where higher in-sample buyer welfare correlates with higher out-of-sample revenue and welfare.
conclusion: Robustness to preference uncertainty endogenously incentivizes firms to improve buyer welfare, via larger assortments in the unconstrained logit setting or lower-priced, higher-utility products under the empirical nominal distribution.

title: An Inexact Proximal Gradient Method For Composite Multiobjective Optimization With Absolute And Relative Stopping Criteria
authors: Zhuoxin Fan, Liping Tang, Xinmin Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proximal gradient methods are widely used for composite optimization. In multiobjective optimization, however, the resulting minimax subproblem generally requires an additional inner method to solve, even when the proximal mapping of each nonsmooth component is available in closed form. In addition, most existing convergence results are obtained only under the assumption that the involved subproblems are solved exactly, which is unrealistic and limits the applicability of the proximal gradient methods. To make the proximal gradient methods practical, we propose an implementable inexact proximal gradient method based on proximal computation. Considering an approximate optimality condition and a hybrid stopping criterion including absolute and relative rules for the subproblem, we address the computational challenge by developing an inner inexact projected gradient method that can exploit the proximal mappings of the individual components. The [MATH] convergence rate is also established for our method under certain conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the computational benefits of solving the subproblems inexactly.
tldr: The paper proposes an implementable inexact proximal gradient method for composite multiobjective optimization with absolute and relative stopping criteria.
motivation: Proximal gradient methods for multiobjective optimization typically require exactly solved subproblems and inner solvers, limiting practical applicability.
method: The authors develop an inexact proximal gradient method using an approximate optimality condition and a hybrid absolute-relative stopping criterion, along with an inner inexact projected gradient method exploiting individual proximal mappings.
result: They establish convergence rate guarantees under certain conditions and demonstrate computational benefits in numerical experiments.
conclusion: The method makes proximal gradient approaches more practical for composite multiobjective optimization by allowing inexact subproblem solutions.

title: A New Premodel For Bounded Type Siegel Disks Of Some Transcendental Entire Functions
authors: Fei Yang, Gaofei Zhang, Yanhua Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the 1980s, Douady and Sullivan conjectured that the Siegel disks of rational maps with degree at least two are Jordan domains. Based on the study of Blaschke models, this conjecture was settled by Zhang under the condition that the Siegel disks are of bounded type, and by Zakeri for a large number of transcendental entire functions under the same condition. The entire functions studied by Zakeri have exactly one finite asymptotic value, which is the center of the fixed Siegel disk. Ch\'{e}ritat, and later with Epstein, also studied the Siegel disk boundaries of such type transcendental entire functions by developing Ghys-like models. In this paper, by introducing a new premodel, we prove that the fixed bounded type Siegel disk centered at the non-zero point [MATH] of [MATH] is a quasi-disk whose boundary contains the critical point [MATH]. The asymptotic value [MATH] is not contained in the Siegel disk of these entire functions, which is essentially different from the previous results. Moreover, we prove that the Julia sets of these functions with a fixed bounded type Siegel disk are locally connected.
tldr: The paper constructs a new premodel to prove that a fixed bounded-type Siegel disk of certain transcendental entire functions is a quasi-disk whose boundary contains the critical point, and that the corresponding Julia sets are locally connected.
motivation: Douady and Sullivan conjectured that bounded-type Siegel disks of rational maps are Jordan domains, settled by Zhang via Blaschke models and extended by Zakeri to transcendental entire functions with a single finite asymptotic value at the Siegel disk center; the authors aim to handle the case where the asymptotic value is not contained in the Siegel disk.
method: The authors introduce a new premodel (in the spirit of Blaschke and Ghys-like models) adapted to transcendental entire functions whose fixed bounded-type Siegel disk is centered at a non-zero point, and analyze the geometry of the resulting model domain.
result: They show the fixed bounded-type Siegel disk centered at the non-zero point is a quasi-disk whose boundary contains the critical point, that the asymptotic value lies outside the Siegel disk (in contrast to earlier results), and that the Julia sets of these functions are locally connected.
conclusion: The new premodel extends Siegel disk boundary regularity and local connectivity results to a class of transcendental entire functions not covered by previous Blaschke- or Ghys-type models.

title: Global Phase-plane Organization Of A Toxin-mediated Plant-herbivore Model
authors: Gabriele Grif\`o
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plant-herbivore interactions with chemical plant defence mechanisms can generate complex population dynamics through the nonlinear interplay between resource availability, herbivore pressure, and defence-induced feedbacks. In this work, we investigate the dynamical organization of a plant-herbivore model characterized by a non-monotone functional response accounting for inhibitory effects on grazing activity. In particular, we perform a qualitative and geometric analysis of the associated homogeneous system, characterizing the dynamical regimes supported by the model and the transitions between them. The results reveal the emergence of oscillatory behaviour through a Hopf bifurcation and the occurrence of stable periodic solutions. We further characterize the global phase-plane organization, providing a complete classification of equilibrium configurations and heteroclinic structures supported by the model. In addition, we identify the conditions under which homoclinic connections may occur and discuss their role in shaping the global dynamics. The analysis provides a unified description of the phase-plane organization and highlights how nonlinear defence feedbacks generate qualitatively distinct ecological outcomes, including extinction, stable coexistence, persistent oscillations, and global bifurcation scenarios organized by heteroclinic and homoclinic structures.
tldr: This paper analyzes the global phase-plane dynamics of a plant-herbivore model with non-monotone functional response and chemical defence feedback.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how nonlinear plant defence feedbacks shape ecological population dynamics, including coexistence, oscillations, and extinction.
method: They perform qualitative and geometric analysis of the homogeneous dynamical system, including equilibrium classification, bifurcation analysis, and identification of heteroclinic and homoclinic structures.
result: The model exhibits Hopf bifurcations, stable periodic solutions, and global bifurcation scenarios organized by heteroclinic and homoclinic connections.
conclusion: The analysis provides a unified geometric description of the model's phase-plane organization and shows how defence feedbacks generate distinct ecological outcomes.

title: A 5/2 Guarantee For Echelon Stock (s,S) Policies In One-Warehouse Multi-Retailer Systems
authors: Ming Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a periodic-review warehouse serving multiple heterogeneous retailers with stochastic demand and fixed costs and lead times at both echelons. We construct a deterministic echelon stock [MATH] policy whose long-run expected average cost is at most [MATH] times the optimum over all nonanticipative policies. The guarantee holds when the common backlog penalty and retailer holding rates are at least the warehouse holding rate and retailer setup costs are at most [MATH] times the supplier's. The retailer-specific setup-cost condition extends beyond supplier setup-cost dominance: a retailer dispatch may cost up to 50 percent more than a supplier order. Demand vectors are i.i.d. over periods with finite positive means, and demands of different retailers may be correlated. Each retailer selects the full cycle of its single-location plan or a shifted cycle of half its width, and the warehouse serves requests in arrival order, allowing partial shipments. The upper bound on the policy's cost includes each retailer's mirror cost, which prices the warehouse imbalance created by its batching. The upper and lower bounds share a pooled supplier problem and add one problem per retailer, giving a factor independent of all lead times and the number of retailers. For arbitrary nonnegative setup costs and associated retailer demands, a consolidation policy holds allocated stock until a dispatch threshold is met and gives a factor below [MATH]. On 864 instances built from Walmart store sales, the simulated cost of an integer-rounded implementation of the FIFO policy averages 1.45 times the lower bound and reaches 1.75, and our analytical upper bound on its cost is below 1.94 times the lower bound. With no simulation search, the policy comes within 8.2 and 12.2 percent, on average over 216 instances, of an echelon batch policy and an integer-ratio policy, both tuned by simulation for each instance.
tldr: The paper derives a 5/2 worst-case approximation guarantee for deterministic echelon-stock (s,S) policies in a one-warehouse multi-retailer inventory system with stochastic demand, fixed costs, and lead times.
motivation: Multi-echelon inventory systems are notoriously hard to optimize optimally, so practitioners need simple policies with provable performance guarantees that are independent of lead times and the number of retailers.
method: The authors construct a deterministic echelon-stock (s,S) policy based on each retailer's single-location plan (full or half-shifted cycle), with FIFO warehouse service and partial shipments, and bound its cost against a pooled lower bound plus per-retailer mirror costs.
result: The policy's long-run average cost is at most 5/2 times the optimum under stated holding/setup-cost conditions, and on 864 Walmart-derived instances the simulated integer-rounded FIFO policy averages 1.45x the lower bound (max 1.75x), within roughly 8–12% of simulation-tuned echelon batch and integer-ratio policies.
conclusion: Simple, simulation-free echelon-stock policies admit strong worst-case guarantees that are independent of lead times and retailer count, making them attractive for practical supply-chain deployment.

title: Learning In-Context Adaptivity For LLMs Through Continual Gameplay
authors: Jiale Liu, Zun Li, John Schultz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks where they must explore, gather experience, and adapt their decisions accordingly. We name this capability in-context adaptivity: improving decisions across episodes from experience accumulated in context. We propose to evaluate it in repeated imperfect-information games against unknown opponents. In these games, fixed game-theoretically optimal policies cannot achieve maximum reward, whereas adapting to the opponent increases returns across games. We design a paired protocol that evaluates each agent with and without memory under identical conditions to isolate experience gain from single-game skill. Evaluation shows that memory brings little performance gain for open-weight models and inconsistent gains for frontier models. Our analysis of the agents' summaries and actions identifies a memory-doing gap in which models accurately record opponent tendencies yet rarely depart from default play. To close this gap, we construct a pool of exploitable opponents and post-train Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. We optimize full-match return across context segments so summary generation and action selection are trained together. On unseen opponents, our 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over supervised fine-tuning in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em. Across 35 opponents, our policy matches or surpasses frontier models, generalizes beyond its training horizon, and retains most of its gain on summaries from frontier models.
tldr: The paper studies in-context adaptivity in LLM agents via repeated imperfect-information games and improves it through continual gameplay post-training.
motivation: LLM agents deployed in long-horizon tasks need to adapt from in-context experience, but fixed game-theoretic policies cannot exploit unknown opponents.
method: It introduces a paired protocol to isolate memory gains, identifies a memory-doing gap, and post-trains Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning plus trajectory-level reinforcement learning over full-match returns.
result: The 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over SFT in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em, matching or surpassing frontier models across 35 opponents.
conclusion: Continual gameplay with trajectory-level RL can close the memory-doing gap and enable stronger in-context adaptivity in LLM agents.

title: PersonaHate: A Scalable Persona-Based Data Synthesis Pipeline For Hate Speech Analysis
authors: Xinyu Zhang, Ziqing Yang, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hate speech remains a persistent and evolving threat on online platforms. The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) further intensifies this problem by making hateful content easier and cheaper to generate at scale. Although stronger hate speech detectors continue to be proposed, their performance remains uneven across target identity groups and different forms of hateful expression, partly because existing training data provides only limited coverage of these cases. Thus, we introduce PersonaHate, a scalable persona-driven data synthesis pipeline for constructing diverse hate speech datasets. PersonaHate begins with a large persona pool of 457K personas drawn from two real-world sources. Conditioned on selected personas from this pool, it prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups and performs multi-judge annotation to obtain reliable labels. The resulting corpus contains 791K samples, from which we curate a 67K group-balanced training set. Our modular design also supports extension to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets. Built upon this dataset, we evaluate two detector training strategies: training from scratch and further fine-tuning. Results show that all trained models achieve competitive performance across four widely used external benchmarks. Notably, a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 model trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% average accuracy, outperforming OpenAI's Moderation API on HateBenchSet and MHS. Furthermore, fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B raises its average F1 from 70.7% to 78.4%, a gain of 7.7 percentage points, surpassing LlamaGuard-3, Meta's official safety model based on the same Llama-3.1-8B architecture, on three of four benchmarks. These results show that PersonaHate can substantially improve the robustness and cross-dataset generalization of hate speech detectors.
tldr: PersonaHate is a persona-driven LLM pipeline that synthesizes a large, identity-balanced hate speech dataset to train more robust hate speech detectors.
motivation: Hate speech detectors generalize unevenly across identity groups and expression types, largely because existing training corpora offer limited coverage of these cases, a gap worsened by cheap LLM-generated hateful content.
method: The pipeline samples from a 457K persona pool, prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups, applies multi-judge annotation for reliable labels, and yields 791K samples from which a 67K group-balanced training set is curated.
result: A 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% accuracy, beating OpenAI's Moderation API on two benchmarks, while fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B raises average F1 from 70.7% to 78.4%.
conclusion: The modular, extensible synthesis pipeline substantially improves detector robustness and cross-dataset generalization, and can be extended to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets.

title: RyBench: Runtime Verification Benchmarking Framework Over Publish/Subscribe Networks
authors: Do\u{g}an Ulus Mehmet Hilmi D\"undar (bo\u{g}azi\c{c}i University)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous systems built as distributed, node-based systems communicate via publish/subscribe middleware. Runtime Verification (RV) tools are used to monitor those systems against formal specifications, receiving monitored events through the pub/sub channel. An RV tool's practical value depends on its monitoring throughput capacity and verdict latency, besides its correctness, so a systematic benchmarking setup is needed to evaluate how efficiently these tools run. This paper presents RyBench, a pub/sub-based benchmarking framework that acts as a synthetic event publisher in place of a monitored system, providing a common benchmarking setup. RyBench separates benchmark generation, serialization, and transport into distinct components, enabling the combination of different event-generation strategies, data formats, and transport layers. We also evaluate the framework's throughput capacity across these configurations using Open Simulation Interface (OSI) schemas and Timescales properties, and illustrate the end-to-end benchmarking flow through an application to Reelay and an integration with MonPoly.
tldr: RyBench is a publish/subscribe-based benchmarking framework that emulates a monitored system to measure throughput and verdict latency of runtime verification tools.
motivation: The practical value of runtime verification tools depends not only on correctness but also on monitoring throughput and verdict latency, yet no common benchmarking setup existed for systematically evaluating these performance aspects.
method: The framework acts as a synthetic event publisher on a pub/sub middleware, separating benchmark generation, serialization, and transport into modular components so different event-generation strategies, data formats, and transport layers can be combined; it is evaluated using OSI schemas and Timescales properties.
result: Throughput capacity is measured across configurations, and end-to-end benchmarking is demonstrated via an application to Reelay and an integration with MonPoly.
conclusion: RyBench provides a reusable, modular benchmarking infrastructure for assessing the efficiency of runtime verification tools in distributed node-based autonomous systems.

title: Automated-Truck Penetration Shapes Human Drivers' Car-Following Margins Near Motorway Ramps: A Driving-Simulator Study
authors: Minhao Chen, Zehao Jiang, Julius Secadiningrat, Elnaz Irannezhad
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated-vehicle dedicated lanes (AVDLs) are proposed as transitional infrastructure for mixed traffic, but their effect near ramps, and that of automated trucks, on the human drivers sharing the road has rarely been observed. In a mixed-design driving-simulator experiment, 63 drivers were assigned to one of four layouts (an AVDL extending beyond, coinciding with, or ending inside a 1.5-km ramp weaving section, or no AVDL) and drove at four automated-truck penetration levels from 20% to 80%. Linear mixed-effects models with participant random effects and multiplicity control were used. Higher penetration reduced the share of car-following time at gaps below 1.5 s from 28.5% to 18.1% (Holm-adjusted p = .006). This was explained by leader composition: drivers spent 8% of following time behind a truck at 20% penetration and 48% at 80%, kept longer gaps behind trucks, and did not change their gaps within leader type. AVDL layout had no detectable effect on safety margins, rear-end conflict rates, travel time or speed (differences bounded within plus or minus 5 s per section) and no significant effect on workload. Between-driver differences accounted for 52% to 77% of the variance in the main outcomes. Mixed-traffic models should therefore represent human car-following as leader-type-dependent and heterogeneous.
tldr: A driving-simulator study shows that higher automated-truck penetration lengthens human drivers' car-following gaps near motorway ramps because humans keep larger distances behind trucks, while dedicated-lane layout has no measurable safety effect.
motivation: Automated-vehicle dedicated lanes (AVDLs) are proposed as transitional infrastructure for mixed traffic, yet their effects near ramps and those of automated trucks on surrounding human drivers are largely unobserved.
method: 63 drivers in a mixed-design driving-simulator experiment were assigned to four AVDL layouts around a 1.5-km ramp weaving section and drove at four automated-truck penetration levels (20%-80%); linear mixed-effects models with participant random effects and multiplicity control were applied.
result: Higher penetration reduced the share of car-following time at gaps below 1.5 s from 28.5% to 18.1% (Holm-adjusted p = .006), explained by leader composition (8% vs 48% of following time behind trucks); AVDL layout had no detectable effect on safety margins, conflicts, travel time, speed, or workload.
conclusion: Mixed-traffic models should represent human car-following as leader-type-dependent and heterogeneous, given that between-driver differences accounted for 52%-77% of variance.

title: A Copper-Inducible Yeast Biosensor With Bioluminescent Readout: Mathematical Modeling, Experimental Validation, And Photodetector Coupling For Molecular Communication In IoBNT
authors: Nikolaos Ntetsikas, Styliana Kyriakoudi, Ariel Klavaris, Antonis Kirmizis, Chrysostomos Chrysostomou, Ian F. Akyildiz, Marios Lestas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.22566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Engineered living biosensors constitute promising model organisms for bringing Molecular Communications (MC) closer to practical applications. However, challenges associated with their development and characterization have resulted in the relevant literature being limited in the MC domain, . In this paper, we contribute in this direction by leveraging engineered yeast as a basis to detect heavy metals such as copper. The biosensor's development is supported by a validated mathematical characterization and analysis for possible integration in an MC system. Different from the existing literature, mathematical representations of the major biological processes within the yeast copper detoxification pathway are integrated into a comprehensive framework that predicts the time evolution of the CUP1 gene, which is treated as the system output. In the engineered circuit, CUP1 was replaced with GFP, therefore making GFP fluorescence the final system output. Experimental analysis including mRNA transcript quantification and fluorometric measurements, validate the GFP reporting model to a satisfactory degree. This establishes the proposed model as a useful tool for virtual experimentation and the developed testbed as a suitable platform for further engineering of yeast-based copper sensors. The theoretical analysis is further extended by incorporating a self-sustained bioluminescent reporter for yeast, replacing GFP and enabling optical output without external light excitation. The optical response is coupled to a photodetector model, rendering the system suitable for integration into mobile monitoring devices such as Smart Pills. The presented characterization of the yeast receiver as a copper biosensor, constitutes the first step towards the development and characterization of a complete end-to-end MC based system for gut theranostics after coupling with suitable engineered probiotic senders.
tldr: This paper develops and validates a copper-inducible engineered yeast biosensor with fluorescent and bioluminescent readouts, models its biological pathway, and couples it to a photodetector for molecular communication in Internet of Bio-Nano Things applications.
motivation: The authors aim to bring molecular communication closer to practical applications by addressing the limited characterization of engineered living biosensors, specifically for heavy-metal detection in gut theranostics and smart-pill monitoring.
method: They engineer yeast with a CUP1-pathway reporter, replace CUP1 with GFP, build a mathematical model of copper detoxification gene expression, validate it with mRNA quantification and fluorometric measurements, and extend the design to a self-sustained bioluminescent reporter coupled to a photodetector model.
result: The GFP reporting model agrees satisfactorily with experimental measurements, and the bioluminescent/photodetector extension provides an optical output suitable for integration into mobile monitoring devices such as smart pills.
conclusion: The work establishes a characterized yeast receiver for copper biosensing as a first step toward end-to-end molecular communication systems for gut theranostics, though it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Cnn Architecture Comparison For Malware Classification With Limited Training Data
authors: Noor Abo Hasan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.21936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional malware classification methods struggle to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats. Image-based malware classification offers a promising alternative by converting malware binaries into grayscale images for analysis with deep learning. While effective, organizations often face practical constraints in acquiring sufficient training data, especially for newer threats. This thesis investigates dual-path CNN architectures with intermediate feature fusion as a potential enhancement for malware classification, with particular focus on how varying training data size affects their comparative performance against traditional single-path approaches. This research implements and compares two models: a baseline single-path using the pre-trained VGG16 architecture and a dual-path model that combines VGG16 with a custom CNN through intermediate feature fusion. Both architectures are evaluated on a binary classification task distinguishing between two malware families (C2Lop.P trojan and Dialplatform.B worm) from the Malimg dataset. Each model is trained across four different training data proportions (20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%), with three training runs per size to ensure statistical robustness, while being evaluated on complementary test sets of varying sizes. Though both architectures achieved perfect classification performance across all training percentages, the study revealed significant differences in secondary metrics including training efficiency, robustness to noise perturbation, and architectural complexity. The findings challenge common assumptions about complex architectures, demonstrating that simpler models can offer superior efficiency and robustness without sacrificing classification performance in image-based malware analysis.
tldr: The thesis compares single-path VGG16 and dual-path CNN architectures for image-based malware classification under varying limited training-data proportions.
motivation: Traditional malware classification struggles with rapidly evolving threats, and image-based deep learning is promising but often constrained by limited training data for new threats.
method: Malware binaries are converted into grayscale images, and a baseline VGG16 model is compared with a dual-path VGG16-plus-custom-CNN model using intermediate feature fusion on two Malimg malware families across 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% training-data proportions.
result: Both architectures achieved perfect classification performance across all training percentages, but differed in training efficiency, noise robustness, and architectural complexity, with the simpler model showing advantages in efficiency and robustness.
conclusion: The findings challenge assumptions that more complex CNN architectures are necessary, suggesting simpler models can be preferable for image-based malware classification with limited training data.
